2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether anarchism means opposition to the state alone, which could include anarcho-capitalism, or also opposition to capitalism and workplace hierarchy, which challenges its place within anarchism. They also disputed where to place the section: some favored grouping it with discussions of capitalism, while others preferred the section on individualist anarchism.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether anarcho-capitalism should be described as a form of anarchism: one argued that many anarchists reject that classification, while another argued that sources support including it among individualist anarchist traditions. They also disputed whether the article’s opening paragraph should flag this disagreement or leave it to the section on anarcho-capitalism and related debates.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to identify anarchism with “libertarianism” near the article’s opening: supporters cited sources describing the terms as frequent synonyms, while opponents said prominent wording could mislead readers because the terms have different uses. They also disputed the article’s treatment of anarcho-capitalism: one editor argued its coverage and opening mention gave too much weight to a controversial, geographically limited current, while another argued it was an important contemporary form that deserved an early place in the section on later schools.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should call Rand a philosopher without qualification: some argued that this could imply academic credentials she did not have, while others said adding “non-academic” gave that distinction too much prominence and risked judging her work. One proposed alternative described her as an author who advanced the philosophy of Objectivism, while another editor argued that philosopher was an accurate, neutral description.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening should call Rand a philosopher: some pointed to sources using that description, while others argued that sources varied and favored saying she developed the philosophical system of Objectivism without applying the disputed label. They also disagreed over how much space to give her philosophical views and criticism of them, with some favoring shorter summaries and others arguing that removing this material would leave important coverage out.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include Rand’s early plans for an unfinished novel and their connection to William Edward Hickman: some considered the details too minor or wanted them shortened, while others argued that a brief, contextual account belonged in the article. They also disputed how to describe Rand’s opposition to collectivism and the welfare state, with one editor arguing that the wording should present these as Rand’s views and another objecting that the cited source did not establish that claim about Rand personally.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should mention Rand’s acceptance of government assistance, with one arguing the issue lacked enough coverage in secondary sources and another saying it mattered because she had criticized such assistance throughout her professional life. They also disputed how much space and quotation the account warranted, with objections to its length and a preference for summarizing the information rather than reproducing extensive quotations.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether Einstein’s 1905 work on relativity was independent or improperly drew on earlier work by Poincaré, with some arguing that Einstein knew of relevant ideas and others pointing to independent or simultaneous discovery as the mainstream account. They also disagreed over whether claims challenging Einstein’s credit belonged in his biography, with one editor describing the priority debate as settled by mainstream historians and arguing that detailed discussion belonged elsewhere.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening history should describe the Hotaki dynasty and Ahmad Shah Durrani: one argued the Hotakis should be included before Durrani, while another said Durrani was the appropriate starting point for the country’s political history. They also disputed estimates of Tajik population share, with one editor citing sources and surveys that put it higher and another favoring estimates around 25–27% and questioning the age or method of the higher figures.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Albania’s 2011 census figures should replace older ethnic estimates in the country’s infobox: one side argued that the new data were reliable, while others said the census was disputed and favored established estimates or no figures there. They also disputed whether to include that 99.26% of people who did not declare an ethnicity had Albanian as their mother tongue; one editor presented it as census information, while another said it did not establish those people’s ethnicity.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over the opening definition: one proposed describing an embryo or fetus as an “unborn human,” while others argued that this wording treated the contested question of personhood as settled and preferred medical terms. Some editors proposed moving ethical arguments to a separate article, while others said the main article needed a brief account of the debate because leaving it out could favor one perspective.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening definition should explicitly say that an abortion results in an embryo’s or fetus’s death: some argued this was needed to distinguish abortion from live birth, while others said it gave undue emphasis to a politically charged point. They also disputed how to describe when pregnancy begins, with proposals differing over whether to present implantation as the standard medical definition and fertilization as an alternative or to give the definitions more equal standing.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening definition should describe abortion as ending a pregnancy before fetal viability or as removing or expelling an embryo or fetus in a way that results in or is caused by its death. Supporters of viability wording cited medical references using that definition, while supporters of death wording argued it distinguishes abortion from live birth; opponents said death was rarely used in standard medical definitions and could carry other meanings.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether tariffs, especially the Morrill Tariff, belonged among the causes of secession: one argued that tariffs were low and rarely cited by secessionists, while another pointed to the bill’s earlier debate and secessionists who raised it. The discussion also questioned how much weight the tariff deserved, with some favoring a brief mention alongside slavery and others arguing that it was too marginal to count as a significant cause.

2005.summary: Editors disputed how the article should describe anarcho-capitalism’s claim to be a form of anarchism. One position argued that the article should state anarcho-capitalists’ own view without repeatedly qualifying it, while another said the claim was controversial and needed context about the established anarchist tradition and competing understandings of authority.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the criticism section should include Austrian responses to criticism, and whether those replies belonged in the main text or in footnotes. Some argued that including replies would give readers useful context and reduce imbalance, while others warned that doing so could give the school’s minority views too much weight.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include Paul Krugman’s criticism that the growth in the money supply after 2008 had not produced the high inflation he said Austrian theory predicted: one editor argued that it misrepresented Mises’s view, while others said it was a notable criticism even if its accuracy was disputed.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should say that Passion plays were used to stir anti-Jewish hostility, or that they sometimes aroused it despite their religious purpose. They also disagreed over whether the opening should explain that “Semitic” can refer to Arabic speakers as well as Jews; opponents said that this linguistic meaning does not change the established use of “antisemitism” for hostility toward Jews.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether research justified describing acupuncture as having effects beyond placebo: one cited a review reporting modest differences between real and sham treatment for chronic pain, while another argued the evidence supported only placebo effects. They also disputed whether the article could state categorically that acupuncture’s effects were due to placebo.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe acupuncture as pseudoscience or report that particular sources use that label. One position was that reliable sources calling it pseudoscience justified including the description; another was that the article should attribute the label to a specific editorial rather than present it as a settled, general conclusion. The disagreement also concerned whether conflicting assessments of acupuncture meant the article should call it “questionable science” instead, or simply report the differing source views.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should cover the symbols commonly called Arabic numerals or the broader numeral system and its history, with some proposing separate pages for those subjects. They also disputed the title: some favored “Arabic numerals” as the common English name, while others argued for “Hindu-Arabic numerals” as the more precise or scholarly term.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should call astrology pseudoscience: some wanted to introduce the subject first and discuss the label later, while others argued it belonged near the beginning. They also disagreed over including criticisms of the Carlson study: proponents said significant objections had been left out, while opponents argued that critiques published in fringe journals did not warrant that weight against a study in Nature.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over what the article’s population figures represented: one position said they counted people whose community’s main language was Arabic, not people who identified as Arab, while another rejected language as a basis for assigning Arab identity. That disagreement was especially visible over Egypt: some editors included Egyptians who identified as Arabs, while others argued that Egyptians were distinct and should not be treated as Arab simply because they spoke Arabic.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to give 8 July as Widdecombe’s date of death, qualify it as approximate, or use 9 July, when she was found deceased; the discussion noted that reports distinguished the suspected attack from when she was found and pronounced dead. Some editors argued that sources supported 8 July, while others said the exact date remained uncertain; one proposed wording that gave 9 July as the date she was found deceased and noted that some sources reported 8 July.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the impeachment section should mention Richard Nixon: one argued that Nixon’s resignation under threat of impeachment provided historical context, while another said the reference was awkward and could suggest an unfavorable comparison with Nixon’s scandal.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether to include Ann Coulter’s claims about Clinton’s sexuality and alleged misconduct in his article, with objections focusing on their placement and whether they merited inclusion. One editor argued that Coulter’s importance in politics made her views worth including if properly contextualized, while others said the claims were more relevant to her own article than to Clinton’s.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to retain the claim that Spears might be too out of breath to sing while dancing: one called it a defensive, opinionated explanation and wanted it removed, while another suggested qualifying it as an argument made by some; the first editor continued to favor deletion.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Spears’s photographed lack of underwear merited mention: some pointed to extensive coverage by major news outlets, while others argued that coverage alone was insufficient without evidence of broader effects, such as disruption to notable websites. They also disputed whether the article should link to the pictures, with one editor saying readers should be able to find them and another arguing that the images added no information beyond the text.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s detailed accounts of Spears’s personal troubles and public conduct were excessive tabloid material or important context for her public image. Some called for this coverage to be sharply reduced, while others argued that events widely reported in the media belonged in the article, with one editor stressing that tabloid-style reports should meet standards of reliability and significance.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Spears’s personal life should have its own section: one proposed separating it from her music career, while another argued that this would overemphasize personal events and preferred covering them chronologically alongside the rest of her biography. The exchange framed the question as how much prominence those events deserved relative to her recording career.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over including an image of Indigenous Brazilians: one argued that their small share of the population could make the image misleading and stereotypical, while another said Indigenous people are part of Brazil and its culture. They also disputed whether the sports section should show the national football team, which supporters described as internationally recognized, or a more general sports image, with an opponent arguing that a football-team picture belonged in an article about football rather than sports overall.

2012.summary: Editors disputed whether the country infobox should list medieval Bulgarian states’ dates alongside the modern state’s establishment, with some arguing the earlier empires belonged in an outline of Bulgaria’s history and others saying the infobox should cover the modern state alone. The disagreement turned on whether shared names, language and other cultural ties showed continuity, or whether gaps in political and legal institutions meant the earlier and modern states were distinct.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether “British Isles” should be presented as a geographical label or as a politically loaded term, with some arguing that its use and the inclusion of the Channel Islands reflected political choices, while others described it as a straightforward geographical term. They also disagreed about how prominently the article should explain objections to the name: some favored alerting readers at the outset, while others argued that the discussion took up too much space and should be shortened or moved elsewhere.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep “British Isles” as the article title: some argued it was the most common name for the full group of islands, while others said the name was objectionable to many Irish people and favored alternatives such as “Britain and Ireland.”

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe the Baháʼí Faith as syncretic: some supported including the label, while others said it was misleading unless the article made clear that the characterization was disputed. They also disagreed over how to present criticism of the faith, with one contributor arguing for a visible criticism section and others favoring factual explanations of beliefs and practices rather than a separate list of praise and criticism.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should call the party “extreme”: supporters said the term reflected how political commentators and scholars described it, while opponents argued it was subjective and should be attributed to sources. A separate proposal to describe the party as white supremacist was also contested; its proponent cited scholarly sources, while opponents argued the label did not fit the party and was not generally applied to it.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether the article’s ideology box should label the British National Party as fascist and white nationalist, or make clearer that the party denied those descriptions; some also proposed replacing white nationalism with ethnic nationalism. The disagreement turned on how to weigh academic sources describing the party as fascist against cited works said to document ideological change, though editors questioned whether those works actually supported that claim.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “Black people” should refer mainly to people of recent African ancestry or also include dark-skinned groups outside Africa who have been described as Black. Some proposed separate articles for these meanings, while others argued that splitting the subject would sidestep the disagreement rather than address it.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “Black” should be defined by recent African ancestry or used more broadly for dark-skinned groups that may not share that ancestry. They also disagreed over whether the article needed a section on biological definitions: one editor considered the existing section balanced, while another said it should be omitted or focus on criticized historical efforts to define race biologically.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether Romania belonged in the usual list of Central European countries: some cited sources that included it, while others pointed to sources classifying it elsewhere or describing it as between Central and Southeastern Europe. A proposed arrangement placed Romania and Croatia among countries sometimes included, separate from the usual list of countries.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s criticism and response sections were too long and argumentative: some called for concise, sourced material or removal, while another argued that criticisms should be answered. They also disputed describing Christianity as an Abrahamic religion, with one editor saying Christians generally do not use that label for themselves and others arguing that Christianity is commonly described that way and traces its faith to Abraham.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether the article’s opening should describe Christianity simply as monotheistic or say that Christians believe in one God, with some arguing that the Trinity makes that label contested. Some editors cited Islamic doctrine describing the Trinity as a three-god belief, while others questioned whether this objection was adequately supported and argued that Christians’ belief in one God fits the standard definition of monotheism.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Christianity article should include a brief section summarizing criticism and linking to a longer article; supporters argued that removing the summary could make criticism less visible and create an unbalanced presentation. Opponents said a general statement that Christianity has been criticized adds little, and preferred placing relevant criticism within the article’s topic sections or providing a link without a separate summary.

2005.summary: Editors questioned the opening paragraph’s description of creationism, with one removing wording that seemed to equate literal belief with physical meaning and to characterize other views as ignorant and materialistic; that editor also questioned including the idea of a demiurge there. Another proposal sought to distinguish intelligent design from creationism as agnostic and open-ended, but a critic challenged several of its claims, including that it was a theory and that it was essentially agnostic.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening definition should describe capitalism: some favored a concise account centered on private ownership and free-market exchange, while others argued that different scholars define the system in different ways. They also disputed whether free markets should be treated as a defining requirement, with some warning that doing so could exclude historical economies described as capitalist.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether capitalism should be defined simply by private ownership and control, or whether the opening definition should contrast it with public or state control; they also disputed whether common, non-state ownership fit that contrast. They also argued over whether wage labor was essential to capitalism: one editor described it as a consequence rather than part of the definition, while another said it was central to the Marxist account and distinguished capitalism from earlier economic systems.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “conspiracy theory” is inherently a dismissive label or can also be used neutrally, including in academic discussion; one view was that it should not be used to characterize claims, while another distinguished neutral description from pejorative use. They also disputed the definition: one position treated any theory alleging a conspiracy as fitting the phrase, while another argued that the label applies only to a narrower kind of argument with particular features.

2017.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should call Columbia “often cited” as one of the world’s most prestigious universities: one argued the cited rankings and publications did not establish that broad characterization and favored listing specific sources, while another said additional sources supported the claim and suggested qualifying it as applying “today.”

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should identify Teachers College as an affiliate; one argued that it should remain labeled that way, citing differences in academic and administrative practices. Another argued that the label was misleading because Teachers College graduates receive Columbia degrees, and said it should be described as affiliated only as Columbia’s Graduate School of Education, not as an academic affiliate.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how the article’s opening should describe Catalonia, including whether to call it a nation, a nationality, or an autonomous community. Some argued that the description should follow Spain’s legal framework, while others said nationhood was not determined solely by constitutions and courts.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should call creation science pseudoscience as an unqualified fact or attribute that characterization to the scientific community. Some argued that standard definitions of science made the label factual, while others said the term was seriously disputed by creation-science adherents and should be presented as a viewpoint.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should describe evidence for chiropractic, including whether to single out reported short-term relief for tension headaches and low back pain while saying there was no scientific agreement about effectiveness. Some argued that the evidence was disputed and that this limitation belonged in the opening paragraph; others objected that the wording gave too much weight to uncertainty and emphasized that supportive research existed.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether research on spinal manipulation generally belonged in Chiropractic’s effectiveness discussion: some argued it was relevant because spinal manipulation is closely tied to chiropractic and researchers use broader evidence to draw conclusions about chiropractic care. Others said this would imply conclusions about chiropractic that the cited studies did not establish, and favored placing the material in the separate spinal-manipulation article.

2007.summary: Editors disputed how to describe the Dominican Republic’s population: one side argued that saying most people had African ancestry obscured European heritage and local mixed-race identities, while another defended that description and cited a demographic study; others pointed to different figures from the CIA Factbook. The disagreement also extended to whether the article should frame identity as self-identification or as a racial issue, with some editors arguing the former better reflected local understandings and others insisting the racial framing mattered.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Sylvester McCoy’s listed years as the Doctor should follow the BBC’s 1987–1996 dates or reflect his screen appearances, with one editor arguing that the longer span misleadingly implied continuous work. They also disputed whether a character counted as a companion in every story featuring them, or only when acting as the Doctor’s companion in that particular story. The discussion cited the BBC’s classification of UNIT characters as companions, while another editor argued for judging each story separately.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe the Doctor’s half-human statement from the television movie as disputed: one wanted to note disagreement about its accuracy, while another said reliable sources did not establish a fan controversy. They also disputed whether the BBC’s note that “purists” disregard the statement supported describing a broader disagreement among fans.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the table of Doctors should include characters and regeneration events, or list only the actors who had served as the programme’s leads; one argument for adding Peter Capaldi was that his casting had been announced, while others said he did not fit the table’s focus. They also disagreed over whether the companion’s infobox should use Jenna or Jenna-Louise, with one position relying on current BBC and other published usage and the other on the most recent on-screen credit until a new episode aired.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Pearl Mackie should appear in the article’s companion listing before her first episode aired: one position pointed to published reports describing her as the companion, while the other argued that the listing should wait until an episode featuring her had been publicly released and credited.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Depeche Mode should be described as a rock band or as synth rock, with one reply arguing that songs or albums containing elements of a genre do not establish that as the band’s overall category. The discussion also questioned whether synth rock had adequate supporting references; one editor cited a Rolling Stone description as evidence for the label.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should focus on Islamic scripture and teaching, with later historical practices separated or left out, or also describe how the system was implemented over time. They also debated whether to avoid judgments based on modern standards and present the historical circumstances instead, or to call the status discriminatory and consider it in relation to present-day equality.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to explain evolution using a distinction between small-scale change within species and larger-scale change involving new species: one editor wanted that distinction in the opening, while others argued the labels were not central to evolutionary biology and did not belong there. They also disputed whether common descent should be described as tracing to one individual or more cautiously to an ancestral gene pool.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should define evolution: some wanted a simpler account of inherited changes, while others argued it should distinguish evolutionary change from the theory explaining it and address changes in gene frequencies. They also differed over how much detail the opening needed, with some favoring a concise, accessible summary and others saying it should explain more of the science before readers reach the rest of the article.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to organize the article into separate sections for observations and inferences, followed by the mechanisms that explain them, or to present evidence alongside the explanations it supports so readers would not encounter ideas without context. They also differed on where to place speciation: one view put it after the basic mechanisms that explain how populations diverge, while another favored introducing it earlier as a concrete result before explaining those mechanisms.

2008.summary: One proposal was to describe the European Union in the opening paragraph as a type of federalism, with its proponent citing scholars who characterized it that way. Other editors opposed adding that description, arguing that federalism was too broad or contested a term to capture the Union accurately and concisely in the opening paragraph.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether nuclear energy should count as energy produced in the EU when most of its uranium was imported: one argued the imports should be counted instead, while another said the statistics count heat generated in EU reactors as production. They also questioned whether the table clearly explained how energy production and dependence were calculated, and discussed adding an explanation of the statistical method.

Editors disagreed over how to describe the Federal Reserve System’s ownership and control: some characterized it as privately controlled or quasi-private, while others distinguished its private regional banks from government components and rejected calling the whole system a private corporation. They also disputed whether historical attacks on central banking generally could be presented as critiques of the Federal Reserve specifically.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether to describe Chopin as Polish, Polish-French, or in another way, with disagreement over how to weigh sources that used different descriptions of his nationality. Some favored identifying him simply as Polish, while others proposed acknowledging his French connection or leaving the nationality discussion to the article body; a compromise proposal described him as a Polish composer who spent much of his mature career in France.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening definition should describe what fascism places above individual interests: one position favored stressing subordination to the collective, while another argued it should cover national, class, gender, and other interests, not only the individual. They also disputed which features belonged in that opening definition, including whether to retain wording about authoritarian repression or instead emphasize national rebirth and cultural decline, and whether claims about culture and religion were sufficiently supported.

2009.summary: Editors disputed how the article should describe fascism’s place on the political spectrum: one proposed saying it is normally considered far right while also noting scholarly accounts of left- and right-wing influences and centrist interpretations. Another argued against presenting a prevailing right-wing view, saying that scholars instead emphasize fascism’s blend of left and right ideas and its poor fit with the spectrum.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should describe claims that Fox News had a conservative bias: one argued it should summarize widely held perceptions without giving less common counterclaims equal prominence, while another urged including sourced accounts from observers who viewed its news coverage as more balanced.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe criticism of Fox News as promoting conservative positions or as aligned with the Republican Party, with one editor arguing that the cited comments supported the latter wording. Another argued that the source also supported the existing account of bias and that the White House remarks were too detailed for the opening paragraph.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Freemasonry article gave enough space to criticism of the fraternity, with one editor arguing that the separate article on opposition to Freemasonry was not adequately summarized. Others said the two articles covered distinct but related subjects and that article length limited how much criticism could be included, while acknowledging that the summary might need work.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe the Union of Concerned Scientists as an activist or politically liberal group when reporting its criticism of Singer; one side argued the description would give readers context, while others questioned its relevance and sourcing in his biography. A broader proposal to remove labels from descriptions of sources also drew opposition, with one editor arguing that brief descriptions help readers understand those sources.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Holocaust should remain in the article and how much space the Nazi period deserved: one argued it must not be erased, while another said the section was already too long relative to other periods and should be summarized. They also disputed adding a brief account of the Herero genocide, with one editor arguing it belonged in Germany’s history and another objecting that it lacked context and was less important than other events of the German Empire period.

Editors differed over adding a trivia section: one proposed collecting interesting facts, while others said entries should be relevant and keep the article serious, and questioned whether being first at something was noteworthy. They also questioned how to describe Washington’s political affiliation, with one editor proposing more explanation of his placement among Federalist candidates and another saying he was not a party member or elected as a Federalist.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should connect climate-change skeptics with skepticism about other issues, especially smoking; supporters cited commentary describing links among organizations, funding and individuals involved in the debates. Opponents argued that listing people who took similar positions did not establish a broader connection, and questioned whether the cited commentary was reliable enough to support one.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s history section should include Great Moravia, a polity that predated Hungary. One editor argued that its influence on the region made it relevant, while another challenged the evidence for its location and extent and said the topic belonged in articles about the region’s pre-Hungarian history.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should cover heavy metal broadly, including later subgenres, or focus on the earlier form of the music; one argued that the article title called for a broad overview, while another distinguished heavy metal from the later styles and defended keeping those styles in separate sections.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Queen should be named in the article’s opening paragraph alongside Judas Priest, with one editor arguing that Queen helped move heavy metal away from blues influence. Another editor replied that the cited biography did not support that claim and that the article should not make it without a source.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to call Hamas a terrorist organization in the opening paragraph: some argued the label belonged there, while others favored describing the group as militant or leaving such labels out as loaded. They also disputed whether Hamas’s covenant called for destroying any secular Palestinian state; some argued it opposed secularism, while others said that did not establish a call to destroy such a state and favored less forceful wording.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over how prominently the opening paragraphs should emphasize scientific objections: some wanted criticism presented immediately, while others argued that the introduction should explain homeopathy first and reserve detailed objections for a later section on controversy. They also disputed whether wording about highly diluted remedies and scientific verification was neutral or unnecessarily confrontational.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to place Homeopathy in the “Quackery” category, with supporters arguing that its scientific standing met the category’s definition. Opponents said the label was controversial and derogatory, and that an unqualified category would present a disputed judgment as fact.

2007.summary: Editors disputed how the article should present research on homeopathy: some pointed to reviews reporting positive results and challenged the interpretation of a 2005 analysis, while others emphasized that positive findings did not establish clear effectiveness. They also disagreed over whether to include individual studies supporting homeopathy or rely on reviews and meta-analyses to summarize the overall evidence, with one argument being that selecting individual results risked giving them undue weight.

2012.summary: One editor proposed adding claims that studies found particles of starting materials in highly diluted remedies, arguing this could explain their effects; others said the studies did not support a broader claim and objected to relying on primary research without reliable secondary sources. Editors also disputed describing homeopathy as generally considered “quackery” in the opening paragraph: some questioned whether the available sourcing established that broad characterization, while others defended it with sources describing how medical or scientific communities view homeopathy.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Italy’s deputy prime ministers should appear in the government infobox: one argued their political influence warranted inclusion, while another objected to highlighting unelected positions and questioned whether the article covered them. Another dispute concerned whether ancient Rome should be included in Italy’s formation history; one editor supported adding it, while a respondent described the modern Italian state as a nineteenth-century creation, despite Rome’s later use by Italian nationalists.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over how much earlier history, including the Roman Empire, belonged in Italy’s opening paragraph: some objected to removing it, while others considered detailed ancient history excessive there. Those favoring a shorter account argued that it should focus on Italy as a unified modern country, while others wanted more context about the peninsula’s past.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether the article’s history should include the Indus Valley Civilization: one argued it was not Indian because its main cities lie in present-day Pakistan and the modern country began in 1947. Others argued that a country overview can trace the history of the region before its current borders, and cited histories of India that include the civilization.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether and how to mention the famines in India’s history section, with objections to the proposed death toll, its account of causes, and the claim that famines ended after independence. Some argued that a brief mention was important, while others said the proposed framing was one-sided or too detailed for a short overview and that explanations belonged in more focused articles; a later draft drew suggestions to include environmental causes and colonial policies without implying a single cause.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over adding earlier famines to the history summary, including estimates of their death toll and whether they belonged in the article’s chronological account; one editor challenged the 70-million figure and the proposed framing of those famines as British-era history. They also disputed calling the 1943 Bengal famine India’s “last” major or catastrophic famine, with objections that the wording was misleading or implied an unsupported connection to British rule.

2024.summary: Editors disputed a historical sentence saying the caste system excluded indigenous peoples: one editor challenged that interpretation and proposed different wording, while another defended the existing account as a summary of a history textbook and asked for comparable sources to support changing it.

2009.summary: Editors disputed whether this article should remain about the state under the title “Republic of Ireland,” with the state’s article moved elsewhere, or instead explain the term itself; one position held that the title helped distinguish the state from the island, while the other argued that the title and article content did not match because “Republic of Ireland” was a description, not the state’s name.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should mention allegations about Iran’s support for terrorism and nuclear weapons, or leave those subjects to separate articles; one editor argued for including them, while another said they belonged in dedicated pages. They also disagreed over how much history the main article should cover: some wanted substantial cuts and more detail moved to history articles, while others argued the section was already short or should be expanded.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether criticism of intelligent design should appear throughout the article or be gathered in a separate section; some said criticism dominated the article and wanted the case for intelligent design presented first. Others argued that placing the scientific community’s objections alongside the claims was necessary to show how the two views are regarded and avoid giving the minority view undue weight.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether the article could say that an overwhelming majority of scientists regarded intelligent design as “pseudoscience” or “junk science,” when cited professional organizations rejected its status as science but did not necessarily use those labels. One editor argued that the terms should be tied to the particular sources that used them, while another restored the broader wording as accurate and supported.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should treat intelligent design broadly as a longstanding argument that life or the universe reflects design, or focus on the modern version promoted by the Discovery Institute; some wanted the opening to identify that narrower scope, while others warned this would obscure the basic proposition. They also disputed whether the opening should present proponents’ description first or foreground the scientific community’s rejection of intelligent design as science.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether violence by pre-state Zionist groups should be labeled terrorism or militancy, with some arguing that attacks on civilians fit the terrorism label and others saying the groups were fighting the British Mandate and that “militancy” covered a broader range of activity. They also disputed how widely the terrorism label had been used: one editor cited an argument that historians apply it selectively, while another said it had been used by mainstream Jewish sources in Palestine from the 1930s for violence by Revisionist groups.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail the country overview should give to Japanese wartime crimes: some favored including the Nanjing Massacre and more information about war-crime trials, while others argued that specific events such as Unit 731 belonged in dedicated articles rather than the overview. They also disagreed over whether and how extensively to discuss discrimination in Japan, with some arguing it merited space in the main article and others accepting only brief mention or favoring coverage in more specific articles.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe Stalin’s actions as genocide or mass murder, with some arguing those terms overstated or prejudged contested interpretations, especially of the Ukrainian famine, and others calling for stronger language about the deaths attributed to his rule. They also disputed whether the opening should give a numerical death toll: some favored a broad estimate, while others argued that differing scholars’ methods made a range misleading and that a general reference to millions of deaths was more appropriate.

2006.summary: Editors disputed how to present deaths under Stalin, particularly whether the article should emphasize estimates of 10–20 million or higher figures; one editor defended the lower range by citing archival researchers, while another argued for a minimum of 15 million. They also disagreed over calling Stalin a dictator in the opening paragraph: supporters said historians used the term, while opponents argued it was a judgment that should not be presented as an objective description.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a lengthy account of John Lennon’s involvement in the James Hanratty case in the article’s discussion of his activism: some argued it gave the case too much space compared with better-known actions, while others said the well-sourced episode merited inclusion.

Editors disagreed over how the opening should describe Jerusalem’s status: some favored calling it Israel’s capital and explaining the non-recognition elsewhere, while others wanted the opening itself to qualify the designation because the international community did not recognize it.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should frame jihad mainly as religious warfare or give equal weight to broader meanings, including personal and nonviolent struggle; some argued that the war-focused meaning was primary, while others rejected reducing the term to holy war. They also disputed whether to include a U.S. prosecutor’s use of “jihad” in a criminal indictment: one view was that it could illustrate contemporary usage if clearly placed in context, while another argued the passage should be removed because it was not a comprehensive definition.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Kurds as an Iranian people, with some treating the label as an important ethnic and linguistic classification and others arguing that it was not a suitable definition of Kurdish identity. They also disputed where the label belonged: some wanted it in the opening paragraph, while others proposed describing Kurds there simply as an ethnic group and explaining the Iranian connection later.

Editors disagreed over whether the opening should call Kosovo a province of Serbia: some argued the term reflected common usage, while others considered it inaccurate or politically loaded given Kosovo’s United Nations administration. They also disputed how to describe Serbia’s role, with one view emphasizing that Serbia had no direct role in governing Kosovo and another arguing its funding and other activities amounted to involvement.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening should describe Kosovo: some favored the neutral terms “region” or “territory,” while others argued that it should be called a country, including with a qualification about recognition. They also disputed whether the article’s map should show Kosovo separately or show its relationship to Serbia, with editors arguing that either presentation could take a side in the status dispute.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should describe Kosovo: some wanted it called a country or state, while others favored “disputed region” or “territory” as less aligned with either side’s position. Supporters of country wording pointed to Kosovo’s government and control of the territory, while opponents argued that calling it a country would endorse one side of the dispute.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should include a section describing Hubbard’s personality from critical sources: some argued that sourced accounts should be included as they became available, while others considered the proposed section one-sided and based on too few critical accounts. They discussed developing the material in a separate draft and including the Church’s positive descriptions alongside critical accounts, while making clear that the views differed.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether the article could support a claim that Led Zeppelin had sold 300 million albums: one challenged the figure and cited an earlier band press release reporting 200 million, while another pointed to a magazine report giving the higher total. They also debated how to divide the band’s history into periods, including whether its “biggest band” years ended in 1975, 1978, or another year, and whether the final section should be called “Latter Days” or refer to the band’s breakup.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe Led Zeppelin as a forerunner of hard rock: one position argued that the style was already established before the band's first album, while another said Zeppelin helped define it despite earlier influences. A separate argument concerned whether to list heavy metal as a genre in the article’s information box, with editors citing published descriptions of the band as metal and others questioning whether that label fit their music.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should describe the LTTE’s accusations against the Sri Lankan government: one proposed saying the international community had not accepted the genocide and state-terrorism charges, while another argued that documented human rights abuses by the government should also be acknowledged. They also disputed how to present the LTTE’s terrorist listings, with one proposed wording noting that 29 countries had listed it and another editor insisting that the United Nations and countries that had not proscribed the group be mentioned too.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Muhammad could be described directly as Islam’s “final prophet” or whether the wording should make clear that this is a belief within Islam; some argued the description was a religious claim, while others treated it as his position in the religion. They also disputed whether “Prophet” should be capitalized, with objections that the capital could imply religious endorsement and arguments that it was a title used consistently with the style guide.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether historical artistic images of Muhammad belonged in his biography: supporters said depictions help readers visualize the subject, while opponents argued that his appearance is unknown and that images could offend Muslims. They also disputed what one illustration showed: one editor placed the depicted event before the conquest of Mecca, while another defended a caption identifying it as Muhammad’s rededication of the Black Stone after the conquest.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how prominently to show historical depictions of Muhammad: one argued that four images crowded near the top overstated a less common artistic tradition and proposed two images placed in different sections. Others argued that the images were historically relevant and that showing both veiled and unveiled depictions, including an early surviving example, gave readers useful context.

2013.summary: Editors disputed how the article should describe Muslims’ belief that Muhammad was the last prophet, including whether to call that belief “almost universal” or instead avoid a qualifier that the sources did not directly establish. They also disagreed over whether the Ahmadiyya, whose members identify as Muslim but hold a different view, warranted mention in the main wording or only in a footnote, and how much emphasis their position should receive.

2015.summary: Editors disputed whether to say Aisha’s marriage to Muhammad was consummated after she reached physical maturity: some argued that detail and historical context belonged in the article, while others considered it irrelevant to a biography of Muhammad. Editors also disagreed over illustrations depicting Muhammad, with some calling for their removal or a way to hide them because they were offensive, and others arguing that historical depictions had educational and artistic value.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should mention alternative names for the language that include “Slavic” or “Slav”: some argued that cited uses justified their inclusion, while others said those names were uncommon and should not receive that prominence. A proposed compromise was to point readers to a fuller discussion of the naming issue without listing the alternative names in the opening paragraph.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether people from the Republic of Macedonia should be described as Macedonian Slavs to distinguish them from Greek Macedonians: one editor considered the label neutral and descriptive, while another argued it misrepresented their mixed background and rejected it as their national identity. The disagreement also concerned how to distinguish the contemporary group from ancient Macedonians without denying the modern use of the name Macedonian.

Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should describe Moldova’s past: one argued it should note a historical connection to Romania, while another rejected that wording and proposed identifying the territory’s earlier history with the Principality of Moldavia instead. They also disputed how to describe poet Mihai Eminescu, with one editor insisting he was Romanian and another arguing he should be described as Moldovan; a suggested compromise was to call him the national poet of both Moldova and Romania.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to combine Moldovans and Romanians into a single Romanian-speaking category in the population figures, or to present the census categories as collected. Some editors also argued that census results on ethnicity and language should be treated cautiously, citing international observers’ reports that some people were advised to declare themselves Moldovan or Moldovan speakers.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether the 1812 transfer of territory to Russia should be described as a cession under the treaty or as an annexation, with one side emphasizing the treaty and the other pointing to Russia’s invasion and formal incorporation of the territory.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over claims about Mariah Carey’s vocal range and the notes she could sing, with one side arguing that audio samples and assessments from musically trained listeners could verify the figures, while another warned that such evaluations were not reliable published sources. The latter position called for removing the claims unless they could be supported by a published, credible source.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s opening definition should describe marriage as a union between individuals or specify a union involving men and women. Supporters of the more specific wording said it captured a core feature of marriage and avoided an overly vague definition, while opponents argued that “individuals” was more inclusive and that specifying both sexes would exclude some marriages.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how much space the article should give to same-sex marriage, with one arguing that its separate subsection gave it too much weight compared with other marriage restrictions. Others defended keeping distinct sections, arguing that same-sex marriage and religious views about it covered different subjects and that brief links to their separate articles should remain.

Editors disagreed over whether Newton Heath had actually gone bankrupt or had only faced a winding-up order, with discussion noting that sources described the club’s financial crisis in different ways. They also disputed the kit history section’s terminology and factual details, and whether online kit-research sites or information from the club museum offered more reliable support for its claims.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should present Rothbard chiefly as an economist or as a political theorist, with some pointing to sources identifying him as an economist and others emphasizing his political legacy; a formal discussion ended without agreement on which description should come first. They also disputed whether sources connected to the Mises Institute adequately supported coverage of his economic contributions: some editors favored independent sources, while others argued that the cited scholars and their published work were suitable evidence.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over how much of a rewritten article to keep: one raised concerns about unsourced information, errors and excessive quotations, while another argued that revisions had addressed promotional wording and proposed removing critics’ quotations instead of discarding the work. The editor who had raised the concerns agreed to that approach but said they could not help further at the time.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over how the infobox should describe Glyndŵr’s claim to the title Prince of Wales: one position favored “in pretence,” while another proposed describing his rule as “de facto” during the years he controlled Wales. One proposal was to remove the title from the infobox altogether; an opposing editor argued it should remain because academic sources call him a pretender and the claim is central to his historical context.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should include a passage about the postwar displacement of ethnic Germans, with opponents calling it outside the campaign’s scope and one editor arguing it cast Germans as victims. Others favored keeping or revising the passage because the displacement contrasted with the invasion’s stated territorial aims, while a critic argued those later events could not be attributed to this campaign alone.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe Poland’s abortion laws as restrictive, with some arguing that this wording reflected reliable sources and others preferring a neutral statement of the legal exceptions. They also disputed whether the overview should mention illegal abortions and estimates of their scale, or leave such detail to the article focused on abortion in Poland.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over which images belonged in the economy section: some favored views representing northern industrial centers, while others objected to the available Maia pictures’ quality and suggested business-park images instead. Editors also disagreed over a culture-section image of musician Chainho, with one proposing a picture of the instrument and another arguing that a person playing guitar would fit the discussion of music.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Portugal’s infobox area should count territorial waters, with some favoring the smaller land-area figure and another editor defending a larger total that includes water. They also disputed how much detail the history section should give to the Lapedo Child and the Knights Templar: one editor argued the material was too detailed or inadequately sourced, while another defended its historical context and inclusion.

2007.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should call Puerto Rico a country: one view reserved that term for sovereign states, while another supported describing it as a non-sovereign country with a separate national identity. They also disagreed over whether Puerto Rico was only partly self-governing or had attained self-governing status in 1952, with the latter view citing its removal from a United Nations list of non-self-governing territories.

2006.summary: Editors disputed how the article should describe the ancient history of the region, including the timing and extent of the Vedic civilization and whether migration from Central Asia or local cultural continuity better explained its development. They also disagreed over how much ancient history belonged in this country overview: one editor sought to shorten the section and move detail to related articles, while another objected to removing material before discussion.

2007.summary: Editors disputed whether claims linking Palestinian ancestry to the Canaanites belonged in the article: one argued they were relevant to ancestry and identity, while others said the claim lacked mainstream scholarly support and warranted only limited coverage. They also disagreed over describing Palestinians as a nation in the opening paragraph, with proponents citing broad recognition and opponents arguing that the term was disputed and should not be presented as fact.

2012.summary: Editors disputed whether Jesus belonged in the article’s infobox: some argued that sources describing him as a Palestinian Jew supported inclusion, while others said that a historical or geographic label did not make him part of the modern Palestinian people. The disagreement turned on whether the article should include historical inhabitants and ancestors of Palestinians, or focus on the modern group, which opponents distinguished from ancient Jews and other residents of the region.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether the article’s opening claim that Palestinians descend from peoples who lived in Palestine over the centuries overstated historical continuity and relied on a single source; one critic distinguished that claim from evidence that Palestinian national identity developed later. Another editor argued that ancestral origins and the later development of nationalism were separate questions, so the article’s wording did not contradict its discussion of Palestinian identity.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Philippines article’s history section should be greatly expanded or kept shorter, with objections that the expanded version was too lengthy and included questionable or biased wording. Some editors argued that a longer section could be justified if details were improved and trimmed, while others preferred placing more historical detail in a separate history article.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to use “the Great” as John Paul II’s formal name or in the opening of the article: supporters pointed to its use in funeral language and public discussion, while opponents argued that it was too early to treat it as established usage. They also disputed how to describe criticism of his position on condoms and HIV, with some arguing that responsibility for AIDS epidemics was widely alleged and deserved specific coverage, and others objecting that the wording was not neutral and needed clearer attribution.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should mention criticism that the PS3 controller’s motion sensing resembled the Wii’s: some argued the comparison and reaction merited a brief note, while others said claims that Sony copied Nintendo were conjecture without supporting sources. They also debated whether to link the controller’s lack of vibration to Sony’s lawsuit with Immersion, with opponents of that explanation calling it speculation rather than an established reason.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to mention that Russia’s free health care could be restricted by the residence-registration system: some argued that this limitation belonged in the article, while others said including it would give the issue too much weight. Supporters described the restrictions as discrimination and said they undermined the guarantee of care for all citizens; opponents argued that the problem affected only a small share of people and concerned registration rules rather than health care generally.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Russia’s map should mark Ukrainian regions it claimed in September 2022, with supporters arguing that the map should display those claims and opponents objecting that the borders were unclear and the areas were not all under Russian control. They also disputed whether the regions should be described as annexed or disputed claims, or as occupied Ukrainian territory, distinguishing Russia’s formal claim from the territory’s status and control on the ground.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the controversy surrounding Limbaugh’s comments about Michael J. Fox belonged in his biography or in the article about his radio show, with one view favoring removal or a brief mention and a link to fuller coverage. Supporters argued that extensive news reporting justified including the incident in the biography, while others said it was more relevant to the show and deserved less space there than other events in Limbaugh’s career.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how specifically to describe the sexual acts in the case: some favored listing the acts and charges, while others argued for less detail, raising concerns about the victim’s privacy and the wording’s effect. They also disagreed over how much space the case deserved in Polanski’s biography, with some calling for shorter coverage or a separate article and others arguing that the case was central to his life and merited fuller treatment.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should spell out Reagan’s economic aims, including lower taxes and reduced regulation, or leave such detail to the article’s main text; one editor argued those positions were essential context, while others objected to the proposed wording or its placement. They also disputed calling Reagan one of the country’s most popular presidents: one editor said the approval figures did not justify the claim, while another pointed to polls showing strong current rankings and argued that his later popularity mattered.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include economic criticisms attributed to Professor Peter Dreier in the article’s discussion of Reagan’s legacy: one objected that Dreier’s views were not significant enough, while others supported including the criticism and argued for presenting it alongside a response from Reagan’s supporters.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Taiwan-related articles should show both simplified and traditional Chinese: one argued simplified characters were unnecessary for Taiwan, while another supported including both scripts. Some editors wanted “Taiwan” included in the article title to reflect its common use and avoid confusion, while others argued the Republic of China title better fit an article covering the entity’s broader history.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Taipei should be labeled the capital, or specifically the de facto capital, of Taiwan and the Republic of China, with some favoring the label and others arguing that it confused readers when sources called Taipei the capital without that qualification. They also disputed how to describe postwar efforts to promote Chinese identity in Taiwan: some editors wanted the account included, while others objected that describing it as “sinicization” presented a contested interpretation as fact and called for more context or attribution.

2010.summary: Editors revised the opening description between calling Taiwan an “island chain” and describing the Republic of China as an internationally unrecognized, disputed state entity; one editor argued that lack of broad international recognition made “state” inappropriate.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the history section should focus on Taiwan, summarizing the Republic of China’s earlier mainland history for context, or cover the Republic of China’s full history as well. They also disputed whether the opening description should call Taiwan a sovereign state, an island country, or simply a state, reflecting disagreement about how to describe its contested status and international recognition.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s infobox map should show only areas administered by Taiwan or also territory it claims, with critics of the second map arguing it would overemphasize claims that are theoretical or disputed. They also disputed how to describe the Republic of China’s claims: some favored saying its claim to mainland territory remained formally in place, while others argued that wording could mislead readers about current government policy and the contested meaning of the constitution.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over how much the opening paragraph should emphasize the People’s Republic of China’s claim to Taiwan and the associated military threat: one argued these topics received too much attention, while another said the claim was inseparable from Taiwan’s diplomatic isolation and merited inclusion in a country summary. They also disputed whether the opening paragraph should retain Taiwan’s postwar economic growth and industrialization as major historical changes, with one editor arguing these were key transformations and another questioning their significance and whether rapid growth was sufficiently specific.

2020.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should call Taiwan a country or state and whether to qualify that description as disputed or partially recognized. Some argued that Taiwan met the criteria for statehood regardless of diplomatic recognition, while others said limited recognition and the sovereignty dispute should be made more prominent.

2012.summary: Editors disputed how to describe Dawkins’s stance on religion: some favored calling him an atheist, while others argued that his own use of “agnostic” should guide the wording, with some proposing a combined label. They also disagreed over whether atheism belonged in the infobox’s religion field, with objections that it was not a religion and that the label was contested.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should devote a section to claims linking Roma people with crime: some questioned whether there was evidence of higher criminality, while others argued that the widespread stereotype itself merited discussion. One proposed approach was to explain the stereotype and challenge its assumptions, rather than present criminality as a characteristic of Roma people.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening sentence should list Romani and Romany alongside Roma: one editor objected that the extra names repeated spellings already covered in a note, while another said readers might not recognize them and that some people use those terms rather than Roma. A further objection was that the wording could imply Rom is the singular form of Romani.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the 1943 11–1 match against Barcelona: one called it surrounded by controversy, while another argued there was no proof of Francoist involvement and that Real Madrid had no more ties to the regime than Barcelona. They also disputed whether the account was adequately supported by references.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over how to identify Rigel’s companion stars: some favored familiar labels such as Rigel B, while others argued for formal double-star catalogue identifiers and questioned whether less-used labels were appropriate. They also disputed how far the informal component names should be used, with one view treating them as useful and readable, and another objecting to their use as consistent labels for the system’s components.

2005.summary: Editors disputed how to frame explanations for group differences in IQ test results: some described the main positions as “environment only” and “partly genetic,” while others argued that “partly genetic” set up a false contrast and proposed “substantially genetic” instead, noting that the competing explanations were not single, uniformly defined theories.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s IQ charts gave a misleading impression that each racial group had a fixed upper score, because the curves did not clearly show how far scores could extend. Some wanted revised graphics or explanatory wording, while others argued that the actual extremes were unknown and the article should emphasize average scores rather than unsupported ranges.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should present differences in average group IQ scores as settled, with only their cause disputed, or make clear that the claimed differences themselves were also contested. One editor framed the disagreement as whether genetic or environmental factors explain the differences, while another rejected the claim that only the cause was in dispute.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail the article should give to arguments for a genetic explanation of group differences in IQ scores: one side sought more coverage of published evidence, while another described the explanation as a minority theory that should receive limited space. They also disputed how to weigh surveys and professional statements when describing how widely the genetic explanation was accepted among researchers.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether a graph of group IQ scores belonged in the opening paragraph: some favored its prominent placement, while others argued it was better suited to the article’s body or could mislead readers about the data and the concepts shown. They also disputed whether reported racial differences in brain size should be presented as established findings; one editor cited research finding no hierarchy or a different one, while another defended the reported pattern.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should mention differences in average test scores between racial or ethnic groups; supporters wanted the differences stated without implying their cause, while critics warned that the wording could suggest race itself causes them. They also disputed whether the opening paragraph should describe genetic explanations as a considerable scientific debate: some editors argued that researchers disagree about the causes, while others said mainstream science does not accept a genetic explanation as a live debate.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s map should shade Western Sahara as territory Spain administers de jure: critics said the map could mislead readers into treating it as part of Spain, while supporters argued it represented Spain’s legal responsibilities and said a note explained the distinction. They also disputed whether and how to mention Spain’s cultural influence in the opening paragraph, with some objecting that labels such as “cultural superpower” were vague praise and others advocating a brief account of cultural reach and related facts.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over how to present stories beyond the films: one argued that material authorized by George Lucas counted as official, while others wanted the article to distinguish the films’ storyline from the wider fictional universe.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether allegations of wartime crimes by Sri Lankan forces belonged in the country article: some argued they should be excluded or kept to the separate war article because they remained allegations, while others argued they were credible and deserved coverage. They also disputed whether the civil war should have its own section or be summarized within the broader history; one position stressed the need for historical context and a concise overview, while another objected that the merged treatment left the war with too little coverage.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening definition should describe biological sex: one proposed version called it a division, usually male or female, while another described it as a trait expressed as male or female that affects reproductive function. The disagreement also involved whether a two-way definition could cover the article’s full range of organisms, including plants and fungi, and whether the wording should instead reflect traits or characteristics found in many different forms.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Nazi Germany should count as socialist: one argued that state direction of production was enough, while others said socialism required worker control and rejected the classification. They also disputed whether the article should explicitly distinguish Nazism from socialism, including whether to explain the Nazi party’s name and the differences between its policies and socialist principles.

2007.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening definition of socialism, which described property and wealth as subject to community control, could fairly capture the movement’s varied traditions; some defended it as a broad shared feature, while others said it misrepresented important views. They also disagreed about whether socialist traditions share a common thread, with one proposal emphasizing collective action to improve society and another arguing that no universal ideas or methods unite all socialists.

Editors disagreed over whether “God Save the Queen” should be identified as Scotland’s anthem: some argued that Scotland’s place within the United Kingdom gave it that status, while others said it was the United Kingdom’s anthem, not Scotland’s. Some supported describing Scotland as having multiple national anthems, while others argued it had no official anthem and that “God Save the Queen” was unofficial in a Scottish context.

2008.summary: Editors disputed how the opening paragraph should describe Scotland’s status: some preferred calling it a country within the United Kingdom, while others argued for “constituent country” as a more specific alternative. They also disagreed over whether “nation” describes the territory or its people, with one position favoring the term for Scotland and another distinguishing Scotland from the Scottish people.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Scotland’s opening paragraph should identify the government elected in 2007 as pro-independence, with some objecting that the wording could mislead readers and others arguing that the brief statement was accurate and did not need extensive qualification. Some sought added context about the government’s minority status and the limits of the Scottish Parliament’s powers, while others considered election details and further explanation inappropriate for the opening paragraph; the wording was revised during the discussion, but the excerpts do not establish a final resolution.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether the economy section’s comparisons with other countries presented South Korea’s rankings selectively and made the article sound promotional; one editor removed many comparisons and favored stating rankings without them. Another editor objected to removing some comparisons, arguing that they could remain when supported by evidence, while the opposing editor said that evidence alone did not make the comparisons suitable for a brief overview.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how much economic and democratic achievement and membership in international organizations belonged in the opening paragraphs: some wanted to reduce that material, while others argued it should remain as part of the article’s overview.
