They also disputed whether the opening should summarize Korea’s earlier history or focus more on present-day South Korea, with one editor arguing history deserved space and another calling it duplicated material with little direct connection to the country today.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over how criticism of the SPLC’s listings should be described: some argued that it came from a wider range of critics and covered more than conservative objections to listings of anti-gay-rights groups, while others said criticism should be included only in proportion to its support in reliable sources and not as a balance to mainstream views.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to restore a previous version of the Sudan article, with one editor favoring it and another objecting to a large batch of changes that included revisions to the opening paragraph, government description, and economic figures. The editor seeking restoration said the older text covered Sudan’s earlier kingdoms and history more concisely, while a reply questioned whether the concern was that precolonial history was too long relative to later periods.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over what the exact SI figure of 299,792,458 metres per second represents: some described it as the speed of light fixed by the metre’s definition, while another argued it is a conversion factor and should not be presented as the physical speed itself. They also disagreed about whether to give the exact figure in the opening paragraph, omit it there, or include it with an explanation of its status.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether war crimes should be presented as central to describing Serbia: one argued they were integral to Serbian nationalism and belonged in the article, while another objected that this would define an entire nation by the actions of a few individuals.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to call Saddam Hussein a dictator in the opening paragraph: one argued it was a judgment that should be avoided there, while another said leaving out the term was a mistake. They also disputed whether the article gave too much attention to his relationship with Western powers and too little to massacres of Iraqis; one editor challenged that emphasis, while another argued both subjects belonged in the account.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list folk-rock and hard rock alongside the Beatles’ broader pop and rock labels: one argued those styles belonged in the article, while others said the range of their music made a short list misleading and difficult to support with sources. They also disputed wording that called the Beatles the most critically acclaimed band ever, with one editor objecting that it stated a subjective ranking too firmly and another suggesting it be qualified as a view held by many critics.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe Jefferson’s slaveholding as a contradiction of his advocacy of liberty, with some arguing the point was important enough to appear prominently and others favoring a shorter, more restrained mention. Opponents of including it in the opening said the article should give greater weight there to his other achievements and discuss slavery later in the article.

2012.summary: Editors disputed how the slavery section should frame Jefferson, with one side urging more context about his treatment of enslaved people and his opposition to slavery, and another arguing the account presented too favorable a picture and omitted harsh conditions at the nailery. They also differed over whether to seek a shared summary or set out contrasting interpretations by scholars.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should name the directors as “the Wachowski Brothers,” the name used in the film credits, or “the Wachowskis,” their current name, with some proposals connecting the two names. Some favored identifying the directors by their current name, while others wanted the historical credit preserved or explained for readers.

2026.summary: Editors proposed and added Dolly Parton to Tennessee’s music section, arguing that her ties to the state and omission alongside other musicians warranted inclusion; another editor agreed.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether terrorism could be given a concise, objective definition—one proposal described it as the systematic use of terror to coerce—or whether the article should explain that definitions vary and no single formulation is universally accepted. Supporters of a concise definition argued it would help readers understand and apply the term, while others said a single formula would oversimplify its complex, subjective use and the article should reflect that complexity.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Timothy Leary should be described as a philosopher in the article’s opening paragraph and information box: supporters cited sources calling him a philosopher, while opponents argued the label was misleading because he was not a professional philosopher and sources used the term more loosely. One suggested compromise was to describe him with a qualifying phrase, rather than present “philosopher” as an unqualified fact.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over which roles belonged in the article’s opening sentence: some argued for adding activism and songwriting, while others favored identifying Shakur chiefly as a rapper. Some also proposed describing him as a poet, but opponents argued that poetry and activism were not covered enough in the article to warrant inclusion there, and supported retaining “rapper and actor.”

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s historical account gave too much weight to an individual-right interpretation tied to resistance against government, at the expense of militia and civic-duty interpretations. One editor wanted to include a scholar’s view that bearing arms was a civic obligation for public defense; another argued the existing discussion of maintaining a militia already covered that point and that repeating it would give it undue weight.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how broadly to describe the Supreme Court’s ruling: one position treated it as a narrow protection for self-defense at home and said it did not settle separate militia-related protections, while another argued that the ruling recognized an individual right not limited to that example. They also differed over how much detail about the rulings belonged in the opening paragraph, with some calling for a brief overview and others arguing that the decisions should be summarized there.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe court interpretations before the 2008 Heller decision: one position was that lower courts had treated the amendment as protecting only a militia-related right, while others argued the cases did not settle whether an individual right existed. They also disagreed about whether that earlier legal history belonged in the article’s opening summary, and whether Miller’s ruling was clear or ambiguous on the individual-versus-collective question.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening description should call the United Kingdom a country or a unitary state. Supporters of “country” argued that it was a familiar term for readers, while supporters of “unitary state” argued that it was more precise and avoided confusion with the constituent countries.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the introduction should describe England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland as countries: some argued this was notable information for readers, while others favored listing the four parts without that label because its meaning could confuse readers.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should mention income and regional inequality alongside the UK’s high rankings on other international measures. One editor argued the addition was unnecessary and made the presentation one-sided, while another said it balanced the positive economic comparisons and was supported by sources.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Ukraine article’s map should shade Crimea differently to show its contested status, with supporters arguing this would represent the dispute neutrally. Opponents said the change was premature without an accepted published map and risked making a fast-moving political dispute too prominent in an article about the country.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to label “Oxford” as an informal name in the article: one view was that the label added useful clarification, while another considered it unnecessary because English universities are commonly referred to by shortened names.

2014.summary: Editors disputed which definition should decide what belongs on the list: some argued that a broad international definition could include systems beyond heavy rail, while others said metro should be distinguished from light and commuter rail. They also disagreed over whether Seoul’s services, run by several operators, should count as one metro system or be listed as separate systems.

2021.summary: Editors disputed whether the party’s position should be described as supporting restrictions on immigration generally or only on illegal immigration: one side pointed to policies affecting legal immigration, while the other argued that the broader wording overstated the party’s position. They also disagreed over whether research describing authoritarian or anti-democratic tendencies in the party warranted a paragraph in the article; supporters cited scholarly evidence, while opponents questioned whether the proposed text gave the claims enough weight or support.

2022.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should describe Republican voting measures as “restrictions on voting rights” or use less charged wording such as “stricter voting laws” or “greater regulation of voting processes.” Some argued the measures should be characterized as voter suppression, while others said that wording assigns a disputed motive and that the article should distinguish stated election-integrity goals from effects critics attribute to the measures.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should mention Republican support for the Great Replacement conspiracy theory, with some arguing that extensive reporting and polling justified including it and others questioning whether the evidence supported that description. Opponents also argued that the material was too recent and prominent for a general account of the party, while supporters disputed that it deserved so little weight and challenged the view that the poll findings did not demonstrate belief in the theory.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe racial appeals as a primary driver of the Republican shift in the South during the 1960s: one argued that this is the majority scholarly view, while another said historians dispute the causes of the realignment. They also disagreed over how much emphasis that interpretation merited in the party’s history, with one editor favoring its inclusion and another urging more cautious wording and less prominence.

2026.summary: Editors disputed whether the party should be described as far-right, with supporters pointing to sources that had applied the label for years and opponents warning that it could overstate the reach of recent political changes. Some argued for a broader “right-wing to far-right” description because the party includes significant factions that are not far-right, while others said the wider label better reflects how the party has changed under Trump.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the party should be described as centre-right, right-wing, or with wording spanning both positions, with debate over whether current academic sources supported the newer right-wing characterization. They also disputed how to represent the party’s position over time, with one proposal calling for a section on changing interpretations and another emphasizing the party’s current position.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over how specifically to classify Urdu: one position placed it within a more detailed language-family hierarchy, while another said it should not be listed as a subcategory of Hindi or Hindustani. Others argued that Urdu and standard Hindi are registers of Hindustani, and that a more detailed classification should reflect their relationship.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should describe Putin’s actions toward the oligarchs and their public standing: one objected to presenting contested assessments as fact, while another defended the claim that oligarchs were widely disliked as important context for his actions. They also disagreed over how much economic change belonged in Putin’s biography and how to attribute it, with some arguing the section should focus on policies attributable to him and others defending broader economic results as relevant to his administration.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s opening paragraph should mention the 2011–12 protests: one side called for including them, while others argued that their scale and significance were being overstated and that the coverage needed context. They also disputed whether critical labels such as “mafia state” belonged in the opening paragraph, with some editors calling the descriptions important perspectives and others regarding them as marginal or inappropriate there.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Panama Papers coverage belonged in Putin’s biography: some said news reports directly connected him to the story, while others stressed that the leaked records named associates, not Putin, and warned that including their dealings could imply guilt by association. One proposed approach was to mention that associates were named and report Putin’s connection as a question raised by media coverage, rather than present the money as his.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how much space the main article should give to claims that someone other than Shakespeare wrote the works attributed to him: some argued the claims had enough academic support to merit fuller coverage, while others preferred a brief summary and a link to a separate article. The shorter-version advocates said extensive treatment would give the claims too much weight in the main article, while supporters of fuller coverage disputed that assessment.

2006.summary: Editors disputed how the opening paragraph should explain the war’s causes: some wanted to emphasize German aggression and Nazi aims, while others argued for a broader account including factors such as nationalism and the effects of the Treaty of Versailles. They also disagreed over whether the paragraph’s wording was biased; one critic objected to its descriptions of aggression and invasion, while another defended those terms as accurate and said a brief overview could not include every historical nuance.

2005.summary: Editors disputed how the article described slotting fees, payments retailers may require from suppliers, and whether to say that the practice was widespread while Walmart did not charge them. One editor objected that the wording cast competing grocers as unethical and revised it; another argued the fees were standard in the industry and supported the description with a report about their widespread use.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening should describe witchcraft broadly, reflecting several meanings, or foreground its commonly understood association with harmful magic. They also disputed whether to present harmful magic as an alleged use of supernatural powers and whether to add a separate statement noting that this harm-focused meaning is common but has exceptions.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should focus on Yahweh as an ancient national deity, or also cover his religious significance in Judaism, Christianity and Islam and the biblical account of him. They also disputed how the article presented scholarly reconstructions of Israelite religion: one editor argued that the account favored the view that Yahweh began as a polytheistic god and left other perspectives out, while others defended its focus on mainstream historical scholarship and asked for sources supporting alternatives.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the war’s outcome: some cited sources characterized it as an Egyptian political or strategic victory and a military stalemate, while others argued for an Israeli victory. They also disputed Israeli casualty figures, with one editor favoring a detailed count from an Israeli source and another arguing that estimates from secondary sources should be included as well.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether Zionism should be defined broadly as support for Israel or Jewish immigration, or also as support for settlements. They also debated whether Palestinian refugee figures should count only those displaced in 1947–48 or include later generations.

2024.summary: Editors debated whether the opening paragraph should describe Zionism’s early settlement project as colonization. Some argued that the term accurately reflected the movement’s historical language; others objected that it could imply imperial control and exploitation.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether natural disasters deserved a dedicated section in the decade article, with one editor warning that this could give them disproportionate weight and turn the article into a list of events. Another argued that the Indian Ocean tsunami’s scale and effects warranted inclusion, and called for a fuller account of the decade rather than the article’s brief treatment.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Barack Obama’s nomination for president belonged in the international year summary: some argued it was historically significant as the first nomination of an African American by a major U.S. party, while others said it was not an international first and belonged in a U.S.-focused article. They also disputed whether the Northern Illinois University shooting merited inclusion, with one editor citing claimed effects and international coverage and others arguing that its impact was primarily domestic and insufficient for the international summary.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Christchurch earthquake belonged in the year’s global events list: supporters pointed to international aid, deaths across multiple countries and overseas discussion, while opponents argued that international news coverage and routine travel warnings did not show the wider significance the list required.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over how to present the number of Pashtuns in India: one side favored an estimate of 3.2 million from a Pashtun organization, while another questioned its reliability and preferred official census figures for Pashto speakers, which do not count ethnicity directly. They also disputed whether Hindu and Sikh people described as Pashtun should be included as Pashtuns, with some citing self-identification and cultural ties and others arguing that those sources did not establish ethnic identity.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether a statement by Heidegger supporting Hitler should appear in the biographical section or only in the separate section on his Nazi involvement; some favored keeping detailed material in that dedicated section, while others wanted a blunt indication earlier in the biography. They also disagreed about how closely the article should connect his political commitment to his philosophical work, with one editor describing this as an unresolved scholarly debate and another arguing that the biography should still keep the details in a separate section.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should say “Radiohead is” or “Radiohead are”: some argued for singular grammar, while others said the plural form was normal in British English. They also disputed whether the band should be described as art rock as well as alternative rock, with one editor seeking both labels and another saying art rock lacked support in the article and its infobox. The discussion also raised whether sources supported the alternative-rock label.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening should call Castro a dictator: some argued that the word accurately described his rule, while others considered it a politically loaded judgment rather than a neutral description. Alternatives included describing him as having governed Cuba or making clear that people disagree over the label.

Editors disagreed over whether the article should say Ratzinger was forced to join the Hitler Youth: some argued membership was required by law, while others said it should state that he joined without presenting compulsion as fact.

2009.summary: Editors disputed how to describe Mercury’s ethnic background, with one arguing that he was ethnically Parsi-Persian and objecting to an Azerbaijani Zoroastrian description, while another said that identifying him as Indian Parsi would repeat information already conveyed by his Parsi descent and upbringing in India. They also debated replacing the article’s photograph: supporters favored a different image, but opponents objected that the proposed picture’s copyright status was not adequately established.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how to summarize research on Transcendental Meditation: some favored saying that studies suggest possible effects but firm conclusions remain uncertain, while others wanted the opening to emphasize a review finding no advantage over health education on several measures. They also disputed the article’s scope, with some preferring it to focus on the meditation technique and keep organizational material in a separate article, while others argued that the term covers both the technique and its associated movement.

Editors disagreed over whether the short entry about the Gaza flotilla raid should say it took place outside Israeli territorial waters and that the violent confrontation occurred on the largest ship; one editor argued leaving out those details could mislead readers about how the raid unfolded. Others opposed adding that context, saying it could suggest a biased interpretation and that the brief entry’s account of the deaths and injuries was enough.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether to include Vietnamese guards’ denials that McCain was tortured: one position was that the denials addressed all American prisoners and belonged in broader coverage of prisoners of war, while another was that statements about McCain specifically should appear alongside his account. Editors also disagreed over whether McCain’s 1985 meeting with Chilean leader Augusto Pinochet belonged in his biography: some said it lacked enough context to warrant space in the main article, while another argued that extensive South American news coverage made it notable.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Nazi restrictions on Jewish gun ownership should count as gun control: some favored a broad definition covering such restrictions, while others argued that targeting Jews as part of wider discrimination was not the same as general firearm regulation. They also disputed where to discuss the episode, with some favoring a factual historical account separate from opinions about its meaning and others arguing that placing it in the history section presented a contested political interpretation as history.

Editors disagreed over whether the year entry should focus on the surveillance disclosures and their international effects or on Snowden’s flight and asylum in Russia. They also contested wording such as “defect” and “fugitive,” with objections that these labels could imply a political judgment rather than neutrally describe the events.

2012.summary: Editors disputed whether the Sandy Hook shooting belonged in the year’s world-events article, with opponents describing it as a domestic event and supporters pointing to its death toll and historical significance. Some argued that a large-scale shooting could merit inclusion despite being domestic, while others said it should be covered only in the United States article unless it had effects beyond the country.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Peshawar school attack belonged in the international events list: one view was that the attack’s ties to a wider militant group and its high death toll supported inclusion, while another held that international media attention and deaths alone did not make a domestic event internationally significant.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include the U.S. same-sex marriage ruling in the 2015 article: some pointed to worldwide media attention and reactions, while others argued that coverage alone did not show international significance without demonstrable effects abroad. The debate also exposed different views of the inclusion standard: whether an event must have consequences in other countries or can qualify because it is recognized internationally as important.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Donald Trump’s election belonged in the international year-in-review article, with supporters arguing that its worldwide coverage and significance warranted inclusion. Opponents said it was a national election and that media attention alone was not enough without tangible international effects.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Las Vegas shooting belonged in the year’s general events list or should be covered only in the United States year article. Supporters pointed to international news coverage and the high death toll, while opponents argued that it was a domestic event without meaningful effects beyond the United States.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a photograph of playwright Neil Simon: one argued for it based on the international reach of his work, while others cited limited space and the number of American entertainers already pictured. A separate exchange over the March for Our Lives included support for listing it, with one editor pointing to its large attendance and international significance.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s deaths section should be removed or narrowed because they considered its growing number of entries unmanageable, and some argued that only deaths or lives widely covered internationally should be included. In the debate over Cameron Boyce, some editors argued that international attention and charitable work supported his inclusion, while others questioned whether coverage before his death showed enough wider significance; editors also debated whether he merited a photograph.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether musician Tim Smith belonged in the year’s deaths list, with one side questioning his international recognition and another pointing to extensive obituary coverage and his band’s following. The discussion reflected a broader disagreement over whether regional or niche prominence was enough for inclusion, or whether the list should favor people known internationally.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Robb Elementary School shooting belonged in the year’s main events list: supporters pointed to the high death toll, the rarity of a shooting at an elementary school, and international attention. Opponents argued that it was a domestic event and that widespread media coverage did not by itself make it internationally important enough for inclusion.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include several developments in ongoing conflicts, with some saying they were incremental events better suited to conflict timelines and others arguing that the size or significance of particular events justified their inclusion. They also disputed whether the European Union’s AI law belonged on the general 2024 page or instead on the science page, with arguments over the usual scope of the year article and the law’s importance.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list the presidential inauguration: some argued that the change of government taking effect made it consequential, while others considered the ceremony a formality after the election. They also disputed whether the Iberian blackout merited a place in the year’s image collage, with one editor pointing to its effects across several countries and another arguing that longer conflicts and events with deaths or major political effects were more deserving.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Spirit Airlines’ shutdown belonged in the year’s global events list: some argued it was mainly a U.S. business story with limited prominence, while another cited its impact across the United States, Mexico and the Caribbean and international reporting. They also differed on whether the hantavirus outbreak warranted immediate inclusion, with one editor pointing to extensive sourcing and others favoring waiting to see whether infections spread beyond the cruise ship.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether Watch Tower publications rule out survival at Armageddon for people who are not Jehovah’s Witnesses or leave their fate uncertain: one side read statements that Witnesses alone have a scriptural basis for survival as excluding others, while another argued that the publications say the outcome for non-Witnesses is unknown.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe Jehovah’s Witnesses outright as Christian: some favored using a secular definition that includes them, while others argued that this wording went beyond what sources supported. Those favoring a direct label pointed to definitions based on belief in Jesus as the Christ; those opposing it said many sources avoided categorizing the group and favored saying that Witnesses profess Christianity instead.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Jehovah’s Witnesses as a Christian denomination, with some favoring that label alongside qualifiers such as “nontrinitarian,” while others argued that it wrongly grouped the Witnesses with Christian churches they regard as separate. They also debated whether to call the group a “religious organization” or “religion” instead of a denomination, disputing whether the opening description should emphasize classification within Christianity or religious independence.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should mention the practice of “reproving” alongside disfellowshipping: one side argued its omission gave disproportionate prominence to the latter, while others said reproving lacked enough attention in secondary sources to merit inclusion there. They also disputed how to describe elders’ responses to members who report little or no preaching activity, with some defending wording about encouragement and others objecting that it presented the response in an uncritically positive way.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s genre listing should mark “punk rock” as disputed: one argued the label was contested and should be flagged, while another said the range of genre labels and discussion elsewhere made a warning unnecessary. They also differed over the music itself, with one arguing that Green Day’s style did not fit the punk-rock description and another pointing to the band’s early punk background while acknowledging that the label fits less comfortably in later years.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening description should say “U2 are” or “U2 is”: one position defended “are” as British English usage, while another argued that “is” is acceptable in British English too and that “are” is doubtful. Editors also debated how to label the band’s music and its albums and songs, with one proposal favoring rock as the default and allowing additional genres, while another argued that “alternative rock” can make a separate rock label redundant and that pop is often overused.

2011.summary: Editors disputed how the opening paragraph should describe Gaddafi’s death: one objected that a proposed account of sexual assault and execution was unsupported and too charged, while another argued that reports supported describing abuse and a deliberate killing. They also disagreed over whether to include such details in the biography’s opening paragraph or leave them to the separate article about his death, citing concerns about neutral wording and emphasis.

2014.summary: Editors disputed how much detail the article should give about Williams’s death, including whether to describe reported wrist injuries and a nearby knife alongside the account of his death by hanging. Some argued that details reported by authorities belonged in the article, while others considered them excessive or potentially suggestive of an unconfirmed explanation and favored limiting the account to basic facts.

2006.summary: Editors disputed how the opening paragraph should describe Falun Gong’s teachings: one proposal emphasized salvation, cosmic judgment and beings being removed, while another framed “Fa-rectification” as renewal and stressed the teachings’ promise of salvation. Practitioners objected that the first framing misrepresented the teaching and its context, while critics argued that omitting judgment and the removal of beings left out important claims by Li Hongzhi.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether describing Falun Gong as a “cult” was a fringe position in scholarship: some argued that scholars mostly rejected or avoided the label, while others said the limited research and differing views did not establish a scholarly consensus. They also disputed how to present the label’s prominence in Chinese government rhetoric alongside academic objections to it, including whether the article clearly distinguished those uses and gave them appropriate weight.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether to retain the “Evergreen City” label: some said online references repeated material from Wikipedia and wanted a credible source, while others argued that Asianet and other published references were sufficient. After newer tourism figures appeared, one editor argued that the article should no longer describe the city as the most visited place, while others favored keeping the information as history or said the existing wording did not claim it still ranked first.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether a photograph of shanty dwellings belonged in the Kochi article, disagreeing over whether it represented a significant feature of the city or was too limited to warrant inclusion. One view was that the image could misrepresent the city by focusing on a few dwellings, while another argued it showed a real aspect of the city and helped give readers a more balanced picture.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether right-wing politics should generally be defined by acceptance of social hierarchy, or whether that framing overlooks a modern classical-liberal emphasis on individual freedom and markets. They also disputed whether to present these as competing meanings in the opening paragraph, with some objecting that the proposed wording went beyond what its cited sources supported.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s information box should include the Turkish Municipality of Nicosia: one argued it was not an official entity of the Republic of Cyprus, while another said it performed municipal duties in the northern part of the city and should be represented. They also disputed how to describe the city’s divided status in the opening paragraph, with proposals ranging from omitting the northern entity to acknowledging its role while noting that its claim to statehood was disputed.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include preliminary statements that there were no signs of suicide, trauma, or foul play before the cause of death was known. Some argued the update could help limit speculation, while others said the article should wait for reliable reporting on what caused his death rather than publish interim details.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s image collage was useful and how to choose figures for it: one editor criticized such galleries as subjective and questioned how to identify a representative Russian, while others objected to Pushkin’s inclusion or challenged the current selection for omitting Tchaikovsky and Dostoevsky.

Editors disputed the article’s estimate of the worldwide Serbian population, with one objecting that figures for several countries did not reflect official census results and questioning how the total of 10–12 million was calculated. Others defended that range using diaspora estimates and argued that language-speaker counts or citizenship records did not measure ethnic Serbs; the discussion also challenged whether the sources used to support the estimates were reliable.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should call PETA radical: one argued its opposition to eating, wearing, riding, and testing animals amounted to thorough reform, while others said the label was subjective and should be used only when attributed to a source.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Gacy’s political affiliation and activity merited inclusion in the article’s information box: some argued that his political involvement made it relevant, while others considered it unrelated to his crimes or insufficiently significant for that summary. They also disputed which of his clown-related names belonged in the information box, with one editor favoring several verifiable aliases and another preferring names connected to his crimes.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening image should be an abstract world map or a military image such as an aircraft carrier. Supporters of the map argued that a military image could imply that military strength alone determines superpower status, while a carrier’s supporters saw it as illustrating the central role of military power and the ability to project it abroad.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether China should be described as a current superpower or whether the article should present that status as contested, with some pointing to recent sources that use the label and others arguing that sources disagree and the article should not state it as fact. They also disagreed over how to frame the opening summary: one proposal distinguished the United States as an established superpower from China as a possible rival, while another favored a more even-handed list of contenders and moving the detailed arguments into the article.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe a tournament used to name the first WWE champion: one proposed calling it fictional, while another argued that it should not be described that way unless WWE acknowledged it had never happened. The discussion favored wording that conveyed uncertainty rather than presenting the tournament as invented.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should add a section describing WWE’s move toward family-friendly programming, with one editor arguing that the change and its effects merited fuller coverage and others objecting that the proposed claims were not adequately supported by reliable sources. They also disagreed over whether to call the change a new “era”: the inclusion advocate said the material could describe a programming change without that label, while critics said the sources did not establish a distinct era or a significant recent shift.

2011.summary: Editors debated whether to retitle the article after the company’s rebranding and whether the title should be “WWE” or “WWE, Inc.”; one editor argued that WWE was the common name, while another raised the difference between the company name and its legal name. They also disagreed over whether the stock exchange listing established a name change: one editor noted that it still displayed the former full name, while another pointed to corporate documents using “WWE, Inc.”

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Money in the Bank section should list Randy Orton and Damien Sandow as holders of separate briefcases, or instead identify Jack Swagger as the holder of a continuing single version; one editor suggested keeping both entries until the next event. Editors also disagreed about whether a picture of WWE’s headquarters belonged in the infobox: one editor asked for its removal, while others restored it and argued there was no good reason to remove it.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Hindustani should describe a living shared language of northern India and Pakistan, with Hindi and Urdu as its standardized forms, or whether that framing confused the common spoken language with its distinct written and literary traditions. One side argued that the term remains useful for the shared language, while another said it is now seldom used and should refer chiefly to a historical British-era name, not a current language.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should describe NLP’s sensory-processing models as involving “engrams”: some argued the concept was implicit and central to NLP, while others said it was a minority interpretation that should not be presented as the field’s general view.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening description should call neuro-linguistic programming controversial: one argued that criticism belonged later in the article, while another said the available sources justified the label. They also disputed how to name and frame criticism of the approach, including whether a section describing criticism as scientific or pseudoscientific accurately reflected its sources; some editors defended that framing, while others challenged it as unsupported or misleading.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Messi’s squad number should be listed as 10, with one challenging the change as unsupported and another citing Barcelona’s website while noting that friendly matches could show different numbers.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether describing changes to the club’s shield introduced political slogans or stated a verifiable historical fact, including that an earlier design replaced the Catalan flag’s four bars with two bars of the Spanish flag.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether Barcelona should be credited with a third Copa Eva Duarte trophy for 1952–53: one editor argued that the Spanish football federation’s account supported the win, while another pointed to the club’s own list, which counted two. They also disagreed over which sources should settle the count, with one favoring the federation’s records and the other treating the club’s published honours list as evidence against including the disputed trophy.

2022.summary: Editors discussed when to list reserve-team players in the first-team squad: one suggested adding them, while another said they should be included once the season began and they appeared in matchday squads; the suggestion’s author agreed to that approach.

2011.summary: Editors disputed how the list should group states, including whether membership in United Nations bodies should determine their placement and whether observers and agency members belonged in the same category. Some argued that placing Kosovo with the Vatican overstated Kosovo’s disputed recognition, while another editor said Kosovo belonged among partially recognized states and was correctly placed there under the proposed categories.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the transfer of Rangers’ assets to a new company meant the football club continued under new ownership or a new club had been formed, and whether the article should treat the club and the companies that owned it as separate entities. They also disputed whether the article could describe former vice-chairman Donald Findlay’s singing as sectarian: one editor questioned whether the evidence supported that description, while another cited an account describing the songs as sectarian.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening description should call Messianic Judaism a Christian movement or leave it as a religious movement; some pointed to outside sources classifying it as Christian, while adherents identified as Jewish. Other editors argued for presenting the competing views without settling the label, noting that some sources left the classification open.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s World Bank high-income list should separate five economies eligible for lending from those that were not. Some argued that borrowing eligibility identified higher-income developing countries and was relevant to whether they counted as developed; others said it was a separate category that should not alter the high-income list.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep the CIA’s list of developed countries in the article; supporters argued that it should remain as a list explicitly using that label, despite its age. Critics called the list outdated and questioned whether the CIA’s choices, including which countries it listed, offered an appropriate basis for describing developed countries, favoring international organizations instead.

2022.summary: Editors disputed whether Steve Jobs should be described as a Pixar founder, with one editor arguing that he was an investor rather than a founder and crediting Ed Catmull and Alvy Ray Smith with creating the company.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Coldplay’s reported 160 million sales as album sales, following a Telegraph article’s wording, or as total sales of albums and singles, which other coverage was said to indicate. Some argued that Wikipedia should preserve the source’s exact wording, while others said conflicting coverage meant the figure should not be presented as album sales alone and questioned whether a different source was needed.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s detailed responses to moon-landing allegations belonged alongside the allegations, or made the page read like an argument against them rather than an account of the claims. Some favored shortening the rebuttals and focusing on the theories as a cultural phenomenon, while others argued that removing the responses would leave readers with the impression that the allegations had no answers.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Billboard Millennium Award merited mention in the article’s opening paragraph: one argued that the award was too new and minor, while others described it as significant to Beyoncé’s music career. They also debated whether to include coverage of rumors about her pregnancy, with one editor calling the material unnecessary and another arguing that the media attention and Beyoncé’s discussion of the rumors in her documentary made them worth including.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep a comparison describing the 777-200LR’s wingspan relative to its length and other Boeing aircraft; some repeatedly restored it, while others called it meaningless trivia and supported removing it.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list the Eagles as active in 2017: some argued that two festival appearances were not enough, while others questioned whether activity should depend on touring or releasing an album. They also disputed whether the band’s reported plans and preparation for future projects were enough to count as being together again, or whether activity required clearer evidence of a reunion.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how much debate about support and opposition belonged in this international overview: some wanted brief summaries pointing to focused articles, while others argued that the page should retain key arguments and counterarguments. They also disputed whether historical same-sex relationships should be called marriages or more cautiously described as unions, because editors differed on how the term fits relationships in earlier societies.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should describe same-sex marriage recognition as largely limited to Western countries, with one editor arguing that the article’s global framing overstated its spread and others objecting to that proposed qualification. The disagreement also involved what “Western” meant, since editors disputed whether countries such as South Africa belonged in that category.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should remain at “Charles III” or use a more specific title and leave that name to distinguish among several historical figures with the same regnal name. Supporters of the shorter title pointed to reader searches and the attention Charles already received before becoming king, while critics argued that recent attention should not determine the title and stressed other figures’ historical significance.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the “Meth Capital” material belonged in the Akron article: one argued that much of it was copied from a source and that only a brief mention connected to Akron was appropriate, while another rejected the plagiarism objection, arguing that restating factual information was not plagiarism.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether to describe the 1915 removals as “relocation” or “deportation” or “forced evacuation”: one contributor argued that Armenians were moved within Ottoman territory, while another said “relocation” wrongly suggested they were successfully resettled. They also disagreed over whether calling the events genocide required a court ruling, with one contributor arguing that a trial must establish guilt and another citing scholarship and Ottoman military tribunal findings in support of the term.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should present the events as genocide without qualification: one argued that the term required a ruling by an international court, while another said historians’ views should guide the article. They also disagreed over whether scholars who rejected the genocide label should be grouped under “opposition” or described as denying it; one editor objected to the latter label, while another argued that the majority view should shape the description.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe morphic resonance as a theory or hypothesis, with some arguing that those terms could suggest scientific standing because the proposal was not well-substantiated or repeatedly confirmed. Others said Sheldrake had named it a hypothesis and cited academic publications using those terms, arguing that the article should reflect that usage.

2007.summary: Editors updated the route figures to distinguish Emirates’ destinations from a larger count that included Emirates SkyCargo, and clarified that two London airports counted as separate destinations but one city; another editor agreed with the update.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article included too much celebratory detail, with one complaint calling accomplishments and praise excessive and others objecting to cuts to information they considered important. They also differed over whether Aguilera's personal life belonged in a separate section: one editor said mixing it into the career narrative made the article hard to follow, while another argued that biographical relationships do not always warrant their own section.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over including videos about Sai Baba’s miracles: some said they helped readers understand what was being described, while others argued the clips presented a one-sided view and that the text already covered the claims. They also disputed whether to include a reported outcome in a sexual-abuse case: one editor argued readers should be told the case was dismissed, while another questioned the reliability of the source and whether the court record supported that account.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the birth-year ranges used to define Millennials in the article’s opening paragraph. One proposal gave the usual starting years as the early 1980s and ending years as the mid-1990s through early 2000s, while another argued that most sources favored 1980 or 1981 through 1996 and treated later end dates as a minority view.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe research on Ashkenazi origins, with one position calling for the article to report studies pointing to both European and Levantine origins without choosing between them. Some argued that a study focused on maternal DNA should be described specifically as such, while others defended broader wording based on the study’s reported interpretation and debated whether discussion belonged in the opening paragraph or only in the genetics section.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include the view that the medieval Bulgars spoke an Iranian language alongside the better-established Turkic-language account, with one editor arguing it merited mention and another saying it should receive much less space. They also disputed whether to add a higher estimate of Bulgaria’s ethnic Bulgarian population by estimating the ethnicity of people who did not answer the census question; one editor proposed such an estimate, while another rejected the calculation as unsupported interpretation.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether to include material connecting homosexuality with child sexual abuse, including claims about studies and the membership of a pedophile organization in a gay rights group. Supporters said the studies and association were relevant to a section about possible causes, while opponents argued that the sources were unreliable and that the association did not establish a link to priests who abused children.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether sections should use objective, date-based titles or titles that describe the band’s development and progress; one editor objected that the proposed titles made subjective claims, while the other argued they better conveyed the band’s development. They also disputed proposed additions based on a fan-club site: editors raised reliability and copyright concerns, while the contributor defended the source as official and said the material was referenced.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to add Liam Gallagher’s remark after an Oasis performance in Dublin to the article’s history: one editor proposed including it, while another argued it was too offhand to merit mention without coverage by secondary sources.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether Islamophobia should be linked to racism, with some arguing that Muslims are not a race and that opposition to Islam as an ideology is not necessarily racist, while others argued that hostility toward a religion can also target its community and resemble racism. The disagreement also concerned whether criticism of Islamic ideas should be distinguished from broader hostility toward Muslims.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should give a straightforward definition of Islamophobia as prejudice or fear directed at Islam or Muslims, or emphasize that its definition was unsettled and identify specific sources for any definition. They also disputed whether survey results about negative attitudes toward Muslims could be presented as evidence of Islamophobia without a source explicitly making that connection, with some editors treating the concepts as closely related and others arguing that the survey evidence was broader.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how the article should define Islamophobia: some wanted the opening to describe prejudice against Muslims, while others argued that definitions also encompass criticism or rejection of Islam and favored qualifying disputed examples as alleged. They also disputed whether the term itself was controversial or whether the disagreement concerned how it was applied, with some arguing that it was often used too broadly to label criticism of Islam as prejudice.

Editors disagreed over what should count as antisemitism in the article: one argued that persecution of Jews counts when it is because they are Jews, even if other groups are also targeted, while another distinguished antisemitism from persecution shared with other groups.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include research linking people’s self-described racial categories to genetic patterns: one side argued it would balance the article, while others said it did not establish a distinct white group and would shift the article into a broader debate about race. They also disputed whether the article could offer a general definition of white people, with some favoring a broad account of changing uses and others seeking shared guidelines for who the term includes.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “white people” should chiefly mean white Europeans or be described as a flexible label used differently in different contexts, including for people with non-European ancestry. They also disputed whether variation in hair and eye color among Europeans belonged in the article: one editor called it relevant, while another argued those traits were not defining and deserved less emphasis.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include photographs of people in the article: some supported adding examples, while others wanted to keep the article without them because choosing who counts as typically white was contentious. One concern was that showing only people whose classification was uncontroversial could suggest that other groups were not white; another editor argued that historical images could be presented as examples of particular past definitions instead.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how much match detail to keep in the main article: some wanted knockout scores and scorers readily visible, while others argued that detailed match information belonged in linked articles and the main page should be an overview. They also disputed how to shorten the article, with some supporting moving sections into separate pages and others objecting to removing material without discussion or leaving only links instead of summaries.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how much space to give the newsletter remarks attributed to Paul: some wanted a shorter account or the exact wording moved to footnotes, while another argued that the remarks belonged prominently in the article. [Avoid citation in prose.] They also disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should list specific political positions; one editor objected that the list was too detailed and could mislead, while another defended including positions and disputed the proposed descriptions of them. [Avoid citation in prose.]

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to add announcement dates to the list of programs in development: one argued that dates would let readers sort projects and see how long they had gone without updates, while another considered the added information unnecessary because readers could check the references. They also differed over when to show a pending renewal status for a current show, with one favoring an update once reporting confirmed a decision was near and the other preferring to wait until the season ended.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Goguryeo should be presented as Korean history, as part of China’s regional history, or as shared history; one editor argued for its importance to both Korean and northeastern Chinese history, while another said historians generally recognize it as a Korean kingdom and reject Chinese claims. They also disputed whether an editor’s diagram based on ancient chronicles could be included: critics said the chronicles needed modern scholarly interpretation and that combining them risked adding unsupported conclusions, while a supporter proposed presenting the material as a traditional Chinese account with direct quotations and citations.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Ted Kennedy’s connection to his nephew William Kennedy Smith’s rape trial merited space in Kennedy’s biography; some argued the trial’s attention and Kennedy’s testimony made it relevant, while others considered it peripheral to Kennedy. Those favoring inclusion proposed a brief statement that he testified, while an opponent argued that even this fact did not make the trial important to Kennedy’s life.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Media Matters was suitable as a source: some argued its transcripts and videos could document what O’Reilly said, while others questioned its transcripts and objected to its commentary and possible bias. Some proposed using it only for specific, neutrally worded claims about what O’Reilly said, while others argued for removing its references or preferring sources such as O’Reilly’s own essays.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the claim that Florida’s taxes fell by $19 billion during Bush’s governorship: one wanted the wording to credit the state government collectively and include analysis questioning how much Bush could claim, while another argued the wording already conveyed his role. They also disputed whether to include a source’s characterization of the tax cuts as benefiting wealthy people and businesses, with one editor calling it opinion and the other defending it as an attributed view.

Editors disagreed over whether the article’s opening should say that Hovind’s views conflict with scientific evidence: one editor argued the assessment was unnecessary there, while others said it was needed to explain how his views are received. They also debated whether repeated criticism of his beliefs and detailed prison information made the article too long, with one editor calling for cuts and others emphasizing that the article should still give substantial attention to his creationism-related work.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether Coulter’s remark about Timothy McVeigh should be described as support for him or as a joke, and whether the article had reliable sourcing for claims about how critics interpreted it. One editor cited a report that Coulter said the remark was a joke, while another argued that the reported exchange did not show her saying that.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include Ann Coulter’s exchange with a Canadian television host about Canada and the Vietnam War: some argued that coverage in outside publications made it relevant, while others questioned its importance and the available sourcing. They also disputed how to present Coulter’s later C-SPAN remarks, with some favoring a brief account and others preferring her words without editorial interpretation because they disagreed about whether she was admitting error or using sarcasm.

2025.summary: An editor challenged revised percentages for the Talysh, Turkic and Kurdish language groups, saying the cited source reported different figures and asking for another source to support the changes.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the new “Med School” season should be treated as a separate series or as the ninth season of Scrubs, with participants citing its different presentation and conflicting descriptions of its status. They also disputed whether the show should be labeled a romance as well as a comedy-drama: one editor pointed to its recurring relationships, while others argued that romance was a subplot rather than the central story.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe UKIP as right-wing or centre-right, with some arguing the latter label needed stronger independent sources and another proposing a combined description. Editors also debated whether academic claims about xenophobia and Islamophobia belonged in the article, and whether they should appear in its main text or in categories and the information box. The claims were supported by some editors as sourced academic assessments, while others questioned their sourcing or prominence.

2012.summary: Editors disputed how the article should describe UKIP’s ideology, especially whether it should call the party right-wing populist or instead emphasize its own description of itself as libertarian. Some editors argued that “populist” was subjective and should be removed or qualified, while others said it was a recognized political term supported by sources and should remain.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe academic research on UKIP voters: some wanted to retain the term “xenophobia,” while others argued it needed explanation because the study used it in a specific sense related to immigration attitudes and hostility to immigrants. They also disputed whether recent opinion-poll gains belonged in the opening paragraph, with supporters calling them important to the party’s significance and opponents arguing that a single poll was too temporary or gave it too much prominence.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether the party’s political position should be described in the information box as “right-wing to far-right”: supporters cited academic sources using the far-right label, while others favored the broader “right-wing” description because sources differed. Some argued that far-right references belonged, if anywhere, in the article text with context, since several cited works mentioned the party only in passing and did not explain the label.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the handball in the Ireland qualifier should be described as a major career event and how quickly to expand coverage, with some seeking more prominence and others cautioning against judging its lasting significance while events were still developing. They also disputed whether the incident belonged in Henry’s opening paragraph: supporters argued that its media attention warranted inclusion, while opponents said that more space would give a recent event too much weight in a biography.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep a notable-filmography section: one wanted it removed amid repeated changes to which films were included, while another said such a summary belonged in an actor’s biography. A separate exchange questioned whether sources supporting a claim about Haasan as a method actor were reliable and appropriate, with one editor emphasizing the need for published secondary sources and strong sourcing for claims about living people.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Moldovan should be described as a separate language or as a variety of Romanian, with some favoring the broader term “variety” and others arguing that the language-versus-dialect distinction could not be settled by linguistic criteria alone. They also disputed how to describe the written forms: one proposal called official Moldovan identical to Romanian except for a spelling difference, while another editor cited grammatical and usage differences as reasons to describe them as nearly identical instead.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how to frame a passage about Hoppe’s private covenant communities: one argued that the section should emphasize his proposal to physically remove homosexuals, while another argued that this singled out one group and obscured the passage’s broader restrictions on democracy, free speech and other groups.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over including an anonymous StudentsReview.com comment calling the university “an abomination”: opponents questioned whether the self-selected reviews represented students, while supporters argued the comment fit alongside other reported survey results and statistics. They also disputed whether to include a section about stereotypes associated with the “909” area code, with one position arguing that the stigma affected students and graduates and the other asking for evidence that it did.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should say Afghanistan is sometimes included in the term “Desi”: one side cited sources that include it, while opponents argued that such sources do not establish a cultural or linguistic definition and that the term refers more narrowly to the Indo-Aryan sphere. A related concern was whether administrative and clinical references gave enough weight to include Afghanistan in a general definition of the term.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether newly elected Rajya Sabha members should be counted as sitting members before their terms began, and whether the BJP’s current strength should be listed as 91, 92, or the official site’s then-listed 95. One editor argued the article should retain outgoing members until their terms ended and add successors only when their terms began; others favored updating the party totals sooner, disputing the count and whether a member had resigned.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should mention uncertainty and differences between Jain sects about Mahavira’s life, or focus more concisely on the broad historical dating and leave those details to the article body. They also disputed the label “proto-Jain”: some argued it suggests an unsupported change in the tradition, while others defended it as a term used by historians for earlier followers of Parshvanatha.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Lita’s moves should be listed under fan or commentator-given names such as “Litasault” and “LitaBomb,” or by more general names such as “moonsault” and “DDT.” One side cited commentators using the special names, while another argued that those labels were inconsistent or did not establish the move’s usual name.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether LeBron James’s listed height and weight should be 6 feet 8 inches and roughly 240–250 pounds, as several published listings gave, or 6 feet 9 inches and 260 pounds, figures he stated in a televised interview. Some argued that the article should use published third-party listings rather than rely on James’s own statement, while others said his statement was more credible because those listings had not measured him.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over how to order the table of states where same-sex marriage was legal, with proposals based on the date of a ruling or law, when marriage became permanently available, or when licenses were first issued. Some favored using the legal decision or enactment date, while others argued for ordering states by when marriages became available; the debate also raised questions about temporary periods when licenses were issued before a stay.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should link to one leading fansite, several sites, or none: some favored the site with the most traffic, while others argued that selecting only a few sites unfairly favored them over comparable alternatives. They also disputed whether to keep favorable press coverage in a section about criticism; some said the reviews made the article read like advertising, while another editor argued that reliable reviews should remain and that negative reviews could balance them.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Assyrians, Chaldeans and Syriacs could be described as one people: one position said the names were used for the same group, while another stressed that people identified as Assyrians and Syriacs as distinct peoples. They also disputed the article’s name and scope, with a combined Assyrian/Chaldean/Syriac title proposed as a compromise and others arguing that the article should not label all Syriacs as Assyrians.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening description should call Northern Cyprus a de facto independent republic, as one editor argued, or describe the area as occupied and outside the Republic of Cyprus’s effective control, as another argued. The debate centered on whether the wording should emphasize its separate government in practice or its disputed legal and international status.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Olbermann as left-leaning or liberal in the opening paragraph: one proposal argued that his public commentary supported such a label, while others objected to applying an ideological label he did not use for himself. They also disputed the order of his job descriptions, with some favoring political commentary and broadcasting ahead of sportscasting, while another editor argued that the order should reflect how long he had worked in each field.

Editors disagreed over whether the article could describe protests and opinion-poll results as anti-Americanism when sources used that label, or whether presenting those classifications as fact amounted to the article taking a side; some favored reporting attributed views, while others warned that sourcing alone did not make such claims neutral. They also disagreed over the article’s scope: some wanted it to cover the range of published uses of the term, while another view favored focusing on people who identify themselves as anti-American or on anti-Americanism as prejudice.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Hunyadi’s ancestry: one argued that early records support a Wallachian or Romanian origin, while another said secondary sources present competing possibilities, including Slavic or Hungarian ancestry, and uncertainty.

2017.summary: An editor requested adding The Uncle Paul Show to the list of former live-action or animated programming, with its premiere and finale dates.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include the announced Children in Need special “Time Crash” in the main episode table before it aired: some argued that it was a Doctor Who television production and should be listed by broadcast date, while others wanted it held out until its place in the series’ continuity was clear. The disagreement turned partly on what the table implied, with some saying it listed broadcast productions rather than story continuity and others warning that inclusion would suggest the special belonged to the established narrative.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over where to list the Doctor Who Adventure Games: some argued they belonged with series five because the production team treated them as extra episodes. Others wanted them in a separate section for interactive stories, arguing that the main list was for televised serials and that the games were not television serials.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list “Demon’s Run” as the title for an upcoming episode or leave it unconfirmed: one argued that the TV Guide website was not a reliable source and cited a magazine report treating the name as a working title, while another said the blog was the closest available source and that titles could later be updated.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether a Gallup poll asking if humans were created within 10,000 years could represent young-Earth creationism: some argued it did not establish belief in a young Earth, while others said the beliefs were closely linked and the poll belonged in the article.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether a fan-voted RiffTrax poll was enough to include the Twilight films: some argued its large vote made it useful evidence, while others said a fan poll and generally mixed reviews did not establish that critics considered them among the worst films ever. For Jack and Jill, one position was that its record Razzie wins and low ratings did not establish an all-time ranking; proponents pointed to reviewers who explicitly called it one of the worst films in cinema history.

2012.summary: Editors debated whether the opening paragraph should simply report that the Southern Poverty Law Center classified the Family Research Council as an anti-gay hate group, or also describe the objections to that designation. Some favored a brief mention and leaving details to the article body, while others argued that the lead should identify the dispute over the label.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how much space to give the controversy about Krugman’s consulting for Enron: some argued that later press references made the dispute worth explaining, while others considered it a minor part of his career and favored a shorter account. They also disputed wording that described his support for freer markets as contrary to his political beliefs; objectors said the claim was unsupported or wrongly inferred from his positions, while a defender argued that it showed he could be pragmatic about market policies.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should say critics viewed Krugman’s economic arguments as politically motivated: some supported that characterization, while others considered it open to debate and warned against presenting interpretation as fact. They also disputed how to describe his partisanship and what context was needed; one editor argued that criticism of his partisanship was a legitimate, important aspect of his biography, while another opposed including it without identifying the critics’ political direction.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how to explain the biblical “mountains of Ararat”: one proposed that the reference was to a region, with a later tradition identifying Mount Masis as the particular peak, while another argued that the evidence did not support parts of that account. They also disputed whether the name Masis predates the identification of the peak as Ararat; one editor said the available evidence did not establish that chronology, while another argued that the timing of the identification remained uncertain.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include accounts alleging that Hannity had a friendly off-air relationship with Hal Turner and gave him a platform on the radio; some argued the material could be included with Hannity’s denial, while others said it largely repeated Turner’s claims and needed independent, reliable support.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe Hannity as a conspiracy theorist and characterize his claims as falsehoods, or use more qualified wording and attribute those judgments to critics. Separately, they disputed whether the article should call his accusations about Jake Tapper a “smear” or describe them as misleading or distorted.

2023.summary: Editors disputed how the article should describe scholarly views on whether Vlachs and Romanians originated north or south of the Danube, particularly whether the migrationist position was supported by only some scholars or by a wider majority. One editor argued that regional historiographies and named scholars supported the migrationist view, while another urged caution, saying the evidence did not establish a general scholarly consensus and that the article should present both views neutrally.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the entry should say that birds are dinosaurs, as scientific classification sources described them, or use wording such as “descended from” and explain that “dinosaur” has both a scientific and an everyday meaning. Some wanted the bird discussion removed as a distracting side issue from the entry’s point about humans and dinosaurs living at different times; others argued the classification information should remain because it reflected the sources.
