2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether roster entries should include wrestlers’ nicknames: some said they were unnecessary and made the list look cluttered, while another supported keeping nicknames closely tied to a wrestler’s ring name. They also disagreed over how to classify inactive talent when status was uncertain: one editor urged using confirmed information and avoiding rumors, while another noted that WWE might not publicly explain when performers were taken off the road.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list wrestlers as suspended based on clues such as their absence from shows, or to leave them unlabelled without confirmation from WWE, which some said was necessary to avoid speculation. They also disagreed over whether Kristal Marshall’s reported release was sufficiently verified to remove her from the roster; some editors favored keeping her listed with her employment status marked unknown.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed about when wrestlers should be listed as active or inactive: one proposal counted appearances and scheduled title matches, while another argued that wrestling was the key measure and questioned using television appearances alone. They also debated replacing the roster lists with tables; supporters proposed sorting personnel by brand and role, while opponents said tables would make the changing roster harder to follow.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to update the women’s champion listing based on reported spoilers before the change appeared on television or WWE.com; one editor argued that a reliable source was enough to use the spoiler.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over adding a “WWE Legends” section for people not assigned to a regular brand but still appearing in current storylines or under special contracts; the proposal set criteria for who would qualify. Opponents argued that occasional appearances did not make someone part of WWE personnel and warned that an open-ended category could prompt further disputes about who belonged in it.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed about whether Vince McMahon and Triple H should appear in both the on-air roster and corporate sections, or be listed only once according to their main roles. Some argued that occasional appearances did not justify placing them with active on-air performers, while others distinguished the Mr. McMahon character from the executive Vince McMahon and argued that continuing television appearances could warrant on-air listings.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Chris Jericho should remain on the active roster list during a break to tour with his band, or move to the unassigned section while he was working outside WWE. Those favoring keeping him on the roster pointed to WWE’s roster listing and argued that a hiatus did not change his role; another editor said the unassigned section was for people without a role and suggested a note could mark the break.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Hulk Hogan belonged among wrestlers or among other on-air personnel: some argued his current role was hosting rather than wrestling, while another favored keeping him with wrestlers because he remained on WWE’s roster and might wrestle later. They also disputed whether the list should mark wrestlers inactive after 30 days without activity, with one proposal to remove those notes and others arguing that the status helps describe the active roster or significant absences.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to classify Lana and Stephanie McMahon as wrestlers or other on-air personnel. One editor argued their feuds and occasional matches supported keeping them with the main roster, while another said those activities did not make them wrestlers and favored classifying them as other on-air personnel.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Stephanie McMahon belonged in the main-roster wrestler section: one argued that she, Shane and Triple H should count as player-coaches because they also wrestle. Another argued that her current authority role and infrequent matches did not make her a wrestler for that section.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether WWE’s website should determine who counted as current personnel: one side treated its roster profiles as stronger evidence than wrestlers’ own social-media descriptions, while another argued the site could be wrong and should not be treated as decisive. The discussion called for consistent standards but did not settle which source should control.

2019.summary: Editors debated whether winning a championship should change where someone appears on the personnel list, including whether an on-screen authority figure should then be listed as a wrestler or moved to another brand. One view was that a title alone should not determine someone’s role or placement without reliable independent sourcing; another was that champions should be listed on the roster as wrestlers, following the page’s longstanding practice.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Paul Heyman should be assigned to a single brand: one argued that, as an agent representing people on different brands, he did not need to switch, while another said he was WWE-hired talent rather than a real agent and should be listed with Raw. They also disputed whether reports about Eva Marie justified keeping her on the personnel list, alongside a broader disagreement over whether PWInsider’s reporting should be considered less reliable after reports editors believed were mistaken.

2021.summary: Discussion concerned whether Rohan Raja and Levi Muir belonged in the NXT UK roster or the WWE Performance Center section.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include the one-off BMF belt in the champions list: some argued it was symbolic and not a standard championship, while others said it belonged because the list also included The Ultimate Fighter winners. The discussion also raised whether those winners should remain, with one position calling for both groups to be included or excluded together and another arguing the BMF belt should be left out while The Ultimate Fighter winners stayed.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include historian Touraj Daryaee’s criticism of the film: supporters considered it a significant scholarly viewpoint, while opponents argued that it did not address what the film actually depicts and should be removed. They also disputed where his comments belonged, with one view treating them as an assessment of historical accuracy and another as commentary on the portrayal of Persians and the film’s modern message.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how much the biography should cover Cruz’s role in the 2013 government shutdown: some argued it was a major part of his record, while others said the article should stick to material clearly connected to him and supported by reliable sources. They also disputed whether to include the shutdown’s wider economic effects and the threatened debt-limit breach, with one side arguing these consequences were tied to Cruz’s actions and the other objecting that the sources did not establish that connection.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the political-positions section should include fact-checking of Cruz’s statements: one argued that reporting his views and related fact-checks belonged there, while another called a specific addition undue and inappropriate, and a third questioned whether that detail was proportionate.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail about the 2016 primary and caucus results belonged in Cruz’s biography: some called for removing or substantially reducing the section, while others argued that a brief account of the outcomes should remain. Editors also debated whether the opening sentence should describe Cruz as Canadian-born; supporters pointed to his birth and citizenship, while opponents argued that the wording could imply he became an American later and that his birthplace was not relevant to his notability.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening wording should use Yahweh or a familiar English term for the deity, such as God or the Lord. Supporters of Yahweh argued that it names the deity identified in the Hebrew text and avoids ambiguity, while opponents said it was unfamiliar to many readers and could suggest a distinct deity or uncertain pronunciation.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include photos of unused school buses and what they implied: some argued the images suggested failures in local evacuation planning, while others said they could unfairly assign blame without enough context. The discussion also questioned whether the evacuation plan called for buses to take residents out of the city or to shelters, with one editor pointing to a state plan that described bus use without fixed destinations.

2010.summary: An editor combined several categories of upcoming shows into one section, saying the existing subsections had little detail, and replaced a creator section with one crediting head writers.

2020.summary: Editors disputed whether Djokovic should be credited with 281 or 282 weeks at No. 1: one argued the article should follow the ATP’s 281-week figure, while another counted the week ending March 22 because Djokovic could not lose the top ranking before Indian Wells was due to end.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should foreground the film’s place in a planned shared DC film universe or focus first on its creators and cast, with some also questioning whether that universe was established enough to merit emphasis. They also disputed whether reports of backlash to casting choices belonged in the article and how much detail was justified, including disagreement over which sources reliably supported the claims.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the cited reports were reliable enough to identify Callan Mulvey as KGBeast in the film; one proposed the identification, while another rejected the reports as unreliable or based on an unreliable source.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether critics’ response should be described as broadly negative rather than polarized, with one editor citing the ratings to argue that negative views predominated and others cautioning against editors interpreting the data themselves. They also disputed how to balance the review examples: one editor wanted negative reviews to appear in proportion to their greater share, while another argued for a reasonable balance of positive and negative reviews instead of selecting examples by the aggregate score.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over describing Hitler’s leadership as “charismatic” near the article’s opening: some called the adjective potentially biased or unnecessary there, even while accepting it could be true or fit elsewhere. Others argued that charisma was a value-neutral, important description of his leadership and should remain near the beginning rather than be omitted.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Hitler’s government: some argued that “fascist” was the more precise label, while others preferred “totalitarian” or objected that neither term should be used without qualification. They also disputed whether the article should say Hitler remained a Christian: one editor argued that this was inaccurate and challenged the relevance of the proposed religious material, while another cited his public professions of Christian faith in support of including it.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Southern Poverty Law Center’s hate-group designation of the Center for Immigration Studies belonged in the opening paragraph: some favored a brief attributed mention, while others considered it too prominent and argued it should remain in the article’s main text. They also disputed how much context to include, with some supporting references to the SPLC’s claims about published writers and alleged ties to nativism, and another proposing narrower wording focused on the designation and the Center’s lawsuit challenging it.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail about the proposed bridges and a $25 million road to one bridge belonged in Palin’s main article; some wanted the road left to a separate article, while others argued that Palin’s decision to proceed with it was important to explain. They also disagreed over whether to retain direct quotations of Palin’s support for the bridges: one view favored her own words as relevant context, while another argued that the brief summary should rely less on quotations from her statements.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Sheamus as a three-time or four-time WWE champion, with the four-time count supported by references that treated earlier World Heavyweight title reigns as part of the same lineage. They also disputed whether “Magic Mohawk” belonged among his nicknames: one editor pointed to Roman Reigns and Triple H using it, while another said use in a promotional segment did not make it an official nickname.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over which dates the episode table should show: one proposal was to list separate United States and United Kingdom air dates, while another favored only the date an episode first aired anywhere. Supporters of the first-airing approach argued that highlighting selected countries would give them undue prominence, while another editor said the United States date mattered because the show was produced there and primarily for that audience.

Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe the practice as involving spirit possession: some defended the term as supported by scholarship, while others said the source discussed mediumship and gender roles rather than Raja Yoga and argued that the wording was misleading in the opening paragraph. One editor proposed using mediumistic channeling instead, while another argued that the discussion of possession should remain in the article, though not necessarily in its opening paragraph.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether the article could describe the founder’s conduct as immoral and intimate: some argued historical accounts supported including the accusations, while others said the article treated contested allegations as fact and relied on an unreliable source. They also disagreed over calling the movement “secretive” in the opening paragraph, with one editor citing academic descriptions of information being withheld and another arguing that this label gave a limited aspect of the group too much prominence.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe the film as a reboot: one view was that it continues earlier storylines and that the term was too vague, while another argued that published sources classified it as a reboot of the franchise. They also disputed where to present that label, with proposals ranging from the opening summary to a reception section that would attribute it to outside sources.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening should describe Islamic views: one position called for noting modern interpretations that the Qur’an aimed to end slavery, while another argued that the article should foreground the traditional acceptance of slavery and cited scholars who still permitted it in some circumstances. They also disputed whether reports of present-day slavery in African countries could be presented as linked to Islam, with one editor objecting that this implied Islam caused the practice and another pointing to cases described as claiming Islamic sanction.

2009.summary: Editors disputed how much dialogue from Roesgen’s Chicago protest report to include, with one proposing a concise account and a link to the full transcript rather than selected excerpts, while another supported including her exchange with a protester so readers could judge it for themselves. They also disagreed over how to characterize commentator Frank Sesno’s reaction: one editor stressed his criticism of Roesgen’s debate with a protester, while another emphasized his view that reporters should challenge serious claims.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Yasuke as a samurai or use a narrower description such as retainer, with some arguing that published sources support the samurai label and others urging that his status remain uncertain. They also disputed whether sources calling him a samurai were dependable, particularly Thomas Lockley’s work, and whether editors could use historical records themselves to challenge those accounts.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “Islamofascism” describes a political movement sharing traits with fascism, such as violence, suppression of dissent and imposed ideology. One editor rejected that description as unsupported and argued that the term was an epithet rather than an established concept.

Editors disputed whether the article should keep the unqualified title “Libertarianism,” which one side said most commonly referred to the philosophy it covered, or become a broader disambiguation page because other political and philosophical traditions also use the term. Some argued that a more balanced account of those alternative uses could address the concern, while others favored a disambiguation page; the discussion also questioned whether the title itself gave one tradition undue prominence.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should include left-libertarian and libertarian-socialist ideas as forms of libertarianism, or focus on the property-rights and limited-government meaning some described as the predominant one; others argued that reliable sources treat several of these ideas as related versions of the broader subject. They also disagreed about how much space the less familiar views deserved, with some arguing they should remain in the article while others said their coverage was disproportionate.

2011.summary: Editors debated whether the article should represent libertarians who support limited public assistance, including a social safety net, alongside those opposing redistribution: one editor argued the existing wording made libertarians appear to favor only a narrowly limited state, while others questioned whether this view was prevalent enough for prominent placement and whether it belonged in the opening paragraph.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should define libertarianism through self-ownership and property rights: one argued that a cited scholarly definition supported including the idea, while another said private property was a varying position, not a central tenet, and did not belong in the opening summary.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over how much government policy belonged in Blair’s biography: one argued criticism should bear personally on him, while another said civil-liberties measures were associated with Blair and needed fuller context. They also questioned describing public opposition to the Iraq invasion as “overwhelming,” with editors favoring less categorical wording and noting that opinion polls did not show uniform opposition.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should reflect a more critical assessment of Blair’s premiership and declining popularity: one argued that its tone was too favorable, while another cautioned that judgments about whether a prime minister was good or bad are subjective and that the article should focus on facts.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to move the article’s section on views of Bush outside the United States to a separate page; one proposal argued that comparable sections were absent from other leaders’ biographies and that the material could serve as anti-Bush commentary. Others argued that international opinion belonged in the article because Bush’s policies affected people beyond the United States.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a Union of Concerned Scientists report alleging that the Bush administration had interfered with science: supporters viewed it as an important criticism backed by prominent scientists, while others questioned its relevance to Bush’s biography and whether its views were adequately balanced. Some editors argued that any account should also explain the White House response and whether other scientists had challenged the report.

2007.summary: Editors disputed whether the economic-policy section should describe the economy as “strong” and its growth as “healthy,” or replace those judgments with figures such as average inflation-adjusted growth and unemployment rates. One editor argued that the favorable descriptions were factual and not biased, while another said they were misleading and preferred neutral statistics for readers to assess.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how strongly to describe historians’ ratings of Bush’s presidency: one argued the wording overstated what a few surveys could show, while another defended it because the polls explicitly used a negative rating category. They also debated whether to include informal History News Network polls alongside a Siena College survey, with a suggested version retaining the results while explaining that the informal polls were not scientific samples.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the infobox should use a cropped or uncropped photograph: one favored the crop and objected to repeating it in another section, while another argued that official photographs in presidential infoboxes should be shown uncropped.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe U.S. actions against Native nations as “stealing” or “seizing”: critics of “stealing” considered it a moral judgment, while a supporter argued that “seizing” softened what had happened. In the economy section, editors disputed a proposed claim that the U.S. financial system gains from exploiting foreign markets, labor and resources; critics said “exploiting” implied unjust abuse, while the proposal’s author defended the word as neutral.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening should qualify the United States’ status as the sole superpower by noting limits on its power; one supported that qualification, while another called it unnecessary and biased and argued it did not belong there. They also disagreed over whether the opening should mention both the expansion of rights and the dispossession of Native Americans and slavery, with one editor defending the inclusion and another saying the sentence was misplaced in the opening.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how the article’s infobox should describe language: one position argued that calling English simply the national language understated how many people used other languages, while others favored “English (de facto)” with a footnote about other languages. They also disputed whether regional languages belonged in the country-wide infobox or should instead be covered in articles about the relevant regions.

2009.summary: Editors debated whether the article should be titled “United States” or “United States of America,” with a proponent of the longer name calling the shorter title an abbreviation. Opponents argued that “United States” is the generally used short form, and the requested move ended with no consensus to change the title.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s history gave too little attention to harms against Native Americans, with some calling for more coverage and another pointing to existing discussion and material. One editor proposed adding a brief account of forced removal and loss of Native lives, while another argued that the history was already addressed elsewhere on the page.

2012.summary: One editor argued that the article called the Iraq war controversial but did not signal similar controversy over the health-care law, and proposed revising one or both descriptions. Others argued that many laws are controversial and that the Iraq wording reflected the war’s human cost; another editor said health-care opposition was especially an American concern, unlike the Iraq war’s international controversy.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether the five modern island territories should be described as part of the United States: one position cited government descriptions and residents’ citizenship as evidence of inclusion, while another argued that the territories’ legal status meant they were not part of the country.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether an aerial photo of Houston's Texas Medical Center belonged in the health section: some considered the center's size and connection to health care relevant, while others called the image generic and noted that the text did not mention it.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should report racial differences in incarceration: some argued the figures needed crime-rate context or belonged in a dedicated article, while others said the racial breakdown was important to include. They also debated how to summarize Hawaii’s overthrow and annexation: some supported saying the United States helped overthrow the monarchy, while others favored describing the overthrow and later annexation without attributing it to the United States as a whole.

2016.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should describe Republicans as center-right, with one proposing “right-wing” instead and another arguing that this description was more accurate than center-right. The discussion also contested calling Democrats center-left: one editor questioned whether selected examples established that label, while another offered published sources applying it to the party.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should describe slavery and its legacy: one proposal called for mentioning slavery’s scale, racism and Jim Crow, while others challenged terms such as “genocide” and “systemic racism” as contentious or inadequately defined. There was also disagreement about how much of the country’s racial history belonged in this short overview, including whether to add more about Reconstruction and the Civil Rights Movement or give that material greater space in the article’s main text.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should say that American influence had diminished in the 21st century: some wanted the wording to reflect a smaller gap in power, while others considered the claim too subjective or difficult to support with sources. They also disputed whether the sports section should name swimmer Michael Phelps; one editor argued his Olympic achievements set him apart, while another objected to listing individual athletes in an article about the country.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the culture section should give African American culture a separate subsection or integrate it into the broader account; supporters argued that the history of enslavement and exclusion helps explain its development, while opponents questioned the need for a separate treatment and its fit in a short overview. They also disputed how to describe American cultural and political ideals: some objected that the opening description presented those ideals too broadly without enough qualification, while others defended them as widely accepted principles.

2015.summary: Editors proposed moving the article from “Kevin Steen” to “Kevin Owens,” arguing that his WWE career made the newer name more recognizable, while the proposal noted he had used Steen longer; the move request was closed as successful.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over which countries’ chart results belonged in the singles table: some favored markets where Lopez had stronger chart positions, while another argued for including larger markets and excluding Ireland or New Zealand when consistent chart data were unavailable. They also disagreed over including the U.S. dance chart, with one editor opposing it because it was not a sales chart and another arguing that Lopez’s dance-chart success made it important to her discography.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether East Germany belonged in the main all-time team table or in a separate section for former countries: some argued that all teams that had played should be included, while others preferred to keep inactive teams separate. Editors also disputed Pelé’s World Cup assist total, with one editor arguing for eight and another pointing to FIFA’s count of six in 1970 and arguing that his total was at least nine.

2005.summary: Editors disputed how to describe Larry Sanger’s role in starting Wikipedia: Sanger said he proposed the wiki encyclopedia and did much of the early work, while another editor argued that his employment meant he should not be called a co-founder. They also disagreed over whether Bomis’s nude and suggestive images should be described as pornography or as nude modeling.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep a section on disputes about who founded Wikipedia and Wales’s editing of his own biography: one removed it, arguing that its sources were unreliable and the material was not notable, while another said the founding dispute had been covered in the press and the editing issue had also been reported. After the section was rewritten with additional sources, an editor accepted that the sourcing concerns were addressed but still questioned whether the coverage gave a relatively minor issue too much space in the biography.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Jimmy Wales’s role in founding Wikipedia: some favored wording that did not settle whether Larry Sanger was a co-founder, while others argued the article should identify Sanger as one. They also disputed whether a section about Wales’s editing of his biography and the related founding and Bomis claims belonged in the article, with objections focused on its neutrality, sourcing, and amount of attention, while other editors said it was sourced and should be revised rather than removed.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Arndt’s psychology credentials: one argued that the article risked implying she had never legitimately worked as a psychologist, while another emphasized that she had not been registered and supported clarifying the rules in force during her earlier career. They also disputed how much space to give recent controversies compared with her earlier career, with one editor seeking more material about her earlier life and another arguing the article should reflect the greater coverage of recent events in published sources.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether describing Adams as raised Mormon in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints was redundant: one argued that either reference alone was enough, while another said the church name clarified which Mormons were meant.

Editors disagreed over whether the phrase “Polish death camp” should be called a misnomer in the opening paragraph, with some arguing it is inaccurate or misleading and others objecting to that label. The objection was that the phrase can describe a camp by its location in Poland, so calling it a misnomer could suggest it is always incorrect.

2016.summary: Editors disputed how to describe whether Hillary Clinton’s campaign had dropped support for a soda tax after Coca-Cola objected: one proposed reporting that an executive said the campaign would stop commenting, while another argued the evidence did not establish a change in its policy. The disagreement also concerned how much weight to give leaked emails and a company executive’s account, with one editor rejecting them as out of context and another arguing they should not be deleted merely because they were not official campaign statements.

Editors disputed when Generation Z begins: one argued that mid-1990s dates were more widely used, while another said the generation did not really begin until around 2000. They also disagreed over how the article arranged its discussion of possible start dates, with one editor objecting that a revision downplayed 1995 and emphasized 2005 dates.

2020.summary: Editors disputed whether Generation Z’s starting year should be given as 1995 or 1996, as some argued, or 1997, which another editor said was supported by most sources cited in the article. With sources using different date ranges, proposals included describing the start as the mid-1990s or giving a range instead of selecting one year.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe a backstage dance segment featuring returning wrestling figures: opponents said it was an unimportant backstage moment, while supporters argued that the reunion and appearances merited mention. A proposed compromise was to list the participants among the event’s other talent and mark their appearance in a short note, which some editors accepted.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over adding material about Nazi views of Chinese and Japanese people: one defended the supporting sources, while others questioned the reliability of a cited study and the use of Hitler’s political testament as a source.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over how prominently the opening paragraph should explain Churchill’s 9/11 essay: some wanted a clear account of the remarks at the heart of the controversy, while others argued that interpretation and detail belonged in the article body rather than the introduction. They also disputed how to describe his claimed American Indian ancestry: some pressed for prominent mention of rejection by Native American groups, while others cautioned that views among those groups were not uniform.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe the film as controversial or mention disputes around it: some wanted the court case and school-showing debate included, while others argued that this overstated the disagreement and gave it too much prominence. They also disputed whether saying the film had generated controversy was meaningfully different from labeling the film controversial.

Editors disputed how the album’s reviews were summarized, with some saying the article gave too much weight to negative criticism and others arguing that the reviews were mostly average, with few strongly positive or negative responses. Some editors described the overall reaction as positive, while another characterized it as mixed and only slightly favorable, reflecting disagreement over whether the article’s wording fairly represented the reviews.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “Radar” should be listed as an official single: one comment said it was not a single, while another argued it should be listed as one. They also offered conflicting estimates of the album’s worldwide sales, with one calculation putting the total below three million and another claiming it exceeded four million.

2016.summary: Editors disputed whether Boy & the World belonged on the list: one editor argued it should not be added without a source identifying it as a children's film, while the film was repeatedly added and removed.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph’s claim that the film became the highest-grossing worldwide should say that the comparison was not adjusted for inflation; one editor argued the qualification was needed to avoid misleading readers. Others argued the record was a factual comparison of dollar earnings, while inflation-adjusted rankings were estimates and belonged in the box-office discussion rather than the opening paragraph.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the plot summary should say Harvey Dent died or describe him as lying motionless, with some pointing to the film’s apparent outcome and others arguing that his fate was uncertain. They also debated whether to report the film’s top ranking on IMDb: supporters considered the audience rating worth noting, while opponents said the user poll could be skewed or manipulated and preferred other measures of audience response.

2018.summary: Editors disputed the listed height: one editor said the only supporting reference was Soccerbase and suggested removing the figure if that source was insufficient, while reporting that other editors had repeatedly changed it.

2021.summary: Editors proposed substantially different figures for Kolkata’s gross domestic product, including $46 billion and $177 billion, and another contributor gave estimates of $47 billion and $48 billion. Other editors questioned whether the cited material supported the figures and declined a proposed change until reliable sources were provided.

2023.summary: Editors proposed and supported changing the article title from “Saudi Professional League” to “Saudi Pro League,” citing common usage and the league’s official website; the move was approved.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Dylan’s religious music after the three albums commonly called his Christian trilogy: one proposed saying that his later albums and songs were mainly secular, while another argued that religious ideas continued in his work and that describing the 1983 album Infidels as predominantly secular was disputed. A later proposal acknowledged Infidels was not secular but said Dylan moved away from religion as the main focus of his new songs; another editor accepted that change in emphasis while rejecting a simple secular label for the album.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Ric Flair’s match with Shawn Michaels: some opposed labeling it a “career-threatening match,” while others wanted that label, and one argument was that it could suggest both wrestlers risked retirement even though only Flair faced that condition. After the event, discussion also questioned whether to call it a retirement match, a career-threatening match, or simply describe Flair’s retirement condition, with participants noting that the condition applied only to Flair.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a sketch of Mahfiruz, with some objecting that its origin and source were not credible and another defending its use and giving it a date of 1619. They also disputed her death date and the reliability of sources used to support different dates, including whether to rely on Baki Tezcan or other historical accounts.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Indigenous Australians’ disparities in imprisonment, unemployment, education and life expectancy as “racial inequality” or qualify the phrase as “perceived”; one argued the statistics supported direct wording, while another said the sentence described a political issue rather than the reality of inequality. They also debated whether to call inequality itself a human-rights issue or instead say that discrimination had been raised as an issue by specific groups, with participants questioning the clarity and sourcing of those descriptions.

2007.summary: Editors disputed whether John Howard’s biography should mention his family’s interests in New Guinea copra plantations, with some supporting a brief factual reference and others arguing the material belonged in his father’s article instead. Supporters linked the detail to coverage questioning Howard’s account of his upbringing, while opponents argued that his father’s dealings had no demonstrated relevance to Howard himself and that the mention could imply wrongdoing.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over which organizations belonged on the list: one favored generally limiting entries to groups with their own articles, while another said the criteria should remain looser, including to keep groups off the United States and Canada list and retain a single-campus fraternity. They also discussed using reliable sources that list Philippine fraternities and sororities to support including organizations without their own articles.

2007.summary: A contributor said the article’s description was repeatedly changed between “Long-Running” and labels such as “Man-Hating” or “Anti-Male,” and asked for the page to be locked; the passage does not explain the reasoning behind either wording.

2019.summary: Editors disputed how the judges table should represent Heidi Klum’s place in the lineup: one proposal put Sharon Osbourne and Mel B in the same column and Klum in a separate fourth-judge column, while another editor objected to merging the third- and fourth-judge fields for earlier seasons as confusing.

2011.summary: Editors debated whether to include reports interpreting Trump’s comments about Obama as race-related, alongside Trump’s denial. The disagreement concerned reporting public reactions without presenting speculation about his intentions as fact.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail the biography should give about the Justice Department’s housing discrimination allegations against Trump and his father: some argued that the specific claims about refusing to rent to Black applicants belonged in the article, while others favored a brief account of the lawsuit and settlement, with fuller details left to a separate legal-affairs article.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the biography should describe the Trump administration’s family-separation policy, with supporters citing extensive coverage and opponents arguing that it belonged in the separate account of his presidency. They also disputed its framing: some described it as a new policy enacted by Trump, while others argued it reflected stricter enforcement of existing immigration law and should not be presented as a distinct policy here.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over how much of the special counsel’s findings belonged in the article’s opening paragraph: one proposal sought a summary of several findings, while opponents argued that a detailed account would give the investigation too much space in a biography. Some favored a brief mention, but others argued that the article’s main text should be updated before deciding whether anything about the investigation belonged in its opening paragraph.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the biography should detail Trump’s call pressuring Georgia’s secretary of state to find votes, with some arguing it merited inclusion and others saying the specific episode was not important enough for this article. They also disputed how to describe the Capitol attack: some favored terms such as “attack” or “insurrection,” while others questioned whether “coup” was accurate and urged more qualified wording.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to mention the Abraham Accords in Trump’s biography: supporters argued they were a significant achievement associated with his administration, while opponents said the subject belonged in articles about his presidency and that the sources did not establish his personal role. Another debate concerned whether to describe Trump as far-right; supporters cited scholarly sources using the label, while opponents argued the sourcing was insufficiently clear and that other political descriptions were more appropriate.

2023.summary: Editors disputed whether the biography should report that the jury found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation but did not find that Carroll had proved rape. Some argued that omitting the rape finding would selectively present the verdict; others said it was unnecessary detail for a short biography and favored focusing on the liability finding and damages.

2024.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should say Trump was convicted of a felony before he was sentenced, with some arguing it should instead say a jury found him guilty. Others argued that the guilty verdict itself meets the legal definition of conviction, while noting that sentencing and further court proceedings remained pending.

2025.summary: Editors debated a proposal to replace the article’s detailed sections on Trump’s political style and rhetoric with a three-paragraph summary. Supporters called the section disorganized and the rewrite an improvement, while opponents argued it would remove substantial, long-standing material and sources and leave out important context.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe the administration’s policies toward transgender people as “persecution” in the article’s own voice, or to use less charged wording such as “restriction” or attribute the characterization to critics; supporters said the term reflected sources, while opponents called it value-laden and insufficiently established by reliable sources. Editors also debated whether to include a summary of media coverage questioning Trump’s mental health: supporters offered a sourced draft describing public and expert concerns, while opponents argued that the coverage did not establish a decline and that speculation should not be included.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how much statistical detail the article should include, with some calling for a shorter list of major records and others arguing that career statistics belonged in a player biography. One editor supported removing repeated or less important statistics but said career statistics should stay, while another pointed to the article’s length and favored keeping only major records.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether Cuba should be described as a democracy: some sources cited in the discussion treated it as democratic or as having democratic features, while others rejected that description because they said political opposition was not permitted. Some editors proposed presenting the competing assessments with sources in the article, while others argued that the opening paragraph should state categorically that Cuba was not a democracy.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should keep the title “God,” which some argued was the most useful title for readers seeking the monotheistic concept, or move to a narrower title and reserve “God” for a page covering other meanings. They also disputed whether the opening description should say “most people” believe in God or use the more limited phrase “many believe.”

Editors challenged claims in the economy section, including its account of trade growth after free-trade agreements, as misleading or unsupported; another editor said the trade claim should be documented because many observers attribute growth to those agreements. Editors also disputed whether to include a ranking of economic freedom: one argued that its criteria conveyed a viewpoint, while others said rankings could be included if they were verifiable and presented without questionable interpretation.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe Canada as a kingdom, particularly in its account of Confederation. Supporters argued that historical materials described Canada as a kingdom in its own right, while opponents said the term was contested and uncommon, favored “constitutional monarchy,” and noted that the proposed official name “Kingdom of Canada” was rejected.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “God Save the Queen” belonged in Canada’s information box as a royal anthem: opponents argued that it had no legal standing and was used as a ceremonial salute, not an anthem. Others argued that Canadian government sources called it the royal anthem by convention, and that it could be included while clarifying that it was not established by law.

2005.summary: Editors debated how much prominence to give dissenting views alongside the scientific consensus on global warming. They also disputed whether to include a graph projecting future storm costs, with objections that its predictions lacked a published scientific basis.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should describe scientists who reject a human contribution as only a small minority; some argued the qualifier carried an unsupported implication, while others said it simply emphasized their numbers.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should describe scientific disagreement: some favored saying that scientists disagree without estimating how many, while others wanted the text to identify the prevailing view and describe dissent as a minority position. They also disputed whether statements by science academies and research reviews justified claims about scientists’ overall views; some treated those sources as evidence of broad agreement, while others said they did not establish how many scientists agreed or disagreed.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “global warming” should be defined as a rise in temperatures without specifying its cause, or as warming caused by human activity. Those favoring a cause-neutral definition argued that the article should explain human influence separately, while others wanted the definition to reflect the view that human activity is the main driver of warming.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the main article should focus primarily on the physical science of warming, leaving politics to related articles, or center the wider political debate and treat science as one part of it. Supporters of the science-focused approach said the article was about a physical phenomenon, while advocates of a broader frame argued that political and social aspects were central to the wider issue.

2005.summary: Editors disputed which name to use for Clinton at different points in her life: one position favored Rodham before 1982, Clinton from 1982 to 1992, and Rodham Clinton afterward, while another favored switching to Clinton after her marriage. They also disagreed over whether to describe the name changes and their political context explicitly or simply use the proposed names in the article, with one editor questioning whether the sources supported explicit claims and the other seeking a separate section on the issue.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe Clinton as polarizing: some argued the label was subjective and not neutral, while others cited political-science research to support describing public responses to her as polarized. The related section also faced criticism for combining sources into editorial conclusions; its defenders said they would trim explanations and keep claims closely tied to what sources said.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the biography should mention the FBI’s examination of Clinton’s handling of classified information, with some arguing that the examination was noteworthy and others saying the separate article already covered it and that more context was needed. They also disputed how to describe the activity, with one editor distinguishing a broad probe from a formal investigation.

2016.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should state in its own voice that Clinton was the Democratic Party’s presumptive nominee or attribute that label to news organizations; they also debated whether her status and the claim that she would be the first woman nominated were premature before the convention vote. Editors also disagreed over how to describe classified information on Clinton’s private email server: some wanted the article to state that classified material was present, while others argued that wording needed to distinguish information later designated classified from information classified when it passed through the server.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether the article’s infobox should classify the Iraq War as part of the broader war on terrorism or leave that claim for discussion in the article. One position was that the classification reflected the stated view of the U.S. and allied governments; another argued that presenting it in the infobox treated a contested government claim as settled and favored including the competing interpretations in the article text.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the infobox’s result field should retain multiple outcome points or replace them with a link to the aftermath section; one side cited guidance against detailed infoboxes, while the other wanted key information kept readily visible.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to date the Democratic Party to Jefferson’s 1790s party, which it was said to trace its roots to, or to the party formed in the 1820s under Andrew Jackson. They also disputed the specific founding date: proposals included 1820 and 1828, while another editor argued that the party emerged gradually and that a precise date was uncertain.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the infobox should describe the party as center-left, center to center-left, or give no political-position label, with some arguing that a broad coalition of factions could not be captured by one label. Supporters pointed to academic sources that explicitly call the party center-left, while opponents argued that some cited sources did not directly support that wording and that other sources described the party as centrist.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Wikipedia’s open editing should be more tightly controlled: one argued that its permissive approach allowed too much poor writing and inaccurate information, while another defended open editing as central to how the site works and to its value as a resource.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should call Wikipedia an encyclopedia or describe it as a website and knowledge database. Supporters argued that “encyclopedia” was more useful and descriptive, while an opposing editor said the label could imply a level of reliability that Wikipedia might not meet.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should mention Larry Sanger’s claim that he co-founded Wikipedia with Jimmy Wales; supporters argued the claim belonged in the article, while one editor said it did not belong in the sentence describing who created the Wikimedia Foundation. The opposing view was that the article should not turn that brief description into a discussion of the founding dispute, though another editor suggested using “a founder” instead of crediting Wales alone.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should call the hijackers “terrorists” in its own voice or attribute that label to the U.S. government and other sources; one editor argued the term was pejorative, while another said avoiding it was itself not neutral. The disagreement also concerned whether a more neutral description, such as “militants,” should be used instead of the label.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over calling the attacks “terrorist”: some said the label makes a value judgment, while others argued that its widespread use by reliable sources supports including it. Editors seeking more discussion of criticism of the official account proposed a separate section, while others argued that the main article should summarize such claims and direct readers to a dedicated article rather than include every detail.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should use “terrorist” in its own narration or attribute the label to sources, with some objecting that the term was pejorative and others arguing its widespread use made attribution unnecessary. They also disputed whether the article’s brief section should focus on conspiracy theories or more broadly describe people questioning the official account, while some argued the section should remain a summary of a separate article.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should call the perpetrators “terrorists” in its own narration or use the more descriptive term “hijackers” and attribute the label to sources. Those favoring “terrorists” argued that mainstream, reliable sources used the term, while opponents said it was judgmental and that “hijackers” was more neutral.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe challenges to the accepted account of AIDS and incorporate material from a separate article presenting dissenting views. One editor called for acknowledging disputes over AIDS’s cause, diagnosis and treatments while giving the mainstream account priority; another argued that the proposed merge would add little and that the main article already covered the dissenting position adequately.

Editors disagreed over whether Kerry’s first shrapnel injury should be described as minor. Supporters of that wording said the evidence supported it; opponents argued that the article should give the treatment details without drawing that conclusion, and that the account describing the injury as minor was not adequately corroborated.

2016.summary: Editors debated whether rows should be colour-coded to distinguish routes running 24 hours from those running only on weekends, with some saying the colours could make the list easier to understand. Others opposed the change, arguing it was unnecessary, repeated information already in the notes, could make searching and citing harder, or raised accessibility concerns.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should list every appearance of the recurring helix symbol or include only appearances they considered significant to characters or the story. Supporters argued that editors could not know which sightings mattered and favored a complete record, while opponents said a full list would add trivia rather than useful reference material.

2022.summary: Editors disputed whether the Chutia kingdom should be listed as a predecessor of the Ahom kingdom: one argued that the Ahom kingdom was established in 1228 and absorbed the Chutia kingdom only in the 16th century, while another cited research placing the Chutiyas among the settled peoples of the region by the 14th century and described Ahom expansion after that period.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe the view that Hitler was a sincere Christian as a small minority interpretation or omit it as too marginal for prominence. Others argued that the interpretation deserved mention as a significant minority view, pointing to academic authors who supported it and to the article’s stated debate over his beliefs.

2006.summary: Some editors argued that “allegations” misdescribed the article’s subject: the policies being discussed were not in dispute, but whether comparing them to apartheid was fair, so they favored a title centered on the comparison. Others argued that dropping “allegations” would imply Israel practiced apartheid, and maintained that the article should describe the claims and their critics rather than present the comparison as established fact.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening summary gave enough space to the case for comparing Israeli policies with South African apartheid, including claims about separate rights and privileges, or gave too much detail to objections to the comparison. They also disputed the title: some argued that “Allegations” cast doubt on the subject, while others said removing it would present a contested claim as fact.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article title should describe comparisons between Israeli policies and South African apartheid or also cover sources arguing that Israel may be committing the international crime of apartheid; some said “analogy” excluded that legal discussion, while others warned a broader title could imply that the disputed connection was established.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether the article’s opening paragraph should describe RT as repeatedly called a propaganda tool, with supporters arguing that the criticism was well sourced and belonged in the summary, while opponents said this wording overstated a subset of views and selectively represented the article’s reception. They also disagreed over whether the summary needed a source analyzing how widespread the criticism was, rather than relying on multiple sources that used the label.

2015.summary: Editors disputed whether criticism of RT belonged in the opening paragraph or in a separate section, with one side arguing its prominence made the article read like an opinion piece and another saying criticism from reliable sources should appear near the start. They also disagreed over whether to describe RT as “state-funded” or use alternatives such as “publicly funded” or “government-funded,” which one editor considered more neutral and another rejected as inaccurate for RT.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe *Reputation* as hip-hop-influenced, with one arguing that sources supported the label and another saying the album had some hip-hop influence but not enough to feature it prominently in the opening paragraph. They also disputed whether the opening paragraph needed to clarify that *Lover* was named the world’s best-selling studio album of 2019, with one editor calling the phrasing potentially misleading and others arguing it was accurate as written.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to name Ariana Grande in a sentence attributing to a music critic the view that Swift helped make space for later pop stars: one editor considered Grande’s inclusion misleading without her own statement of influence, while another argued the claim was clearly attributed and removing her could misrepresent the critic’s words.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should foreground Swift’s sales, billionaire status and touring record or mention those achievements later; some called their prominent placement promotional, while others argued that the milestones explain her influence. They also disputed descriptions of her as influential and a subject of widespread public interest: critics considered such claims generic or fan-oriented, while supporters argued that her cultural impact and popularity were well documented and worth stating.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over how strongly the article should present biological explanations of sexual orientation: one argued that prenatal hormones had the strongest scientific support, while another objected to language that treated biological accounts as conclusive or dismissed other explanations. The latter editor urged room for psychological or environmental influences, while the biological account’s proponent challenged the inclusion of what they saw as unsupported claims about those influences.

2006.summary: One editor argued that homosexuality should be called a disorder because, in their view, it does not serve reproduction; they distinguished this from claiming that it was a disease or that anything was wrong with gay people. Other editors objected that the label suggests a malfunction and noted that mainstream psychological organizations do not classify homosexuality as a disorder.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the criticism of Rubio’s account of his parents’ immigration history and how much detail to include. One editor argued that the article should briefly note Rubio’s response, while another sought a fuller account, saying the shorter version left out information needed for balance.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether leaders who took office before their countries became independent should be dated from their appointment or from independence; some favored one consistent rule, while another argued that continued service before recognition should count. They also disputed whether personal honorifics such as “Sir,” “Sheikh” and “Ayatollah” belonged beside leaders’ names, with one position calling them outside the list’s scope and another arguing that familiar titles should remain.

Editors objected to material they described as promotional, copied from other websites, and unsupported by sources, and one editor questioned whether a claim about letters from admirers could be included. In the filmography, editors disagreed over including a co-stars column and other extra details: one argued that such information was trivia unless supported and relevant, while another invited sourced observations about recurring collaborations.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Iraqi Turkmen should be described as a dialect of Turkish or South Azerbaijani, or as a distinct language; one editor argued there was no separate Iraqi Turkic language, while another cited sources supporting differing classifications. The discussion also raised whether the article should present these competing classifications rather than choose one.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening should describe Melchizedek as a micronation directly linked to banking fraud or as an entity aspiring to ecclesiastical statehood that licensed banks involved in fraud. They also disputed what diplomatic recognition from the Central African Republic meant: one editor cited it as established recognition, while another argued that such recognition did not establish the entity’s legitimacy.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over which flags to show for races such as the European and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix: one proposed using the European and Abu Dhabi flags, while another restored the existing flag pending a wider discussion.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the main Islam article should include a section on penalties for apostasy and blasphemy, or instead link to a separate article on apostasy. Those arguing for inclusion described apostasy as important to Islam, while others said the detail did not belong in a broad overview and should be handled consistently with other religion articles.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should have a section on criticism of Islam: some argued that documented criticism belongs in the overview, while others felt the section made the article more negative than comparable religion articles. They also disputed how to define its scope, with one view calling for criticism to be distinguished by whether it addressed Islamic beliefs, practices, communities, or governments, and for specific historical and cultural contexts to be made clear.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Sunni and Shia proportions in the article, with some arguing that exact percentages lacked reliable support and others seeking wording that conveyed Sunni numerical majority without making the groups sound equal in size. A separate dispute concerned whether to present the Five Pillars as shared by Sunni and Shia Muslims or describe distinct practices for each; editors challenged the wording and sources used to support those descriptions.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether discussion of slavery and concubinage, including rules about sex with enslaved women, belonged in the article’s “Family life” section or should be covered elsewhere; some considered it relevant to household relations, while others argued that the section gave the topic too much weight. The archived discussion of proposed text closed without agreement on whether to include it.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Islam’s article should retain a separate “Criticism” section: one argued it should be removed in favor of links to dedicated critique articles, while another said such a section was relevant for major religions.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Nelliel belonged in the list’s Espada section: one argued she should not be grouped there because she was introduced by another name and a different character held the same rank, while another supported listing her as an Espada because she had previously held that rank.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to call the events a war or a conflict and whether the title should name Israel and Lebanon or Israel and Hezbollah; some favored the latter pairing because they viewed Hezbollah as the other main combatant, while others said the fighting involved both countries. They also disputed whether the Israeli soldiers were “captured” or “kidnapped”: some saw capture as more neutral for soldiers taken in armed conflict, while others argued kidnapping better conveyed an unlawful taking for ransom.

2017.summary: Editors debated whether allegations about Moore’s sexual conduct with teenagers should be included in the article, with some urging inclusion based on extensive reporting and others calling for caution because the claims were disputed and coverage was still developing. They also disagreed over whether the allegations belonged in the opening paragraph: supporters argued their prominence in news coverage warranted prominent placement, while opponents warned that doing so would give recent, unproven claims too much weight.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should be retitled to describe the events as an anti-Muslim pogrom, with proponents citing academic works and opponents favoring the broader, religiously neutral term “violence” and arguing that Hindus were also victims. They also disputed whether scholarly accounts describing the violence as preplanned and involving state officials should be included alongside accounts of official investigations and their findings.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether shared genetic patterns between southwestern Europeans and Yoruba samples supported gene flow from Africa, or whether the study’s charts and alternative explanations argued against that interpretation. They also disputed whether European branches of Y-chromosome group E should be described as evidence of ancestry from sub-Saharan Africa or treated as lineages with North African or West Asian origins.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to state as fact that about 150 Mujahideen fighters fought with the NLA, or to describe their involvement as an allegation because some sources question or qualify it. They also disputed whether NATO belonged in the article’s list of belligerents: some editors cited NATO actions against rebels, while others argued those actions did not make NATO an ally of Macedonia.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe studies by the Ramazzini Foundation that reported possible cancer effects: some sought more detail on the findings and researchers’ responses to criticism, while others argued for a shorter account centered on assessments that challenged the studies’ methods and results. They also disputed whether to include a lengthy statement from New Zealand’s food-safety authority criticizing the research, with some favoring the full quotation and others preferring a shorter summary as more focused and readable.

Editors disagreed over whether World War II bombings and other violence by states should be included as terrorism: one position urged inclusion where sources described acts as terror, while others argued that terror bombing or wartime crimes should not automatically be classified as terrorism. The disagreement also concerned the article’s scope, with one proposal seeking coverage of state terrorism alongside non-state groups and another favoring a history focused on non-state terrorism, with only brief treatment of state terrorism and terror bombing.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Maduro remained president after being taken into U.S. custody: some said he remained legally in office until Venezuelan authorities removed him, while others argued that his tenure had ended when Rodríguez became acting president. They also disputed how to describe his seizure, with some favoring “capture” as the term used by most news sources and others arguing for “abduction” or “kidnapping” to convey their view that the action was unlawful.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Wade’s article on COVID-19 origins should link to a page about misinformation or to an account of investigations into the lab-leak hypothesis. Some argued that his claims about a deliberately engineered virus and scientists suppressing dissent were misinformation; others said he discussed a possible accidental release and that applying the misinformation label lacked adequate secondary-source support. The disagreement also involved whether describing the lab-leak hypothesis as misinformation wrongly treated an accidental lab release and deliberate engineering as the same claim.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over adding a photograph: one wanted an image, including a temporary still from a music video, while another removed it as non-free and said a freely usable replacement was needed for the article.

Editors disagreed over how to present reactions to Wright’s sermons: one argued that the responses section leaned too heavily toward defenders and failed to explain critics’ objections, while still supporting inclusion of criticism from reliable sources. Others argued that the section should be limited to people with a direct connection to Wright or the controversy, rather than collecting opinions from commentators with little connection to either.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the hardware section should retain its extensive technical specifications or present a shorter, more accessible overview. Some argued that detailed figures were important information and should not simply be removed, while others said that many specifications lacked context and did not belong in an article about a consumer product.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Syrian National Council should be presented as a rival government alongside Bashar al-Assad’s government, with some arguing it lacked a rival leadership and governing authority and others saying it represented the opposition and deserved recognition in the article. That disagreement extended to the infobox: some wanted it to show only the Syrian Arab Republic, while others argued that the opposition’s territorial control and foreign recognition justified a split presentation.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe the Golan Heights as “occupied,” “disputed,” or both, and whether those labels should appear as statements or be attributed to governments and other sources; some also argued that the article should say the territory was Syrian, while others challenged whether cited sources established that claim. A related disagreement concerned how much prominence to give sources describing the area as occupied Syrian territory, with editors disputing whether references to particular governments and international bodies supported that wording.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Robert Spencer’s writing could be used directly to describe criticism of the Quran: one view treated his work as a reliable source for critical viewpoints, while another called it a primary source and argued that the article should rely on scholarly assessments of such criticism. The discussion also questioned whether his work had been reviewed by scholars and whether critics’ prominence alone was enough to establish a source’s reliability.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail the opening paragraph should give Luther’s writings against Jews and their later use by the Nazis; some wanted examples of his proposed actions included there, while others argued that a brief mention of their use, with fuller discussion below, would suffice. They also disputed whether the wording should spell out Luther’s anti-Jewish statements or describe their later use without examples, with one editor arguing that readers needed to know what the Nazis had drawn on.

Editors disagreed over whether the cartoons should be displayed prominently at the top of the article or shown farther down, with one position arguing that readers need to see them and another favoring a less prominent placement. Supporters of moving them also proposed featuring an image of protests instead, while opponents said the cartoons were central to the article and necessary for readers to understand the controversy.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether close state poll results justified labeling a state as having majority support: one argued that Wisconsin’s result established only a plurality, while another said its reported support level should count as a majority. They also differed over whether to show margins of error in the results: one editor argued they were needed to support claims about the polls, while another said including them made the table confusing.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should classify Ahmadinejad as an antisemitic person or discuss antisemitism without applying that label to him. Some argued that his remarks and how sources characterized them justified the label, while others said opposition to Zionism and Israel was not by itself proof of hostility toward Jews and that the classification lacked adequate reliable sourcing.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe Ahmadinejad as calling for Israel to be “wiped off the map” as an established statement or signal that the wording and translation were disputed. One side pointed to reliable sources reporting the call, while another argued that the cited sources did not substantiate that wording and that the translation controversy needed context.

Editors disagreed over whether the 2006 parliamentary recognition of the Québécois as a nation belonged near the opening of the article or later in the introduction, and whether uncertainty about its meaning should be noted there. They also disputed whether the recognition described Quebec itself or its people, and whether it could be presented as a straightforward fact or needed context about competing political interpretations.

2008.summary: Editors disputed how to describe English’s legal use in Quebec: some favored labels such as “quasi-official,” while others argued that such terms overstated its status and preferred describing specific rights and services instead. They also disagreed over whether a federal motion recognizing the Québécois as a nation could be described as recognizing the people of Quebec as a nation, with some arguing that the wording could include all residents and others distinguishing the province’s population from the Québécois.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to retain a section about misconduct allegations: some argued that the allegations were unsubstantiated and did not belong on the page, while others said the coverage and investigation made them notable, though the section should be shortened or rewritten. They also disputed how much to explain the 1945 championship selection: some favored a concise account naming the American Football Coaches Association, while others wanted the Blue Ribbon Commission’s role and the retrospective award process explained.

2009.summary: Editors disputed whether the victims should be described outright as informers or whether that claim should be attributed to Meda Ryan and qualified, since contributors questioned whether the article established it for all those killed. They also disagreed over how to frame the motive: some accounts were cited as supporting Ryan’s informer explanation, while others were presented as linking the killings to Michael O’Neill’s death or suggesting sectarian violence.

2007.summary: Editors disputed whether to list the Wii Points cost beside each game in the tables or show prices in another way. Supporters said per-game costs were useful information and easier to present in the tables, while opponents argued that listing prices made the article too much like a price guide and repeated information that could be summarized.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include “Rhapsody Originals”: one argued that limited success or fame was not a reason to exclude them, while another said an additional source was needed to support their release.
