2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should mention an online death hoax: one noted that the Associated Press had covered it and said they would not remove a properly sourced addition, while others argued it was trivial and that repeating it would give attention to the hoax.

2017.summary: Editors differed over whether a line about a vice-presidential vacancy belonged with the entries around it or in the paragraph about vacancies before the 25th Amendment; it was restored in that paragraph.

2009.summary: Editors disputed which names to use for the Campos and Manor teams after FIA releases and a report from Autosport gave conflicting versions, including Campos Grand Prix, Campos Meta, Manor F1 Team and Manor Grand Prix. Some argued the reports could not be ranked reliably, while another editor proposed using the names from a later entry list for the table and keeping the Campos article under a different name until the team’s naming was clearer.

2010.summary: Editors discussed shortening the article by combining tables; one also suggested separating the results from the season overview, while another supported combining some tables but opposed splitting those sections into separate articles.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s use of “FYROM” blurred the distinction between that abbreviation and the full provisional reference, with one editor calling the abbreviation incorrect and offensive and others defending its use, including when introducing it or quoting sources. They also disputed how to classify countries whose official statements or documents used different names for the Republic of Macedonia, with conflicting reports about Mexico and Congo leading to calls for further confirmation or leaving cases unresolved.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over how the article should characterize medical evidence: some argued that professional bodies’ opposition to routine newborn circumcision did not mean they found no net benefit, while another editor read their statements as showing that benefits did not outweigh harms. They also disputed how much detail about potential benefits belonged near the beginning of the article, with one editor arguing that the summary should represent arguments in favor and another saying those benefits were repeated elsewhere and not balanced by discussion of harms.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should state broadly that circumcision is painful or qualify the claim by distinguishing procedures performed with and without anesthesia. Some argued that circumcision without anesthesia is painful and often performed without it, while others objected that a blanket statement could imply all procedures are painful even with anesthesia and pointed to reports describing procedures as painless.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening summary should describe arguments for and against circumcision, including which claims to include and how much space each side should receive. They also disputed how prominently to present the World Health Organization’s HIV recommendation and whether the summary accurately described the U.S. health agency’s position alongside it.

2009.summary: Editors disputed whether information about circumcision and HIV prevention belonged in the article’s opening paragraph: one argued its public-health relevance was limited in many countries and its placement gave it too much prominence, while another said the article should reflect the issue’s global relevance.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether HIV prevention deserved its own paragraph in the opening paragraph: one argued that health sources give it substantial attention, while another said its relevance was limited for most English-speaking readers and it belonged in the article body. They also disputed whether presenting equal numbers of arguments for and against circumcision produced balanced coverage or distorted the factual picture.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should focus on recent reviews of circumcision and HIV, or retain a broader account of arguments for and against circumcision and medical organizations’ positions. Supporters of the review-focused version argued that older sources were unsuitable for summarizing medical claims, while supporters of the broader version said it better covered the article’s main issues and controversy.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe preventive circumcision as controversial generally: one argued that this would overstate disagreement, since the cited criticism concerned routine circumcision in developed countries, while voluntary adult circumcision for HIV prevention was presented as less controversial. They also disputed how to describe the ethical debate, with one editor objecting that wording about disease prevention, group rights and religious freedom was not supported by the cited source and arguing for language about informed consent and children’s rights instead.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should state without qualification that circumcision does not affect sexual function, sensation, desire, or pleasure. Some argued that the literature was inconclusive and the wording should be qualified; others said major medical organizations and research supported the claim and that contrary views should not be given undue weight.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over how much the article should discuss press comparisons between O’Leary and Donald Trump, with one position describing the similarities as superficial and warning that the comparison could misrepresent O’Leary’s political views. The opposing position argued that frequent comparisons across the political spectrum were worth noting, provided the article also explained differences between the two men.

2007.summary: Editors debated whether to add monsters seen at a game demo to the article’s roster, including entries described as only probably playable. Others argued against including them before official announcements, noting that Atari had warned that some demo information might not match the final game.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening description should call the group jihadist without qualification or note that some Muslim scholars reject applying that term to it; suggestions included an explanatory footnote, while others argued the term was established in English usage and needed no qualification. They also debated how specifically to summarize criticism in the opening paragraph: some wanted explicit mention that Muslim communities say the group does not represent Islam, while others favored a broader statement that its actions and claims were widely criticized.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should have a separate section describing the group’s religious arguments for slavery and other acts, or whether that material belonged in other articles or existing sections. Some argued that a dedicated section gave those arguments too much weight, while others said the group’s religious reasoning should be covered in a careful, properly contextualized way.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Carano as “fired” by Lucasfilm or say she would not return to the role, with one position emphasizing reports that she was not under an active deal and the other pointing to coverage that called it a firing. They also disputed how to describe her shared Instagram post: some favored including the full post, while others preferred a summary of news coverage, which variously described it as comparing conservatives or the divided political climate to the persecution of Jews in Nazi Germany.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a section on China’s market reforms, with supporters arguing it showed how communism was changing and opponents saying the country-specific details belonged elsewhere and did not fit an overview of communist ideas and movements. They also disputed whether describing the reforms as a development of communism wrongly assumed that China’s current policies represented communism, or merely noted that the ruling party called itself communist.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the album’s genre should be described as thrash metal alone or as heavy metal with thrash elements. They also debated whether to mention audio clipping: one editor said forum discussions were not enough support, while another later argued that coverage from multiple sources justified a section on the sound issues.

Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe rumors about Obama as false, rather than report them as allegations without that label. One editor argued that the label was justified when claims were demonstrably false, while another said it could wrongly characterize allegations for which the article had not established falsity.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should say that non-Jewish Israelis enjoy full political and civic equality; one objected that the wording was misleading in light of discrimination. Other comments distinguished the ability to vote from equal treatment in practice, and one editor suggested describing both formal rights and discrimination rather than making an unqualified claim.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the country article should summarize human rights criticisms, including reports about treatment in the occupied territories: some argued that notable findings from rights groups belonged in a balanced section, while others warned against singling Israel out when other countries also faced criticism. They also disputed describing Israel as the region’s only democracy, with one view arguing that a Freedom House assessment supported the claim and another noting that Turkey and Lebanon were also considered democracies by some sources.

2007.summary: Editors disputed the introduction’s comparison of Israel with most Middle Eastern countries, with one editor arguing that the wording made the passage sound less objective and added little useful information. Another editor defended the comparison as a source-supported way to describe how Israel’s form of government and development differed from those of most countries in the region.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening and infobox should describe Jerusalem: some wanted to call it Israel’s capital while noting that other countries do not recognize it as such, while others argued the wording should state plainly that it is the capital. They also disputed whether that lack of international recognition merited prominent treatment in the article or was already adequately covered elsewhere.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening history should describe the region as the birthplace of the Jewish people or also recognize Palestinian connections, and whether its ancient history should focus mainly on Jewish kingdoms. They also disputed whether the account of the 1947 partition plan and the 1948 war unfairly assigned blame to Arab leaders, and whether the number of Palestinians expelled or displaced should be stated more specifically.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a controversy involving Vanessa Hudgens in the film article: some said it was no longer relevant or belonged on her own page, while others argued it affected her involvement in the film. They also disputed whether Kelsi should be counted among the film’s starring characters, with one side pointing to her promotion and merchandise and the other noting that the film’s poster and cited press coverage named six stars.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening description should call Breitbart far-right or use right-wing or conservative. Supporters cited published sources describing it as far-right, while opponents pointed to sources calling it conservative and argued that far-right was too contentious.

2017.summary: Editors requested removing “Archie Bunker’s Place” and “Bosom Buddies” from the list, saying the programs did not belong there.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over how to format the driver list: one proposal was to list Ken Schrader and Jon Wood separately, as they are in the game, while keeping cars with different drivers across game versions grouped together.

Editors disagreed over how strongly the opening should characterize scientific criticism: some favored saying most of the film’s scientific claims had been refuted, while others argued that “most” and “refuted” overstated what the cited critiques established. They also debated whether the first sentence should call the film “controversial” or use a more interpretive label such as “polemical,” with objections that such wording could impose a viewpoint.

2012.summary: Editors disputed whether to count the 1902 match as an official meeting, a choice that changed the head-to-head totals. One position relied on claims that the Spanish federation did not recognize the tournament; others pointed to published 86–86 counts and noted that the federation did not publish a record of the teams’ meetings.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over accounts of the 11–1 match: one cited a report based on a Barcelona player’s recollection that described hard play and an aggressive crowd, while another argued that English-language sources instead linked the match to political pressure after Barcelona fans jeered Madrid players. They also disputed whether the cited report was reliable and whether claims about what happened should be presented as established or qualified as claims.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a newsletter’s personal Christmas greeting as evidence relevant to who wrote the disputed newsletters: one argued the detail mattered, while another said it risked implying disputed authorship without analysis from a secondary source.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe a 1986 church document’s discussion of responsibility for same-sex activity: one interpretation said sexual orientation did not lessen culpability, while another argued the document only rejected treating such activity as automatically compelled and without blame. The discussion also noted that the document allowed individual circumstances to reduce or remove culpability, making an absolute summary disputed.

2007.summary: Editors disputed how the opening paragraph should describe the Holocaust’s scope: one proposed wording emphasized that many scholars define it as the genocide of Jews, while another included scholars who define it to include some or all other persecuted groups. The disagreement also concerned whether the wording should foreground exclusion or make the range of scholarly definitions clearer.

Editors disagreed over whether the opening should frame the controversy around the false credentials themselves or around The New Yorker’s correction of its earlier article. They also disputed whether wording that said the credentials were “forged” or “faked” accurately described the issue, with some preferring wording that said he had lied about them.

Editors disagreed over which songs belonged on the album: some favored the record label’s published track list, while others argued it was outdated and proposed using tracks they said 50 Cent had confirmed, or separating confirmed songs from rumored ones. They also disputed whether “I Get Money” was part of the album or a separate promotional release, with editors citing conflicting claims and sources.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the album’s promotion deserved a dedicated section: some said it took up too much space and should be shortened or removed, while another noted that some editors wanted the information kept and suggested limiting it to a few sentences.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the history section should state that Armenians were killed in the Armenian Genocide or qualify the wording to describe the events as forced migration whose classification as genocide is disputed. They also differed on how much space the Turkey article should give the Turkish government’s rejection of the genocide label and to claims that some historians dispute it, with one editor arguing that a brief mention of the government’s position was enough.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether ethnic-group percentages belonged in Turkey’s opening paragraph and infobox: one side favored figures from the CIA World Factbook, while another argued that uncertain estimates should be left out, especially where Turkey had no official ethnic census. They also disputed how to present a KONDA survey: one editor treated 9% as a minimum estimate for Kurds, while others said the study’s stated estimate was about 15.6% for Kurds and Zaza combined.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the expanded article, particularly its culture and economy sections, needed substantial shortening and material moved to separate articles, or whether its length and detail were reasonable compared with other countries’ articles. They also disagreed over whether relations with the Kurdistan Region of Iraq merited a sentence in Turkey’s foreign-relations section or were too detailed for the country overview.

2015.summary: Editors disputed how the article described Armenian deaths and competing totals: one proposed attributing a high estimate to Armenians and some international sources while also giving Turkey’s lower figure, whereas others objected that this wording understated broad scholarly acceptance of genocide and challenged the cited death estimates. They also debated labeling Kurdish-inhabited southeastern areas “Turkish Kurdistan” and showing them on a map; supporters called the term commonly used and the map useful, while an opponent warned that its borders were imprecise and could confuse readers.

2017.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening description should call Turkey a democracy: one side proposed the more specific term parliamentary democracy, while another cited sources questioning its democratic status; a later close favored parliamentary republic without calling it a democracy. They also disputed how to summarize wartime genocides, with some favoring one concise sentence about Armenian, Assyrian and Pontic Greek victims, while others argued for distinctions and mention of the Turkish government’s denial.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail the Turkey article’s human-rights section should retain: one proposed moving material to a separate article and shortening the section, while others objected that the changes removed relevant information, including material about destroyed villages and events in Syria. Editors also disputed whether to include an image related to the Armenian Genocide; supporters described it as informative and historically significant, while an opponent argued that the event was too indirectly related to the country article and was already mentioned in its text.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep the article under “Meghan Markle,” which some argued remained the name readers and sources knew, or use her new duchess title, which others favored for consistency with other royal biographies. They also disputed whether “Meghan, Duchess of Sussex” was an accurate form for the title, with some arguing that the wording was associated with divorced duchesses and others defending its use.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should include negative material such as racism allegations and a restraining order: one argued these topics were unnecessary or settled, while another said they belonged in a fuller account of Hilton and pointed to a link about the restraining order. The discussion also showed disagreement over the article’s overall framing, with one editor seeking a balanced account of both positive and negative aspects and another rejecting the restoration of a controversies section.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over who belonged in the article’s roster: one position was to include everyone on FCW’s talent page, including performers also appearing on WWE’s main shows or NXT, while another was to list only wrestlers who were part of FCW’s developmental roster. The disagreement also involved whether appearing in FCW programming was enough for inclusion, or whether performers no longer in development should be left off.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over whether figures from RSSSF, which uses a different counting method from IFFHS, should appear in a separate table or alongside the main figures in one table. They also differed over ranking players: one editor argued that conflicting goal totals made rankings unreliable, while another favored ranked tables based on major sources.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “Get Up” and “I Get It In” should appear as singles from the album: one argued that, because they were not on the album, they should be listed only as promotional singles, while another said they were singles regardless of whether they appeared on it.

Editors disagreed over whether the list of unverified age claims should be limited to people in high-income countries, with one position favoring an eligibility rule to keep the list manageable. The opposing position argued that claims should not be excluded because of a person’s country and that cited claims should be presented even when they had not been verified.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how long to keep people on the list when recent reports did not confirm they were still alive: one proposed removal after one or two months without a new birthday report, while another favored allowing more than a year. They also disagreed over whether Gertrude Weaver should remain listed based on her last report, which showed her as having reached 110.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the list should include and rank people whose ages appeared in news reports but had not been verified by a longevity research group: some favored separating or excluding those claims, while others argued that reliable reporting could support inclusion even without that group’s confirmation. They also debated whether a ranked table would misleadingly suggest a complete worldwide order, or could be retained if it reflected a cited outside ranking or was clearly qualified.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed about whether published reports from reliable sources were enough to include a person’s claimed age, or whether the claim needed validation by a specialist organization focused on longevity. They also disputed whether the incomplete list could support claims about people’s exact worldwide ranks: some argued the ranks were misleading without evidence that the list covered everyone, while another proposal was to keep the numbers only as labels for the entries.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether reliable reporting alone justified listing an extremely old person whose age exceeded records recognized by organizations such as Guinness, or whether such a claim should be excluded as unsubstantiated; they also disputed whether to cap the article at 100 entries and how to describe that limit. For people whose recent lives or deaths were uncertain, editors debated whether forum posts could establish that someone was alive or dead, and whether a missing recent confirmation or indirect clues justified removing a person from the list.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Maria Emilia Quesada belonged on the list: one editor argued that several reliable reports supported including her, while another said an unverified claim of such extreme age belonged elsewhere. Some editors considered reliable reporting sufficient, while others argued that claims of extreme longevity require stronger, specialist verification before being presented on the list.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether several people should remain on the list when their entries relied on sources one editor considered unreliable or incomplete; another editor objected to the removal of two entries but said they would not contest it.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Fauja Singh should be included: one said he was still living at 114 and had been left off the list, while another said his age was unverified.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the page should be renamed to describe a wider X-Men universe, including films such as Deadpool that one editor said were not X-Men movies, or remain about a film series whose spin-offs belonged together. Some argued that Deadpool was part of the same film series as the X-Men and Wolverine films, while others distinguished sharing a fictional universe from being part of the X-Men film series.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether television shows such as Legion belonged in the article: some argued they were separate from the films unless a connection was demonstrated, while others said the shows were installments in the wider franchise. That disagreement fed into a proposed title change: supporters wanted a name broad enough to cover related television, while opponents argued that “franchise” could imply coverage of X-Men media beyond the film-related material and favored keeping the article focused on the films.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over which tracks counted as singles for the album’s summary box: some treated tracks released for sale and confirmed by reliable sources as singles, while others wanted to list only three tracks and regarded “Beautiful” and “Old Time’s Sake” as previews rather than singles. They also disputed whether less-established review sites met the standards for inclusion, with some editors arguing that a site with multiple writers qualified and others questioning its professionalism and reliability.

Editors disputed how the elimination chart should rank contestants eliminated in the same week: some favored a shared range such as 12th–13th because the show had not established their vote totals, while another argued that the order of elimination showed who ranked lower. They also disagreed over whether the chart should use separate colors for the bottom two and bottom three, with supporters saying the distinction mattered and opponents arguing the labels were sufficient and the similar shades made the chart harder to read.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the health-effects section should include organizations’ concerns about possible nicotine addiction and a path from vaping to smoking, or distinguish those hypothetical risks from effects observed in research. Some argued that the article should reflect major health organizations’ positions and avoid using individual studies to challenge them; others said those precautionary views should be presented alongside research on the current evidence, which they felt was being left out.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should put health effects before construction and usage: some argued that health dominated reliable coverage and deserved prominence, while others said the page should first explain the consumer device and how it works. The disagreement also concerned applying medical-article guidance to the whole page, since some supported that approach based on health-focused sourcing while others viewed health as one aspect of a consumer-product article.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to mark the Sound Five as absent from the upcoming game or leave their status uncertain: one editor said there was no evidence they were included, while another argued against marking them absent because they might still be added. A later reply said they had been ruled out, citing a stated roster limit of 35 characters and a leaked roster of that size.

2021.summary: Editors debated whether the article’s opening paragraph should stay at one sentence or be expanded to three or four. Supporters of keeping it short said it introduced Elizabeth without overloading the paragraph or listing every country; those favoring a longer version argued that a one-sentence opening was too abrupt and could not provide enough context.

2022.summary: After Elizabeth II’s death, editors debated whether the article’s main photograph should show her as a younger monarch or retain a more recent image. Supporters of an earlier portrait favored its formal, historical representation, while supporters of the recent image said it better reflected the Queen people recognized and her long reign.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the season article should include car-launch schedules and detailed testing information: some argued for including those details, while others said the page should focus on a balanced account of the season and omit minor or duplicative material. They also disputed whether the article’s calendar should mention uncertainty about the Bahrain race, with some supporting a note about the threat to the event and others considering such forward-looking information speculative.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the FA Cup runner-up or the next-highest league team should receive a Europa League place when the cup winner also finished fifth; one editor argued the league team should qualify, while another questioned whether that interpretation was documented.

Editors disagreed over how much detail the plot summary should retain: one wanted major locations, characters and outcomes preserved, while another argued for a shorter account that omitted such detail unless essential. They also debated whether character descriptions should include toy biographies when the film gives little personality information; some supported using them, while others said material about the toys belonged on separate character pages.

2010.summary: Editors disputed how to present Enthiran’s first-week box-office figures alongside Dabangg’s, including whether the article should compare the films’ collections. One editor cautioned that net collections could mislead because of differences in entertainment taxes and said comparable gross figures were unavailable, while another argued the tax difference should be explained and the figures compared on that basis.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Watts or his blog as promoting climate-change denial, or instead use terms such as “skeptic”; they disputed how reliable sources used those labels and whether “denier” was too contentious. They also disagreed about putting Michael Mann’s characterization of the blog in the opening paragraph: supporters said it conveyed the blog’s significance, while opponents argued that one critic’s opinion was not important enough for that prominent position.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include Braun Strowman as a current champion for the Greatest Royal Rumble title: supporters pointed to WWE’s website listing him as champion and tracking his reign, while opponents argued the prize was not a regular championship because it was not defended or treated like other titles on WWE programming.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to identify Nintendo as the game’s developer or leave the developer unknown: one side argued that sources describing a new Nintendo team supported naming Nintendo, while others said the evidence did not state this explicitly and was not enough to establish the developer.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the reception section gave too much space to criticism: some called for more positive reviews, while others argued that the section already contained too much negativity. They also disputed whether to include the Zero Punctuation review, with one editor defending it as a legitimate review and another objecting that it was satire rather than a serious assessment.

2015.summary: Editors disputed whether Adele should be described as English or British, with one editor proposing “English” based on sources describing her that way and another arguing the cited material was insufficient to change the article’s existing wording. A source quoting Adele as saying she was proud to be British was offered in support of retaining “British.”

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should include criticism of Scientology and Hubbard’s remarks about religion as a way to make money; one editor argued that placing this material there created a negative impression. Another argued the remark might explain Scientology’s origins, while others said the allegation was disputed and belonged later in the article rather than in its opening.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether criticism of Scientology should be concentrated in a short section or discussed throughout the article, with one side arguing that this would give a clearer account of the movement and the other that its controversies were integral to that account. They also disputed whether the article should call Scientology a cult near its opening: some wanted a scholarly explanation and recognition that Scientologists reject the label, while others argued that omitting it would distort coverage of the term’s use.

2007.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraphs should mention allegations of harassment and harm: one argued they should be omitted unless proven, while another said leaving out the controversy would give readers a misleading picture. They also disputed whether to include the Church’s responses there, including its claims that negative coverage was motivated by interest groups; one editor wanted those counterpoints in the main article instead, while another argued that removing them left the summary unbalanced.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether multi-part iCarly movies should count as one episode or several, citing different ways of grouping them and sources that treated them as a single item. They also differed over whether social-media posts and blogs could support episode-list references, with one editor objecting to their use and another accepting posts by the series’ creators or cast.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether episodes shown as the second and third seasons should be listed together as one season or kept separate. Those favoring a merger cited outside episode listings, while defenders of the split pointed to production codes, new opening credits, and statements describing separate seasons as they aired.

2018.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should highlight which major teams missed the semifinals; one proposed revising the list of teams named, while another argued the fact was temporary trivia that did not belong there. Editors also disagreed about adding a final standings table: some tried to include one, while others said the rankings needed an official FIFA source and otherwise amounted to calculations not established by a published source.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s overview should first summarize the film’s arguments without comment or interleave criticism as it described them. Some argued that immediate context was needed to prevent the film’s presentation from misleading readers, while others said the repeated claim-and-rebuttal format made the overview read like a critique rather than a summary.

2009.summary: Editors disputed whether the reception section should use more negative review examples to reflect the film’s mostly unfavorable critical reviews, or retain positive examples alongside the overall rating. They also disagreed over whether the critic-review aggregate was a reliable guide to reception and whether its figures should be balanced with examples from individual publications.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s title should omit “Episode VII,” as one editor said the film’s announced title did, or include it, as another argued that episode numbers were part of the title and helped distinguish the film. The discussion also considered how the episode number should be mentioned in the article if it was not part of the title.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s opening paragraph should give “Star Wars Episode VII: The Force Awakens” as an alternate title alongside “Star Wars: The Force Awakens.” Supporters cited the episode number in the film’s opening crawl and sources using the longer name, while opponents argued that the official title excludes it and that the longer wording appears inconsistently and in relatively few sources.

2016.summary: Editors disputed whether the plot summary should call the Republic in the film the “New Republic”: supporters said the more specific name clarified the reference and was supported by other sources, while opponents argued that the film itself uses only “the Republic.” They also disagreed over the film’s budget, with one side favoring the roughly $200 million estimates from film-industry sources and another arguing that audited British production filings supported a higher figure; the dispute involved how to interpret and convert those figures.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over changes to the article’s sidebar: one argued it should remain as it was, while another said proposed changes should be discussed and could be accepted. One editor objected to separating judges and presenters into current and former groups, arguing that their periods on the show were already stated.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed about where to place Sharon Osbourne in the judges’ infobox, with suggestions tied to her return to the show and the order of the current panel. Another proposal was to order judges by when they joined the programme, while for the tenth series one editor preferred placing Osbourne last.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether the article’s definition of “Holodomor denial” as claiming that the famine did not occur was supported by sources, or whether those sources only documented that the famine had been denied. They also disagreed over whether the article should cover claims that no famine occurred or include the separate question of whether the famine was genocide.

Editors disagreed over whether a separate table of housemates’ jail visits belonged in the article: one argued the information was trivial and already covered in weekly summaries, while others considered it useful for tracking a recurring feature of the series. They also debated how much explanation to include beneath the nomination table, with one editor calling repeated notes unnecessary and another supporting a note about the Head of House and the task assigned to housemates in Hell.

2005.summary: After personal-life and controversy material was moved to a separate article, editors disagreed over whether Jackson’s biography should cover only his music or include fuller coverage of his personal life and controversies. They also disputed whether allegations of child sexual abuse belonged in the opening paragraph: one editor argued they were not relevant there, while another said they were important to an overview of Jackson’s public profile.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over how to organize Jackson’s biography: one proposal mixed music and personal events in a chronological account, while another objected to moving too much personal material out of the main article and argued that it should remain summarized there. They also disputed what to move into separate articles, with critics saying the main article remained too focused on albums and that this structure left too little context about his life.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening summary should frame Jackson’s life: some wanted it to foreground his entertainment achievements, while others argued that personal issues and controversies were receiving too little attention. They also disputed how to summarize the 1993 allegations, including whether to mention the civil settlement alongside the state’s decision not to bring charges for lack of evidence and the accuser’s later withdrawal from cooperation.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether Jackson’s estimated record sales should remain at over 750 million or be raised to over 780 million or 800 million, with some arguing that newer sales figures supported an increase and others questioning the reliability of the much higher estimates. A separate argument concerned whether the opening paragraph should call him the most successful entertainer of all time: some wanted that accolade included with clearer attribution, while others questioned the claim or said such superlatives were matters of opinion.

2006.summary: Editors disputed whether to call the article “Dokdo” or “Liancourt Rocks,” with the disagreement focused on whether a name associated with neither Korea nor Japan would frame the subject more neutrally. Supporters of “Liancourt Rocks” argued that it avoided choosing either country’s name, while opponents said the article should remain “Dokdo” after the earlier move and argued that its title should follow the same approach as the Senkaku Islands article.

2007.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should be titled “Dokdo,” which one editor supported based on its usage and South Korea’s control, or “Liancourt Rocks” or a paired name, which others argued would avoid favoring either country’s claim. They also disagreed over whether the information box should include Japan’s administrative classification: some said it records how each country classifies the islands, while others argued that South Korea administers them and Japan’s classification should not be presented as administration.

Editors disagreed over whether the opening should treat atheism chiefly as a belief that no God exists, with one editor arguing that standard philosophical references distinguish this from simple nonbelief and agnosticism. Others argued that published definitions vary and that the opening should describe a range, including absence of belief, rejection of theism, and belief in nonexistence without declaring one the sole definition.

2011.summary: Editors debated how to define atheism in the article’s opening paragraph: one proposal grouped rejection of belief in deities, the view that none exist, and simply lacking belief in deities under one description. Others argued that these are distinct definitions with different scopes and should be treated separately, rather than combined as though they were complementary understandings. The disagreement concerned how the article should present the range of meanings, not just the wording of a definition.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include information about Grover’s tattoos: some considered it irrelevant personal detail, while another argued that it had been reported and belonged in the article. They also disputed how much to say about his departure from and return to the television show Dill Mill Gayye, with one editor supporting mention of his dismissal and another arguing that the circumstances of his return should be included too.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s map and country lists should distinguish states that had rejected Kosovo, those still undecided, and those that had said nothing, or group all states that had not formally recognized it together. Supporters of the simpler scheme argued that it relied on verifiable recognition and avoided editors’ subjective interpretations of government statements. The opposing view was that grouping all non-recognizers together obscured meaningful differences in their positions.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over adding details about episodes that had not yet aired: one wanted to post information based on a preview, while another said eliminations should not be listed without a reliable source. They also disagreed over whether Owen had been unfairly voted off; one editor described his vote as unfair, while another argued that the other contestants chose to use their votes on Courtney.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the colored tables summarizing career sections should remain: one editor said their placement delayed the prose and raised concerns about readability and the use of color. Another argued that the tables clearly summarized results and that color made team standings easier to see.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should use the Serbian spelling Đoković, which one editor said better reflected the surname’s pronunciation, or the English-language form Djokovic, which others said was used in English media. Supporters of Djokovic argued that English-language sourcing should guide the article’s name, while the diacritic spelling was also raised in a discussion about consistency across tennis players’ names.

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should link to fan sites, with supporters arguing that sites such as Lostpedia merited inclusion and opponents saying such links were inappropriate or offered little encyclopedic value. Supporters challenged the claim that allowing one site would require adding many others, arguing that editors could judge each link on its merits; opponents warned that fan-site links could invite repeated demands for more.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe reviews as ranging from negative to positive: one said that wording made the album sound bad and did not belong there, while another argued that review scores and differences between UK and US responses supported describing reception as generally poor. They also disputed whether to include a reported track listing before official confirmation, with one editor accepting retailer listings and another arguing that listings from other sites were not enough.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to display co-director credits alongside directors’ names, with one favoring that approach and another arguing it would take up too much space and make the list less clear.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should say the R179s would replace all remaining R32s or only some, with one side relying on an MTA board meeting recording and another disputing that it established full retirement. They also disagreed over whether the recording was a suitable source: one editor considered an official meeting record reliable even when hosted on YouTube, while another objected to using YouTube without corroboration.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether a film’s year should be based on its North American release or its earliest release anywhere, with some favoring the North American date and others arguing for the first release date globally. They also disputed whether the worldwide article should show box-office figures for selected individual countries: supporters said such comparisons were useful, while opponents argued that highlighting only some markets was unrepresentative and favored worldwide totals instead.

2007.summary: Editors disputed whether the title should present state terrorism by the United States as fact or frame it as an allegation, with arguments for both approaches. They also disagreed over sourcing: some wanted claims tied explicitly to the United States, while others supported reporting authors’ claims and relevant criticism of them.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether human-rights reporting about abuses in the Philippines could provide background for claims that U.S. support amounted to state terrorism, even when those reports did not accuse the United States of terrorism. Some argued that a separate source made that connection and the reports added detail; others said combining sources in this way wrongly attributed the abuses to the United States.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how much to expand the article’s account of objections to casting white actors in the Asian-influenced story: one editor proposed adding coverage of boycotts and protests, while another said some proposed details repeated existing material and questioned including a fan site’s activities. They also disagreed over whether the casting controversy warranted its own section or should remain covered within the casting and reception sections.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether a Kommersant article supported saying that Washington recognized Russia as a superpower: critics argued its text described Russia only as a political and economic force, while a supporter relied on the headline’s claim of recognition.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Japan’s strong economy and public polling support justified its inclusion, with one arguing that global political and military reach mattered more and that the European Union had greater support from academics. They also questioned whether the European Union belonged on the list as a union rather than a country, while another editor pointed to reliable sources supporting its inclusion.

2020.summary: Editors disputed removals of material on Eritrean history, including Bahta Hagos, as well as images, text and sources: one asked for reasons for the removals, while another said the changes removed additions from a sock puppet and image spamming.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether to include a list of album sales figures: one post supplied totals for four releases and credited Generation Network, while another said the figures would be removed without a reliable source.

2020.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should describe Gunatitanand Swami as Swaminarayan’s spiritual successor, or attribute that claim specifically to BAPS and its followers rather than present it as a general historical account. One editor argued that sources did not support a broader claim about a spiritual succession system, while another proposal drew on scholarly sources describing differing accounts of succession among the branches.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should include photographs: one argued that images of an erect penis could offend readers, while another said an encyclopedia should use photographs to illustrate the subject. Separately, editors debated whether to keep a close-up image of the glans, the tip of the penis; one thought it added little and crowded the page, while others considered it useful or favored repositioning it.

2008.summary: Editors debated whether reports of an alleged fight involving Sharon Osbourne and Megan should be included in the show’s article, with some arguing for coverage because multiple outlets had reported it and others preferring to wait until the reunion episode aired. They also disagreed over how to present the story, including whether a proposed sentence based on a newspaper blog was suitably sourced and gave the incident appropriate weight.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to identify the jury members’ unshown votes for Sandra based on the likely vote pattern, or leave them unspecified because that conclusion was an inference rather than directly confirmed information. A later comment said an official recap confirmed Sandra’s six-vote total, which, combined with the votes shown on the broadcast, could establish the remaining votes.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether countries that had competed in 2008 but had not publicly announced plans for 2009 belonged in an “undecided” category. Some argued that silence did not prove a broadcaster was unsure, while others treated the lack of an announcement as undecided participation. They also disputed whether those countries should be listed at all: one view limited the article to countries that had expressed possible withdrawal, while another held that recent participants without public plans should still be mentioned.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should frame criticism of Qatar’s hosting: some wanted it described as primarily Western and wanted responses characterizing the criticism as hypocritical or prejudiced included, while others objected to that framing and challenged the paragraph’s balance. They also disagreed over whether the article’s detailed section on controversies should be shortened to a summary linking to a separate article or retained as important to the tournament article.

2009.summary: Editors disputed whether the article’s sources were reliable: one editor questioned claims based on a humor column and challenged Digital Spy, while another defended the sources, including Digital Spy, as dependable. They also disagreed over whether to mention a widely discussed but unsubstantiated rumor about Gaga’s sex characteristics: some argued that its media coverage merited a brief account, while others said it did not belong in her biography.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s discussion of Gaga’s connection to the gay community was too long and gave it too much weight, or whether her influence and relationship with that community warranted coverage. They also debated whether to include a brief mention of a rumor about her sex characteristics: some argued that media coverage and her response made it notable, while others said that including it would give an untrue rumor undue prominence in a short biography.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over what photo should represent Lady Gaga in the article’s infobox, with some favoring a newer image that reflected her changing look and others questioning whether suggested photos showed her clearly or were suitable. One editor argued that a proposed image with teal hair was not appropriate because Gaga was most notable as a blonde, while another preferred a recent image that showed her face clearly and distinctive clothing.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed about whether to count the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup in the club trophy table: one argued it should be excluded because UEFA did not recognize it as an official title, while another said the table included major competitions recognized by FIFA, including the Fairs Cup. They also disputed how to describe the fastest player to reach 100 league goals: one editor argued that Ronaldo’s fewer seasons merited a separate record, while another focused on appearances and said that claim was not established by sources.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Galloway’s meetings with Saddam Hussein should appear in the article’s opening paragraph: one side argued they were central to how the public viewed him, while others said that prominence unfairly framed his biography around the meetings. Supporters of including them said the encounters were a defining part of his public image; opponents argued that the opening instead overemphasized a negative episode and made the article seem unbalanced.

2026.summary: Editors disputed wording that said far-left politics “in certain instances” includes particular ideologies, with one objecting to the phrase as biased and another arguing that it reflected the less settled definition in academic sources and should not simply mirror the far-right article. A proposed rewrite described the ideologies more directly and treated authoritarian rule as an outcome of some revolutions rather than as an ideology in itself.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over replacing the team-by-team sections with a single table: one supported the proposed table as smaller and cleaner, while others argued it would be harder to use and edit and would disrupt links to competition rounds.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Allan Lichtman’s 2016 prediction should be described as correct because Donald Trump won the presidency, or incorrect because he lost the popular vote; one view argued Lichtman’s pre-election statements established that the system predicted the popular vote, while another emphasized that the prediction’s meaning and accuracy were contested. They also disputed how prominently to feature the issue and whether the article should state one conclusion or describe the competing interpretations without endorsing either.

2005.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include comparisons between Palpatine and real-world politicians: one objected to the George W. Bush and Franklin D. Roosevelt comparisons, while another suggested describing them as parallels people had drawn and noting that Lucas said Bush was not an influence.

2015.summary: Editors questioned whether to keep Howie listed after he had not appeared for 13 months; another editor pointed to a recent industry list naming him as still expected and argued the article should follow that source.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether characters still appearing on the show should have their known 2018 exit dates listed in the current-characters section, or remain marked as continuing until they had left, with exits noted in the departing-characters section. They also disputed whether character entries should name every actor who had played a role or only the current actor; one editor argued for including all performers, while another noted that the list specified the current actor and said including everyone would still make sense.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether character names in the list should match the names used in the characters’ article titles or the names currently shown in the programme’s credits. Supporters of article-title names argued that consistent, commonly recognisable names would help readers, while opponents said the current-character list should reflect the credits so viewers could find characters under the names they had just seen.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Vicky, Natalie and Jan belonged in the list as regular characters or should be classified as recurring characters. One editor pointed to their ongoing filming or storylines as evidence of regular roles, while another argued they should remain recurring until the show confirmed their status.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Sophie Webster should remain on the list of current characters after actor Brooke Vincent’s contract was said to have expired and she had not announced a return date. One editor argued that this meant she was no longer a current character, while another said a spokesperson’s statement that she was not leaving and the lack of reliable confirmation of a departure meant she should stay listed.

2008.summary: Editors disputed whether Bessie and other characters were playable in the game: some challenged their inclusion and said the game featured only five series, while another asked why Bessie could not appear. An administrator said the additions could not be treated as false without sources, describing them as unsourced material rather than established vandalism.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail to include about Starmer’s Labour leadership: one sought fuller coverage, while others favored a shorter account and opposed duplicating material covered in separate articles. They also debated whether to mention his earlier refusal to call for a Gaza ceasefire in the article’s opening paragraph, with one editor arguing that the fact was notable and another preferring to keep it in the main text.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article title should name Russia and Georgia as the main participants, following a widely used name, or focus on South Ossetia, where one editor said most of the fighting took place. Supporters of the existing South Ossetia title described it as a neutral, descriptive choice, while others argued that common usage favored a Russia–Georgia title.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should be titled for South Ossetia or for Russia and Georgia, with supporters of the latter arguing that it better reflected the conflict’s wider scope and the two main parties. Defenders of the South Ossetia title argued that it was more descriptive and neutral, while others said it could make the conflict seem limited to that region and frame Russia’s role as merely protective.

Editors disagreed over whether studies of living Egyptians and neighboring Nile Valley groups belonged in the article: one argued that genetic patterns could help reconstruct historical migrations, while another said the studies measured only modern people and could not establish ancient Egyptians’ genetic profile or racial classification.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should mention commentary calling the party’s abortion-platform language the Akin plank: some favored a brief mention, while others argued the platform was longstanding and the label was not part of the convention’s own wording.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Johnson’s support for a parliamentary motion about Owen Paterson: one said it postponed consideration of the recommended suspension, while another argued it prevented the suspension, citing how news reports characterized the vote. They also disputed whether the article should say an investigation had found Paterson broke the rules or had only alleged that he did, with one editor pointing to news coverage that used “found.”

2006.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Iranian peoples could be described as one ethno-linguistic group: some read a source describing Kurds as part of an Iranian ethno-linguistic group, alongside Persians and others, as support for the wider label, while others said it did not establish that Iranian peoples as a whole form one such group. They also disagreed over whether Azeris belonged in the article’s grouping: one view treated speaking an Iranian language as the basis for inclusion, while another argued that Azeris’ historical and cultural ties could also make them Iranian peoples.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “neoliberal” belonged in the party’s ideology box: one removed the label, citing Gordon Brown’s statement that neoliberalism had collapsed, while others argued that published sources still described Labour’s ideology that way. Another editor distinguished between Labour having adopted neoliberal economic policies in the past and describing its current ideology as neoliberal.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to mention the album’s November leak: some argued that a full-album leak merited inclusion, while another said leaks were too common to be notable and cited a guideline against covering them. They also disputed which reviews belonged in the article, with one editor objecting that prominent newspaper reviews had been removed while less professional outlets remained, as others had added reviews such as USA Today’s.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Britney Spears’s official website was reliable enough to confirm “If You Seek Amy” as the album’s next single: some argued that the site was official, while others wanted confirmation from a more reliable source before adding the claim. They also disputed whether Lady Gaga’s vocals on “Quicksand” justified crediting her as a featured performer, with one editor pointing to her audible singing and others arguing that the album credits did not identify her as featured.

Editors disagreed over whether the discography should include songs Gaga wrote for other performers. One position was that it should list only her major recordings, while another argued her songwriting career justified including those credits. The discussion also raised whether such material belonged in a separate list.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “Chillin’,” on which Gaga was credited as a featured performer, should count among her singles: some argued it was Wale’s single, while others said a featured performer should be counted too. They also disputed whether to list it alongside her other singles or in a separate section for featured singles; arguments against separating it included that it was her only such single at the time.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to raise the reported worldwide sales of *Born This Way* from five million to roughly seven or eight million, with the higher estimate supported by an interview quoting Gaga’s manager. Other comments objected that sales above five million were not confirmed by official organizations, and one editor put sales at between 4.5 and five million.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe the Weather Underground as “violent” in the opening paragraph, with some arguing that this could imply Ayers personally committed violence and others saying the group’s actions warranted the label; a more specific description of its bombing campaign was also proposed. They also disputed how to frame Ayers’s connection to Barack Obama: some considered their contacts and shared board service worth mentioning, while others said the campaign controversy—not the contacts themselves—was the relevant subject for the article.

2007.summary: Editors disputed whether to describe the Israeli attack as indiscriminate based on findings by international human-rights organizations, or to attribute that characterization only to Palestinian sources and a limited number of international sources. They also disagreed over whether investigations had disproved claims of a massacre or merely found no evidence for them, and whether to describe the organizations’ findings as evidence of possible war crimes or as findings that war crimes occurred.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over how to present the article’s campaign issues: one defended the section’s importance but said it was a poorly organized list of promises, while another criticized its wording and coverage as favoring the NDP and Liberals. The criticism called for organizing the material around major topics and including more context and party positions, rather than keeping a list that mixed issues with individual promises.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Wurzelbacher as a plumber based on the work he did, or to qualify that label because he lacked an individual license and was not currently doing plumbing work. They also disputed whether the article should primarily describe Wurzelbacher as a person or emphasize how “Joe the Plumber” was used as a political symbol, with some arguing the symbol had to be understood through the man behind it.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Chandrayaan-2 as the first landing in the Moon’s south polar region or as the southernmost lunar landing. One argued that the region was too vague to claim the distinction, while another considered “south polar region” acceptable despite the planned landing site being outside an informal polar circle.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether a table of Diana Vickers’s tour dates belonged in the article: one supported adding the cited dates, while another said a complete schedule fit better in an article about a tour and could be confusing in a table. Both later expressed support for describing the tour information in a paragraph instead.

2009.summary: Editors disputed how to describe safety concerns about Obama’s proposed fuel-efficiency rules: one proposal said studies linked fuel-economy standards to additional crash deaths and warned the new rules could worsen the toll, while others said the cited source did not establish that the proposal would cause more deaths and urged broader, balanced sourcing.

2011.summary: Editors debated whether the candidate list should be narrowed by requiring candidates to meet a minimum polling threshold, alongside other eligibility conditions. Opponents argued that a polling cutoff would be arbitrary and could exclude candidates they considered serious, favoring the existing approach instead.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list candidates as “presumptive nominees” in the infobox before their party conventions: some wanted to wait for formal nominations, while others argued that candidates already described as presumptive should be included with that status clearly marked. They also disputed which minor-party candidates belonged in the infobox, with proposals ranging from limiting it to the major candidates or debate invitees to including candidates who could mathematically win enough electoral votes.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether a candidate’s general notability was enough for inclusion, or whether the candidacy itself needed to be significant; one side argued Jonathon Sharkey’s public profile did not establish relevance to the Republican field, while another defended listing notable candidates under the existing standard. Proposals to require polling support or broader campaign coverage also drew objections, with one editor warning that polling could exclude candidates who had received media attention and arguing for decisions based on coverage and each case.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to call states won according to which candidate led in the popular vote or which candidate could show support from the most delegates, a distinction made more consequential by the party’s five-state rule for qualifying for a convention nomination ballot. Some favored delegate counts as the more meaningful measure of the nomination process, while others argued that popular-vote maps matched earlier election coverage; a proposal to show both measures offered a way to distinguish them.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the music-video section should include its initially planned filming date, February 10, as well as the actual start date, February 7. Some argued that the original date added unnecessary detail because the difference was only three days, while another editor defended including it as a sourced fact about the video.

Editors debated whether the article should remain fully protected or return to semi-protection after repeated replacement of its infobox image; some said semi-protection could be bypassed, while another suggested established accounts could be trusted to edit.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should characterize the citizenship theories as racist or as a racial reaction to Obama’s presidency. Some argued that this interpretation was important and supported by commentary, while others objected that emphasizing it in the opening paragraph gave it too much weight or made an overly broad accusation.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list celebrities who attended concerts, with some defending the entries as true and others questioning their sourcing and whether the details belonged in the article.

Editors disputed whether to describe Madoff as Jewish-American in the opening, with some arguing his identity mattered because of his connections to Jewish organizations and victims, and others saying it was not a defining characteristic and should be addressed in the article text instead. They also disagreed over whether his Jewish identity belonged in the first sentence: one editor argued it was relevant to the scheme, while another urged that the opening focus first on what he did.

Editors disagreed over whether the opening should present “Gaza massacre” as a name Hamas used for the conflict alongside Israel’s “Operation Cast Lead.” Supporters said including Hamas’s terminology reflected a major party’s viewpoint, while opponents argued that “massacre” was a description rather than an established name and belonged in the article body with context.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should mention attacks on schools, mosques, United Nations facilities and homes, and whether that wording needed to include Israel’s stated explanation that some sites were used by militants. They also disputed whether “Gaza Massacre” belonged among the event’s alternative names: some editors cited sources describing it as a name used in the Arab world, while others questioned whether those sources adequately supported that broad claim.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the academy should be described as Mormon-related: some pointed to missionaries and other claimed ties, while others argued that these did not establish an official relationship with the church. They also disputed how to present former students’ abuse allegations and older material about the academy’s practices, with a school representative arguing that past information needed context and other editors saying the allegations merited mention while emphasizing that they were allegations.

2018.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should describe Judaism or ancient Israel as a foundation of Western civilization, or instead characterize its role as influence; they also disagreed over whether a related image belonged at the top of the article. A separate image dispute concerned whether the Delphic oracle was representative enough to appear near the start of the article’s main text, with one editor saying it was added to give pre-Christian beliefs more weight and another proposing a replacement.

2009.summary: A contributor posted an alternate track list and an August 2009 release date, while another called the cover and track list fake and said the November 24 date was sourced.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to lower the list’s 700-solar-radius cutoff to include more stars or keep the list shorter; proposals ranged from 200 to 400, while another editor argued against expanding it. They also differed over which estimate to use for the star [W60] B90: one editor cautioned that a recent radius estimate came from crude methods and conflicted with other sources, while another favored using the most recent estimate.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether candidate information should stay in a list with a separate photo gallery or move into a table: supporters said the table grouped each candidate’s details, while opponents argued it made the page harder to edit and separated information and sources. They also disagreed about circular versus rectangular portraits: supporters preferred the circular appearance, while critics said circles made it harder to replace photos and could hinder neutral image selection.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list the known write-in vote totals of people such as Bernie Sanders and John Kasich, who received electoral votes from electors but did not run as presidential candidates. Some argued that recorded write-in votes should be included alongside those electoral votes, while others said the votes were unrelated and listing them could wrongly present these people as candidates.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how specifically to label the album’s genre in its information box: some favored the broad label “rock,” arguing that sources gave varied descriptions, while others argued that the sources supported “punk rock.”

Editors disagreed over whether to include discussion of Lambert’s sexual orientation: some argued that media coverage of the speculation warranted a neutral account, while others considered the available reporting too uncertain or unreliable to support it. They also disputed whether to describe Lambert as Jewish, with some treating his response in an interview as confirmation and others questioning the sourcing and whether the information belonged in the article.

Editors disagreed over whether to call the subject a 2012 doomsday prediction or use a broader name, with some arguing that many of the ideas discussed were not predictions of the world ending and that no common name was established by reliable sources. They also disputed the opening paragraph’s wording: some wanted it to state that science offered no support for doomsday or spiritual-transformation claims, while others argued that this framing overstated what the article’s examples showed and should be based on verifiable claims.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over how to present contestants’ results: one proposal listed contestants alongside episode outcomes, while another view favored keeping the existing table because the show involved teams rather than individual competition. A proposed version would use simple labels for team wins, safe contestants, those at risk, and eliminations, instead of including every detail in the table.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a much higher estimate of the September 12 crowd alongside estimates around 75,000, with some arguing it was a reportable outlier and others saying it was unreliable or based on mistaken claims. They also disputed describing the protests as locally organized: one editor proposed removing that wording because of allegations of national political organization, while another argued the allegations alone did not justify removing it.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how much space the article should give reports of alleged misconduct at Tea Party protests: some called the section excessive and proposed a brief account, while another argued that the examples were significant and should not be stripped of participants’ comments. They also disputed whether the accounts were adequately substantiated, with one editor describing them as allegations and rumor and another pointing to eyewitness accounts and objecting to wording that misrepresented a source.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the post-credits figure should be named Thanos in the plot: some argued the film did not identify him and that naming him required a reliable source, while others argued that the character was recognizable and should be identified. They also disputed the UK title: some cited classification and other sources for “Marvel Avengers Assemble,” while others pointed to Disney’s use of “Marvel’s Avengers Assemble” and questioned whether the classification board’s listing established the film’s title.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether review scores alone should convey the film’s reception or whether the article should summarize critical opinion in words, with some favoring a description such as “critical acclaim” and others objecting to interpretive labels or seeking supporting commentary from publications. Editors also disputed how the film’s title should be presented in the opening paragraph: one position favored the commonly used title first and treated the formal or UK title as secondary, while others argued that the formal name should come first and the UK naming should remain.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether ancient Yadava dynasties and groups claiming descent from Yadu belonged in this article: some argued that modern Yadavs shared a continuous history with them, while others said shared descent claims did not prove they were the same community and favored treating them separately.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should give a fuller account of the movement’s proposed social and economic system: one editor offered an extensive description, while others rejected it as interpretation that would make the article promotional. They also disagreed over whether criticism of the films belonged in the movement’s article: one editor argued it should remain in the film articles, while others said the movement’s connection to the films made some criticism relevant.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether criticism of the first Zeitgeist film belonged in the movement’s article: one position was that the film was unrelated to the movement, while another was that published sources connected the two and the criticism should remain. They also disagreed over whether the movement’s own materials could explain its philosophy when outside sources did not describe it in detail, or whether the article should rely mainly on independent analysis and limit those self-published accounts.
