2019.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the United Kingdom’s parliamentary ratification step, with suggestions including “passed,” “not rejected,” and wording that no negative resolution was tabled. They also differed over whether country names in the ratification table should be colored, with one editor defending color as a way to indicate completed ratification and another objecting to the styling.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how to introduce Boyle, with some arguing that the opening paragraph should emphasize her singing and fame from the talent show rather than her church volunteering, while another view favored describing her as a church volunteer and amateur singer. They also disputed whether to include details about oxygen deprivation at birth: some objected to expanding on the medical account as irrelevant or unsupported, while others argued that a brief, sourced mention of the reported birth complication and learning difficulties belonged in the biography.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether descriptions of two matches were neutral, with one commenter objecting that the article called one a “great match” and another “very slow”; the comment says the wording was then changed. There was also disagreement over when to list rumored matches, with a request to add an Undertaker–Triple H match met by replies that it should wait for official confirmation from WWE.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include television ratings, with one arguing that including only one rating system could make the article biased and another proposing limited updates to the ratings information. They also debated how to present ratings: one suggestion was to include both systems without mentioning rival shows or rankings, while another editor objected that the existing presentation cited only one system and compared the show with a rival.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over which professional roles to include in the opening sentence: one argued it should follow the cited New York Times description and include only roles integral to her notability, while another cited Britannica’s descriptions of Minaj as a television personality, singer-songwriter, and actress in support of restoring those titles.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether the movement should be described as grassroots: some said it grew from local organizers, while others argued that claims of outside organizing made an unqualified description misleading. They also disagreed over whether support from established political organizations showed that the movement was being directed or funded from outside, or instead represented assistance to local groups.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether the article could describe the Tea Party movement as having been viewed as “astroturf,” or whether the cited book actually supported that wording; some argued it should be removed or framed specifically as a claim by political critics. Others maintained that the book reported survey responses and accusations from multiple sources, so the article could report that the description had been made without presenting it as fact about the movement.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how to label and color a contestant declared safe when only two contestants were grouped at risk: one view treated that contestant as the last person saved, while another said they were the first—and only—person declared safe. Some editors also questioned whether the order of announcements showed contestants’ relative vote totals, arguing that it could instead be arranged for dramatic effect.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over what birth year to give Kapoor, citing conflicting reports that put her at 24 in 2013 or 21 that year. One editor proposed describing her birth as around 1990 while acknowledging the conflicting reports; another requested removal of the date sourced to CINTAA, which they considered unreliable for information about a living person.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include contestants missing from the pageant’s official website: one argued the site was still being built and that other reports supported the list, while another questioned whether those sources were reliable and favored waiting for official confirmation.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph’s infobox should show the candidates promoted for European Commission president or the leaders of the European Parliament groups whose seats it reported. Those favoring group leaders argued that the candidates did not lead the groups, while supporters of the candidates said they had led their parties’ election campaigns and should be featured.

2026.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should call Khamenei an Ayatollah or Grand Ayatollah, or use the lower clerical title Hojjatoleslam. Some pointed to reports of a promotion by a Qom seminary and the titles used by Iranian state media, while others argued those reports did not establish that he had earned or been recognized at those ranks.

2018.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should qualify its description of David de Gea as the world’s best goalkeeper with the phrase “regarded by many as,” with one editor objecting to repeated removals of that wording.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should say that the country adopted the name “Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia,” or explain that the United Nations used it while the country retained its constitutional name. They also disagreed over whether to use that full provisional name or its abbreviation, and whether international use of it meant the country was recognized by that name or only referred to that way in certain settings.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the leading-scorers table should include players’ appearances: one proposed adding the column to match earlier Champions League articles, while another argued it was unnecessary because appearances do not affect ranking.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include criticism of Bieber’s 2010 Video Music Awards performance: some said lip-syncing was common and the incident was not notable, while another argued that a source’s criticism of how poorly he lip-synced was worth mentioning.

2009.summary: Editors disputed whether killings in different communist-ruled countries could be treated as a shared subject linked to communist ideology, or whether grouping them implied a connection that sources had not established; one cited account argued that communist ideology and party organization could enable mass killings. They also disagreed over whether famine deaths belonged in the article: some argued famines were not killings unless deliberately caused, while others cited accounts describing famine as a means of targeting suspected enemies and forcing compliance.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether grouping killings under communist regimes implied that communist ideology caused them, and whether the article’s framing presented that connection as an accepted scholarly view. Others argued that the article covered killings occurring under regimes labeled communist, not a necessary link to the ideology, and that it treated explanations as proposals from different scholars.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Greece should count as a participant: one argued that its broadcaster had only provisional membership and might therefore be unable to compete, while another pointed to an invitation and expected membership approval as grounds to include it. They also disputed how to interpret published participant counts, with one editor arguing that Greece and Bosnia were already included in a provisional count and another questioning whether that count matched the event organizer’s confirmed list.

2011.summary: Editors debated whether to divide the episode list into separate pages for each season, with the proposal describing the existing article as too long and difficult to maintain. Opponents argued that the list was still too short to justify splitting, and one editor said its readable text was well below the size range that would prompt consideration of a split.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the film belonged within the episode list at its chronological point or should be listed elsewhere or after the episodes.

2019.summary: Editors disputed whether to list films that were still in development, with opponents arguing that the projects were uncertain and the available sources too weak to support their inclusion. The section was added again, but the discussion contains no explanation from its proponents for why it belonged.

2010.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening description should call the EDL “far-right” or the broader “right-wing”; some favored the broader wording, while others argued that “far-right” was better supported and more precise. They also disagreed over whether to call it political: some considered the label unnecessary or unclear alongside “far-right,” while others argued that its stated aims made it useful and supported by sources.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over describing the English Defence League as far right: some argued that this label was misleading and preferred “right wing,” while others said academic and other sources supported the stronger label. They also disputed how to describe the group’s stated opposition to Islamism and Sharia law, with one proposal presenting it directly and other editors arguing that the wording should make clear this was the group’s own claim rather than an established fact.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether season-five contestant team assignments belonged in the list: one argued that a script and image identified several contestants’ teams, while another said the available information did not establish team assignments and removed them.

Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should describe the Catholic Center Party’s role in Hitler’s rise and the circumstances surrounding its support for the 1933 Enabling Act. One editor argued the account should convey intimidation while keeping detail in the main article; another said intimidation did not remove the party’s choices and pointed to historians’ interpretations of its role in enabling Hitler’s rise.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the list should include wage figures from national statistical agencies alongside international datasets: some argued that differing national methods made comparisons unreliable, while another supported including them with clear sourcing. They also disputed how wages should be converted for international comparison, with one position favoring purchasing-power adjustments and another arguing that figures in current US dollars from official sources should remain.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Windows 8.1 merited its own article: supporters described it as more than a service pack, while opponents considered it an update whose material did not justify a separate page. They also disputed calling Windows 8’s app environment a “walled garden”: one editor argued the phrase was used in published commentary, while another considered it pejorative and too specific for Wikipedia’s own wording.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the season-effects table should list individual hurricane landfalls and “direct hits,” or instead use broader descriptions of areas affected, because direct hits could be hard to verify and the existing entries might omit impacts beyond landfall sites. They also questioned whether the table’s damage and casualty figures could be checked through the article’s references, with one editor arguing that the data were not adequately tied to sources.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe emails discussing efforts to keep some research out of journals: some saw them as evidence of attempts to restrict peer review, while others said they concerned excluding weak research through review. One editor argued the issue merited coverage but cautioned that the discussion did not establish that any such efforts had succeeded.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article title should focus on the hacking or on the controversy surrounding the emails and documents; supporters of a controversy-focused title said the public attention centered on the contents and their fallout, not just how the files were obtained. Others argued for keeping the incident framing and objected to labels such as “Climategate” or “scandal,” which they considered prejudicial; proposals for alternative titles also differed over whether to describe the subject as an email or document controversy.

Editors disagreed over whether the song’s long music-video section justified a separate article: some argued that the video had extensive coverage and distinct material, while others said it was too soon to judge its lasting importance and that the section could instead be shortened. A separate dispute concerned using both the monochrome digital-release cover and the colored physical-release cover; editors differed over whether showing both added enough information to justify two copyrighted images, and the discussion’s organizer declared that only one should be used.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the “death panels” claim: some wanted the article to distinguish the claim that Sarah Palin made from broader debate about health-care rationing and the law’s advisory board, while others argued that expanding this discussion would give fringe views too much weight. They also debated the section’s label, with “common misconceptions” proposed as a less charged alternative to “myths.”

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Grande’s account of why she left Catholicism: one proposed wording that made clear the claim reflected her understanding, while another argued that the article should not evaluate whether her understanding of the cited account was correct.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to replace the article’s existing 2015 image with a newer photograph, including a 2023 image from Vogue Taiwan. Supporters of a change pointed to the alternatives’ greater clarity or recency, while others preferred the existing image of Grande performing and argued that the proposed options were not clear improvements.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether performance tables should name earlier performers of each song: some wanted original performers credited, while others favored leaving artist names out or using the version named by the show. The disagreement reflected uncertainty over what such a credit would mean, since an original performer might not be the artist whose arrangement a contestant used, and editors argued that naming singers could therefore mislead readers.

2005.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should include the Apostle Paul’s distinction between outward and spiritual Jewish identity: one objection was that, after the split between Christianity and Judaism, Paul should not define Jewish identity, while another view was that the passage represented a belief held by Messianic Jews and belonged in the article.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep information about the U.S. executive order after its proponents abandoned it: one argued the page should focus on current visa policies, while another said the recent history still belonged in the encyclopedia. They also disagreed about where it belonged, with one proposing a separate section and the other arguing it should not remain in the visa table’s notes.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over which source to use for the film’s worldwide box-office total: one request cited a figure from Eros, while others favored BoxOfficeIndia’s lower figure, pointing to an earlier decision to rely on that source and concerns about Eros’s figures. They also disputed how to describe the reviews, with one editor arguing that a majority were positive and citing an aggregate rating, while others called for summaries based on sources discussing the overall reaction and reviews from the film’s home country.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should mention the Swedish arrest warrant and sexual allegations: some argued the widely reported case was a major controversy, while others said giving it prominence before a trial would overemphasize a developing event. They also disputed how to describe the case, including whether to use the word “rape” and say Assange faced charges, or instead explain that he was wanted for questioning and that the allegations were contested.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the biography should explicitly describe the Swedish allegations as including rape or use broader wording about sexual allegations; some argued that naming rape was necessary to explain the case, while others considered the term potentially misleading without more context. The disagreement also involved how much legal detail to include, with some favoring a concise account and others saying readers needed explanation of the offenses and the legal process.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe Assange as a journalist: some cited news sources and journalism awards using that label, while others argued the awards did not establish that it was an appropriate description. They also disputed whether the opening paragraph should report a UN rapporteur’s warning that Assange’s life was at risk in prison; supporters cited the rapporteur’s assessment and medical team, while opponents said the wording was misleading and gave too much weight to one assessment.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should report Yahoo News’s account that CIA officials discussed kidnapping or killing Assange: some argued that coverage by other reliable outlets made it significant, while others said reliance on one investigation and a lack of independent confirmation made it too weak or disproportionate. They also disputed how much space to give UN rapporteur Nils Melzer’s assessments, with some favoring coverage of his widely reported views and others calling the repeated detail excessive.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to use a track list shown in an image attributed to Kanye West as the album’s official track list, with some treating it as the latest version and others questioning whether it was final and reliable enough to include. The disagreement also concerned whether the article should rely on that image or wait for confirmation from the record label or a published third-party source.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over which flag to show for the European Grand Prix in Valencia: some argued flags should identify the host country, Spain, while others favored the European flag because of the race’s name and its use at the event.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe Croatian as part of the broader Serbo-Croatian language group or present it as a distinct South Slavic language. Supporters of the group framing cited linguistic similarities and English-language usage, while opponents argued that Croatian has its own history and standard and that the Serbo-Croatian label carries political associations; the disagreement extended to how prominently that label should appear in the opening paragraph.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should report favorable coverage of Gabbard by Russian media outlets, with one side arguing the coverage was relevant and another questioning its wording and whether it deserved space. They also debated whether to describe Gabbard’s connections to the Science of Identity Foundation and its founder: some proposed including those ties and her reported relationship with the founder, while others objected that such wording could imply more than the sources established.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe the Coffee Party as liberal: one position cited media descriptions of it as a liberal alternative, while another pointed to the organization’s rejection of ideological labels and its stated welcome to people with differing political views. The disagreement also concerned whether the article should present those media descriptions as fact or explain that sources used a range of labels, including centrist, moderate and left-leaning.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether episode entries should identify main cast members who do not appear: one called that information trivia without encyclopedic value absent outside commentary, while another said other episode lists mark cast absences and argued it was acceptable here.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether hour-long specials should count as one episode or two: one position favored counting them as two, while another argued that a special shown with one set of credits should count as one. The arguments included whether the series’ stated episode total and production codes supported separate counts, or whether the final edited and broadcast version should determine the listing.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed about whether to add bronze medals as soon as a place was secured or wait until the entire event was complete and the medals were formally awarded; some pointed to the Rio 2016 table, which listed bronze medals earlier. The disagreement also surfaced over whether this article should follow that table, with one editor arguing for matching its counts and another explaining that the article’s practice was to wait until the event was finished.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “Animales” qualified as a promotional single: one relied on a Rolling Stone label, while another questioned its reported release date and argued it was not officially available before the album. Editors also disputed whether the worldwide sales figure for The Pinkprint could include streams; one editor said streams count toward industry certifications, while another argued the article’s sales section should include only album purchases.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the biography should print the explicit sexual definition behind the online campaign linked to Santorum’s name, with some arguing that readers needed the actual wording to understand the episode and others opposing its inclusion in the main article. Those favoring a brief description and a link argued that this would explain the issue without reproducing all the detail, which they considered better suited to a separate article.

2025.summary: Editors disputed whether Igodomigodo’s starting date should be placed around 40 BCE or around the 10th century CE, weighing older historical works against more recent academic sources and a newer account proposing the earlier date. They also disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe the Ogiso dynasty as native to the Edo or avoid a settled origin claim, with one editor citing scholarship that characterized some early rulers as outsiders.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether BP should be named in the article title: supporters argued that it was more neutral to name the company, citing its public acceptance of cleanup responsibility, while opponents said the title would unfairly single it out when other companies were involved. Opponents also argued that placing BP directly before “Deepwater Horizon” could imply that BP owned the rig, which they said was not the case.

Editors debated how the article should describe the risk of racial profiling, with one arguing that it be presented as critics’ claims alongside supporters’ denials rather than as an established fact. They also questioned whether the sources supported the specific explanation that the risk arose from the law’s wording, enforcement and historical precedent, and the phrasing was removed.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Melor as having both “Nonoy” and “Nona” as names after both appeared in advisories, or to use only “Nona”; one editor said “Nonoy” was immediately dropped and that including both names would be confusing.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the season article should count and date tropical depressions using the Japan Meteorological Agency’s later revisions of its weather maps, which sometimes changed whether a system was classified as a depression. One editor proposed revising the article to reflect those post-analysis maps, while another questioned whether the changes altered a system’s duration; the discussion also raised whether the archived map data could be verified.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to place storm 36W in the 2018 or 2019 season article: one proposed moving it to 2019 if it received a 2019 designation, while another argued that Pabuk should appear in the timeline because it formed in 2018.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “The Annoying Orange Sitcom Version” should be classified as an extended episode of “Annoying Valentine”: one said it was not, while another argued that its greater length qualified it.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the film’s critical reception should be called “mixed-to-positive,” with one position pointing to its lower review score than the earlier films and another objecting to that label. The opposing view argued that review scores alone should not be used to create a reception summary, and that the wording should instead rely on sources that aggregate reviews and state an overall assessment.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether contestant names should come before their numbers in tables: proponents said this would make them easier for screen-reader users, while opponents argued the format was not required by guidance and departed from the customary layout. They also disputed whether to include a report from TMZ about a possible change to the finalists, with one editor treating the source as adequate and another arguing the claim needed supporting evidence.

2022.summary: A reference-formatting notice asked an editor to review differing versions of a citation and add the correct version to the article.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to use “Ground Zero Mosque” in the opening description: some argued it was a widely used name, while others considered it misleading or politically charged and wanted it qualified. They also disputed whether to describe the project as including a mosque or instead as a community center with a Muslim prayer area; some cited news coverage calling it a mosque, while others favored the project’s description of the space as a prayer area.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Hurricane Marie should be described as a remnant low or as post-tropical, with one editor objecting to calling it a remnant low without an official source and others arguing that the terms could apply to the same system. The discussion also cited Marie’s remaining tropical-storm-force winds and the National Hurricane Center’s definition of a remnant low when considering which description was supported.

Editors disagreed over whether to recreate a separate article about the show's characters: one began drafting one and wanted a wider vote, while another opposed restoring it without reliable sources on the cast and production, describing the draft as mostly plot-based summaries. Another editor said a separate article would need substantial coverage of the characters in independent secondary sources.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should mention comparisons between the film and the game: supporters pointed to reports in gaming publications, while opponents said the sources mainly reflected fan reactions and did not substantiate a controversy. One editor proposed a neutral section about comparisons rather than a controversy section, but another argued that even a comparison could overstate the evidence without a reliable source making a stronger claim of copying.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether the article title should change from Bradley Manning to Chelsea Manning after Manning publicly stated her name and gender identity. Supporters of retaining Bradley cited common-name and reader-recognition concerns and distinguished the title from pronouns used in the article; supporters of Chelsea argued that her stated identity and Wikipedia’s guidance supported using that name.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to add an account of Noem’s comments on a China trade agreement: one objected that the proposed text was unclear, potentially viewpoint-driven, and insufficiently relevant, while the contributor argued that it updated an attribution about her position and belonged in the article. The objector suggested a shorter, more narrowly worded version.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list when and on which program each battle-royal participant was announced: one saw that sequence as useful context, while another argued it added little and was not sourced. They also differed over how to present the event: some favored identifying several matches as main events and retaining key moments, while others preferred chronological match listings and a much shorter account focused on finishes and major developments.

2022.summary: Editors disputed whether white Colombians make up 45–50% of the population or a smaller share: one position cited recent studies of European ancestry, while another argued that external estimates put the figure around 20%, with some reaching about 35%. They also disagreed over whether genetic ancestry results could establish the size of an ethnic group, with one editor saying ancestry does not reflect ethnic composition and another objecting that the census does not separately count white and mestizo Colombians.

2013.summary: Editors disputed how to describe the season’s accumulated cyclone energy: one commenter said the article’s “67%” figure should say that the total was 67% below average, while another pointed to the hurricane center’s wording, and the discussion clarified that this was equivalent to 33% of average.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should list the contestant quotes used as episode titles: one editor opposed adding them, calling them trivia unrelated to the game, while another argued they belonged in an article about the season. The editor supporting inclusion also suggested a separate page listing quotes from all seasons if others opposed adding them here.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s opening should link Bitcoin prominently to criminal activity: one argued it was routinely used in criminal contexts, while another said criminal use was comparable to other currencies and that its public transaction record undercut claims of anonymity. They also disputed what transaction estimates showed, with one editor arguing that drug-market activity and gambling merited emphasis, while another questioned treating gambling as criminal and pointed to estimates placing drug-market transactions at a smaller share of activity.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the section title “Speculative bubble” presented a contested judgment as fact: one argued the cited views differed and suggested a neutral title, while another defended the title but also proposed phrasing it as a question.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over how Bitcoin should be described at the start of the article: one argued that it should be introduced as a distributed public ledger, while others favored describing it as a payment system that uses such a ledger. They also disputed whether separate sections on child pornography and terrorist financing gave those criminal-use topics too much prominence, with some arguing they should be covered within broader sections instead.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should present critical claims—particularly about Bitcoin’s use for illicit payments and its energy use—as facts, or qualify them as disputed interpretations. One editor defended a concise critical summary as supported by reliable coverage, while others argued that the wording overstated contested claims and should reflect contrary views.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether the post-credits scene should identify the waking figure as the same Booker played throughout the game or leave his identity ambiguous; some argued the wording implied a different person, while others said the game and available sources did not establish which Booker it was. They also disagreed over whether the scene’s calendar date should be presented as evidence connecting it to the earlier events: one editor said the date was important to the story, while another argued that drawing that connection would go beyond what the game confirms.

2023.summary: Editors disputed whether Qeparo should be described as “mainly” Albanian-speaking and whether the article should note Greek-speaking residents in Upper Qeparo. Some argued that fieldwork and scholarship supported that distinction, while others said more recent sources described the village as Albanian-speaking and that the older reports did not establish the present-day situation.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over how to present conflicting estimates of rally attendance, especially whether CBS’s lower figure should receive greater prominence because its method was explained, or whether that would overemphasize one estimate. Some argued that the article should give more space to estimates and methods discussed in detail by sources; others said the article should reflect how prominently competing estimates appeared in reliable coverage, rather than treating the CBS figure as the prevailing view.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over a photo for the BD-08 rifle: one defended the image as official and higher-resolution, while another said the proposed alternative was unsuitable and preferred leaving the image space blank. They also disagreed over the support for added equipment information: one editor said it had relevant official references, while another argued that most sources were old or unofficial and that much of the information was biased.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to label the film American in its opening paragraph: some argued that its British-American production made a single nationality misleading, while another argued that its primary production role justified calling it American. They also disputed whether its reception should be described as positive or as critical acclaim, with objections that acclaim overstated what a limited sample of reviews could show and supporters pointing to an aggregate review site's ratings and description.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening should describe autism: one proposal favored “neurodevelopmental disability” over “neurodevelopmental disorder,” arguing that the latter presents a contested viewpoint as fact and can be inappropriate language for describing medical conditions. Others argued that “neurodevelopmental disorder” is the formal diagnostic classification and should remain prominent, while some supported “condition” as a less pathologizing alternative or as a way to avoid repeating “disorder.”

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should say Meloni would preserve civil unions: one view treated her recent remarks as her current position, while another argued that a response to a rally protester did not establish an official change from her earlier support for repealing the law.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over the date for “Split It Up”: one cited its earlier iTunes availability, while another said the list records the Disney Channel broadcast date.

2011.summary: Editors disputed whether Portugal would participate: one commenter argued that the cited report said no delegate had yet been found and selection information was still forthcoming, not that Portugal would be absent.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over how far ahead the table’s round-by-round positions should be shown: one objected to including positions that depended on possible future results, while another argued that Real Madrid’s first place was certain for the following week. The exchange concluded that Real Madrid’s position two weeks later was not certain, so the ranking should show them first for only the next week.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed about how prominently to cover the Britney Spears remix, with some calling for a dedicated section as it gained radio play and chart attention, while others argued it should not receive prominence as a remix of the original song. One editor suggested waiting for more information before creating a section, while others supported adding one as coverage developed.

Editors disagreed over whether to list the program as “Primetime” or “Primetime: What Would You Do?”; one argued it was part of the broader program, while another said ABC promoted it under the longer title. They also disagreed over whether to include start dates for news magazine shows: one editor considered the dates unnecessary because episodes aired regularly, while another said summer episodes could reuse previously aired stories.

2009.summary: Editors disagreed over how strongly to present cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for chronic fatigue syndrome: some argued that reviews rated the supporting trials low or very low in quality, while others said the treatment had evidence of benefit and that the caveats should not outweigh it. They also disputed how to describe the limits of the evidence, including the lack of research on CBT for severely affected patients.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Rob Grayson should have a separate article: some supported splitting him off, while others considered him a minor guest character who should remain on the list, and one suggested turning the material into an article about the storyline instead.

Editors disagreed over whether the article should include week-by-week song details and individual judges’ scores: one editor wanted that information retained, while another argued that the extensive recap did not belong in the article. They also disputed whether the cited reports supported the detailed scores, with one editor saying the links did not show individual judges’ scores and another pointing to reports said to cover weekly competition details.

2013.summary: Editors disputed how the article described the view that China could not produce high-powered jet engines, with one editor questioning who held that view and whether the cited 2011 article supported it. Another editor defended describing it as a shared view, arguing that several cited authors expressed it and naming each would distract from the aircraft description.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether rankings from the Brazil Billboard chart could be used when readers could not check the physical magazine: one editor questioned whether the figures were verifiable, while replies said published magazines could be reliable sources and that the same standard could apply to Turkey’s chart. A separate request argued that South Africa’s 5fm Top 40 should count as a national chart, while a reply said single-network charts were excluded from the article’s chart table.

Editors disagreed over how to characterize the song’s early critical reception: some argued it was positive because positive reviews outnumbered negative ones, while others called the response mixed and said a positive description would be biased. Later discussion continued over whether to describe reviews as generally positive or mixed to positive, with participants citing negative criticism and comparisons to other songs as reasons not to use a purely positive label.

Editors disagreed over whether the map should classify Libya as a revolution after the war and the Gaddafi government’s rule ended, or continue to show it as a civil war. Supporters of changing the map said the conflict had ended in the overthrow of the government; an opponent argued that reliable sources still mainly described it as a civil war and noted that some sources also described the revolution as over.

Editors disputed whether to call the events a civil war or use a broader term such as “conflict”: some argued that the fighting and sources supported “civil war,” while others questioned that label, pointing to international involvement and the wording used in news coverage. They also disputed whether al-Qaeda belonged among the listed combatants; one editor cited reports and allegations as grounds for including it, while others said the cited material did not show that the organization itself was actively involved.

Editors disagreed over how to label a single’s radio date in the album infobox: one argued it should be identified as a radio date, or omitted, because it was not a sales release, while another objected to removing the date and argued the song should not appear there without one. The disagreement also concerned whether the song’s inclusion required a separate release date, since one editor considered its radio date insufficient for the infobox.

2012.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should be titled as a civil war or an uprising: one proposal argued that “civil war” was becoming the more common and accurate description, while an opponent said Wikipedia should follow how reliable sources described the conflict and noted that many did not call it a civil war.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether Israel belonged in the article’s list of forces involved in the war: some pointed to Israeli air strikes and exchanges of fire with Syrian forces as evidence of military involvement. Others argued these were limited border responses or strikes linked to Israel’s conflict with Hezbollah, not participation in Syria’s civil war, and proposed covering them in a separate section on border incidents.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over how the article’s infobox should group the Kurdish forces, Syrian opposition and Islamic State: one proposal grouped Kurdish forces with the opposition and separated Islamic State, while an opposing editor argued the Kurds should not be grouped with the opposition because they were not allied with it and had clashed with rebel groups.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should emphasize critics’ descriptions of Gorka’s expertise and views or explain his arguments and how they differed from previous administrations’ approaches. They also disputed whether to include reporting linking him to antisemitic groups: some editors cited its pickup by other outlets, while others argued the coverage repeated a single source and questioned its accuracy and reliability.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether episode-list entries should use brief descriptions or longer, more complete plot summaries, with one editor arguing that longer summaries were appropriate and another opposing them. The disagreement also touched on spoilers: one editor objected to the longer summaries partly because they revealed plot details, while others argued that spoiler concerns should not determine how much information the summaries include.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should describe the Souliotes’ identity, including whether to call them an Albanian tribal community and how to present their later identification with the Greek nation. They also disputed whether participation in the Greek War of Independence was the key setting for that identification, or whether the account should emphasize the clans’ military and political circumstances and their later settlement in Greece.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Robert Sarvis belonged in the election infobox: some argued his polling and coverage warranted inclusion, while others said the available coverage and polling did not justify listing him alongside the two major-party candidates.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Ernst’s remarks about weapons of mass destruction in Iraq should be accompanied by coverage describing the response as negative or controversial: some said the criticism was significant and sourced, while others objected to the wording and weight. They also disputed whether the biography should include a news article’s critical framing of Ernst’s Agenda 21 remarks, or simply report her stated position without commentary on the issue.

2025.summary: Editors noted that Season 28’s coaches appeared in different chair orders across the article’s lists and tables; one editor favored the order in the season infobox, while another said the order was not yet known.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the section on public response should be removed or revised, with one objection describing its opening quotation and cultural explanations as misleading, while others favored keeping sourced material in a shorter or reworded form. They also disputed whether to retain the term “gaman”: one editor called it misleading and unnecessary, while another pointed to its use in a source’s title.

Editors disagreed over whether to include a Hollywood Reporter review in the tour’s critical response section after the performer’s manager reportedly challenged its accuracy. One editor argued that the criticism did not make the reviewer’s opinion less valid, noting that the manager was defending his client.

Editors disagreed over how much detail the article should include about demonstrations of the device: some favored reducing the long list, while another argued that the article should report the demonstrations neutrally. Others objected that extensive demonstration data could suggest the device worked despite the lack of independent scientific verification, and argued that the doubts about those demonstrations needed clear emphasis.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the film’s critical reception: one participant called it extremely negative, while another argued against interpreting Rotten Tomatoes’ scores and favored relying on its percentage and review summary. They also disputed whether to include commentary by a Rotten Tomatoes editor who disagreed with critics’ response; supporters considered the remarks worth noting, while an opponent viewed the material as an unnecessary counterweight and too prominent.

2021.summary: Editors disagreed over how to divide the career section: one favored the earlier album-based headings, while another objected that the latest heading referred to After Hours despite also covering the newer “Dawn” era; a proposed title change was offered as a fix. They also debated whether to group albums into fewer, longer sections or keep the sections more evenly sized, with one editor arguing that too many short sections hindered readability and another defending the existing layout.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over the infobox’s meeting totals and head-to-head records: one argued that sourced competitive-match figures should be shown, while another said the displayed competitive figures were wrong and supplied different counts. The exchange also called for references and argued that both competitive-only and all-time records should appear.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include critic Taran Adarsh’s reviews: one opposed including them, calling him a “sold out” critic, while others argued that he was a reliable critic.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list the songs contestants performed during the judges’ houses stage, with supporters arguing that the songs mattered in a singing competition. Opponents said the available lists could be incomplete or misleading because contestants performed multiple songs, not all performances were shown, and those performances did not determine who was eliminated.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening scene should be described, particularly whether the planet was Earth and whether the alien was deliberately seeding it with life; some cited filmmaker comments while others argued that the scene left those details uncertain. They also disputed whether the scene belonged in the plot summary: some considered the black liquid and its apparent link to DNA central to the story, while others said the scene’s place, timing, and connection to later events were unclear.

Editors disagreed over whether the effort should be framed as a campaign to establish a new word or as a personal attack or slur; others argued that such labels were judgmental and that the title should describe an effort without implying that the word had become established. They also disputed how prominently to present the proposed definition: some wanted it near the start so readers could find it, while others objected that placing it first would make the article appear to promote the redefinition.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the season article should include the order in which contestants were called safe, with some repeatedly restoring the information after others removed it. Those against including it called the order trivia that did not affect the results, while a supporter argued it belonged in the article even though it could be found elsewhere.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe South American ticket sales: some wanted reports of low demand and promotional discounts retained, while others accepted that information but argued the section should be shortened and attendance estimates removed as unofficial. One editor cited differences between local media estimates and figures later reported by Billboard to argue that the estimates were unreliable.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over what should define a console generation: some emphasized whether reliable sources group or compare devices, while others argued that release timing and the way products are marketed also matter. They also disagreed about whether smaller or less conventional systems released alongside the major consoles belonged in this article’s generation listing or should be treated separately; one editor supported including them in an “Other” category, while another proposed separating microconsoles from console generations.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over the episode summaries’ length and detail: one said several were too long and trimmed them, while another proposed shorter, more thematic versions. Other editors objected that the proposed summary left out important events and used promotional-sounding language.

2008.summary: Editors disagreed over revisions adding episodes from Joseph Smith’s life: some said the additions emphasized negative details and would make an already long biography bloated, while the revising editor said the goal was to remove trivia and shorten the article. One critic argued that selecting only certain details from a single biography skewed the account, while the revising editor defended using that source and invited others to choose material they considered appropriate.

2010.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraphs placed too much emphasis on Smith’s controversies and crises: one view called for foregrounding his religious legacy, while another argued that the crises were major parts of his life and belonged in the summary. They also disputed whether to mention his planned millennial government there, with one editor saying it helped explain events leading to his death and another arguing it was not important enough to feature prominently.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Joseph Smith’s early treasure-seeking and use of supernatural methods belonged in the article’s opening paragraph: one argued this context mattered to understanding the golden plates, while others said it gave too much prominence to an early-life topic already covered in the article. They also disputed how to describe the Smith family’s religious background, with one editor arguing that Christian practices should be acknowledged alongside folk magic and that the latter needed historical context.

Editors disputed whether the article should describe Breivik as a Christian fundamentalist. Some argued the label relied on an early police statement and conflicted with his own descriptions of his beliefs; others favored retaining it because news outlets reported the authorities’ characterization.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over describing Robinson as far-right: some objected that the label was pejorative and favored attributing it to media sources, while others argued that reliable sources used it and it was not a slur. They also debated whether to mention police injuries at a rally held while Robinson was jailed, with some seeing the violence as relevant context and others objecting that he was not involved and the detail could suggest responsibility.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to use familiar news-reporting terms such as “convicted” and “imprisoned” for Robinson’s contempt proceedings, or to distinguish a finding of contempt from a criminal conviction and committal to prison. Some argued that changing the wording required reliable secondary sources, while others said the legal distinction mattered to his appeal and release and that the article should reflect it.

2012.summary: Editors questioned which budget figure to use, noting that reports differed; an edit request proposed a budget of Rs 80 crore. One editor described the figures as differing and said the article’s existing sources were unreliable, while adding budget information based on the submitted source.

Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe the counter-jihad movement as Islamophobic and far-right outright or say that scholars had applied those labels, with one editor arguing that doing otherwise generalized across groups with differing views. Others argued that researchers characterize the movement in those terms and that the labels referred to a specific political current, not everyone opposed to Islam or Islamic extremism.

Editors disagreed over whether Caroline Sullivan’s remark that Adele “now has the advantage” in ballads could be paraphrased as saying Adele was better at them. One editor argued that this went beyond Sullivan’s wording, while another defended the paraphrase as a comment on Lewis’s former strength in ballads.

Editors disputed whether to call Newcastle United’s stadium the Sports Direct Arena: one side pointed to an official club source and supported using the sponsored name, while another argued that people did not use that name.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Heng Samrin belonged in the main list: some argued that his office qualified because Kampuchea was formally independent, while another objected that the state was not recognized by the United Nations and challenged the legitimacy of his tenure.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe inequality, unemployment, corruption, and corporate influence as the protests’ targets without qualification, or make clear that these were protesters’ perceptions rather than established facts about conditions in the United States. One editor argued that further qualification would cast doubt on the protesters’ stated aims, while another said presenting the claims without qualification risked implying they were proven.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s opening should describe Occupy Wall Street as defined by anarchism: one argued that this framing was too broad and belonged in the article body, while others supported including the characterization in the opening paragraph. They also disputed how to describe the 2012 anniversary gathering, with some favoring detailed accounts of arrests and police conduct and others arguing that the article should avoid a one-sided account or include only a brief mention.

Editors disagreed over whether to include the unreleased album *Sirens* in Lana Del Rey’s discography: one editor argued it was unconfirmed and released under the name May Jailer, while another questioned whether the article should cover her work under other names.

Editors disagreed over whether the plot summary should identify Eve as Miss Moneypenny when she first appears or wait until the end, where the film reveals her identity. Those favoring an early identification said summaries need not follow the film’s exact sequence; those favoring a late reveal said naming her earlier would misrepresent how the story unfolds.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe reported disagreements inside the OPERA collaboration: some argued the accounts were rumor, vague, or inconsistent, while others favored including them because news sources had reported them. They also disputed whether to explain that the reported result would challenge special relativity or avoid drawing theoretical conclusions while the result remained uncertain.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether to list “Lawhead” as an alternate name, with some arguing that its appearance in very few sources did not justify including it and others saying sources used the name and it could be listed without replacing “Lipscomb.” They also disagreed over how much of her full name and birth date to include: some favored retaining those details as sourced biographical information, while others supported limiting the article to her birth year and omitting her middle names and exact date.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over which non-racing drivers belonged in the season’s team table: some favored limiting it to drivers who took part in practice or served as designated reserves, while others argued that development or testing roles also qualified, or that the whole category should be removed.

2011.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Nintendo 3DS version should be described as confirmed or still a rumor: one editor cited reports and magazine scans, while another remained unconvinced because there was no gameplay footage and questioned whether the images were genuine. They also disputed whether the PC release’s Steam requirement belonged in the article, with one editor seeking to mention it and another arguing it was irrelevant to the game’s release format.

2019.summary: Editors disputed whether Buttigieg should be described as a “combat veteran”: one argued that the term requires a Navy combat-action ribbon, while another said it commonly includes veterans deployed to a combat zone. The latter editor said the article followed the usage found in reliable sources.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Pool as far-right, with one editor objecting that the cited coverage did not establish his political affiliation and others defending the description as supported by reliable reporting. They also debated whether to include coverage connecting Pool to a Russian-funded media company: some favored an attributed account based on multiple news reports, while others argued the allegations were unproven and did not establish that Pool knew about the funding.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Billy Eichner belonged in the cast list before his role size was known: one editor said he might be a recurring character or guest, while another pointed to the article’s upcoming-cast section. The same discussion said Billie Lourd had been confirmed as a lead and added her.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list departures from the judging panel based on media reporting and a judge’s Twitter statement, or to wait for direct confirmation from Fox; one editor said reporting confirmed two departures, while another said Twitter was insufficient and questioned whether Paula Abdul had left.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether non-English programs should be grouped in a separate section or placed alongside English-language programs by genre. Supporters of a separate section pointed to the article’s English-language focus and the majority of titles being in English, while opponents argued that shows should be grouped by genre regardless of language.

2019.summary: Editors debated whether the tables should distinguish canceled series from series that had concluded, with one proposal defining the difference by whether a show reached an ending and a reply questioning whether editors could reliably make that distinction.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed about how to divide the growing list: some favored separating current and former programming, while another editor argued for dividing it by decade instead. Supporters of the current/former split said it was a good starting point, while the decade-split advocate said it would make the former-programming lists a fixed size and be easier to carry out.

2024.summary: Editors disputed when series should move to the ended-programming list: one questioned removing 2024 Korean series and pointed to the return of renewed Bloodhounds, while another said the agreed threshold was nine months and that limited series without a planned second season count as ended.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the series’ architecture: one comment called its parts rebadged Fermi chips for the original-equipment market, while another said Kepler was the generation’s name but had not been confirmed for the 600 series.

Editors disagreed over match durations being added during the live event, including whether stopwatch measurements were suitable sources; a participant said the timing-based edits and reversions had led to the page being locked. Another participant objected that the lock prevented timely updates, while an administrator said the temporary lock was used to address repeated editing and review the situation.
Editors disputed the spellings of Pefko, Pesce and Alegre; one editor argued for those forms over alternatives such as Pefkos, Peche and Allégre.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a section identifying a tropical low near the boundary of the Australian region as the same system as Cyclone Uesi: one argued that Australian Bureau of Meteorology records placed the low in the region, while another said the sources did not explicitly link it to Uesi and making that connection would be unsupported.

2014.summary: Editors debated whether to cover interpretations of the film as having LGBT themes, with some arguing that the discussion merited a place in the article and others questioning whether it was substantial enough to include. They also disputed how to frame the material, including whether wording should make clear that these were viewers’ interpretations rather than an established portrayal of Elsa as an LGBT character.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Ron Paul should be marked “out” in an article about the primaries: one argued he had not left the race during the primary process, while another said he was out and suggested labeling him “Defeated” or “Lost.”

An editor questioned whether the event merited an article without reliable secondary sources, arguing that news reports did not establish its notability; other participants pointed to extensive coverage from major outlets. Another editor maintained that reports about mixed martial arts events often analyze and compare information, and therefore can qualify as secondary sources. The disagreement concerned whether the available news coverage met the sourcing standard for establishing the event’s notability.

2013.summary: Editors disputed the film’s first-day box-office total: many publications reported 33.12 crore, while Box Office India reported 29.25 crore, producing different claims about whether the film set an opening-day record. Some argued that the article should include both reported figures, while others favored relying on Box Office India alone to keep figures consistent across Hindi-film articles and to use independent data.

Editors disagreed over whether to describe Angie Miller’s elimination as controversial: one argued the criticism was supported by sources, while another said the available coverage was mainly from blogs and minor outlets and treated the elimination as a surprise rather than an established controversy.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should mention the separate story about Barack Obama eating dog meat as a child: some argued that news coverage connected the two episodes and that the response belonged in the article, while others said the childhood story was unrelated to the specific Romney incident and outside the article’s scope.

Editors disagreed over whether to describe some tour dates as not sold out: one side cited news reports of unsold seats, while others said official box-office figures showed those dates had sold out. They also disputed what “sold out” meant, with one editor questioning a promoter’s use of the term when only the number of tickets offered for sale had been sold, and another describing that reporting method as an industry standard.

Editors disagreed over whether audition dates and guest judges should be shown in a table or in prose: one preferred the table, while another argued for prose. They also discussed whether to include the wildcard phone vote in the results table; one editor suggested including it, while others noted that the acts were not finalists and had not performed.

Editors disagreed over whether reported counts of Limbaugh’s insults should be treated as attacks on Fluke, since some remarks referred to Georgetown women generally, and whether Media Matters could reliably count them; others argued that the count showed the extent of the remarks. They also debated whether a count belonged in the opening paragraph or only in the article body, noting that published totals differed, including figures of 47 and more than 20.

Editors disagreed over whether to describe the physical encounter as a “fight,” which some said implied a mutual confrontation, or use a more neutral term such as “encounter”; others argued that “fight” was used by the sources and reflected the accounts of those involved. They also disputed whether to include Martin’s earlier school suspensions: some considered them unrelated to the shooting, while others argued they could help readers assess competing accounts, though they did not suggest Zimmerman knew about the suspensions.

Editors disagreed over whether to keep a separate page listing all episodes or redirect it to the first book’s episode section: one view was that the separate page duplicated content while only one book had aired, while others argued that a combined list should remain available. They also disputed how to group the books, with one editor arguing that buying more episodes did not make a new season and another saying sources described two seasons divided into four books.

2016.summary: Editors disputed whether the New Day–League of Nations match should be described as a four-on-three handicap match and whether the tag team titles were at stake: one editor said the evidence pointed to a handicap match, while another cited a source describing a handicap match with the titles not at stake. Editors also disagreed over whether Charlotte should be marked as a defending champion in the results table, with one view treating her as defending the Divas title and the other saying only the newly introduced Women’s title was being contested.

2017.summary: Editors disputed whether the article should describe the André the Giant Battle Royal as having 30 participants: one questioned whether that total was supported by sources, while another pointed out that WWE’s page listed only 24.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Conor’s departure after he took the £50,000: some argued it should be recorded as an eviction, while others favored “walked” or wording that described his choice to leave with the money. They also disagreed over how much of the series’ controversy section to retain, with one editor cutting it to two incidents and another arguing that more of the reported controversy should be included.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening definition should describe restrictions on women’s rights as an established effect of Republican initiatives or qualify that description as a viewpoint, since the initiatives’ effects and the meaning of “rights” were contested. They also disagreed over the article’s scope: some argued it should focus on the political phrase and how it is used, while others said it should cover the policies the phrase refers to as well.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list Unforgettable’s summer 2013 episodes and renewal on the 2012–13 schedule or under the prior season, since it had not been renewed to air beyond the start of the 2013–14 season. Some argued it belonged on the earlier schedule, while others wanted it kept here to explain its unusual cancellation and renewal.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should state that the PlayStation 4 was about 50% more powerful than the Xbox One: some argued that reports supported including the comparison, while others questioned its evidence and opposed including it, or at least placing it in the opening paragraph.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to place the season in a category for LGBT-related television, with one side arguing that its openly gay contestants and winning same-sex couple made that classification appropriate, while others said the show was not produced to include LGBT people. Those opposing the category also argued that the contestants’ identities or relationship did not make LGBT issues significant to the season’s subject; supporters pointed to the couple’s relationship and reasons for racing as important parts of the season.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Manu Bennett’s Slade should be listed as recurring cast: some argued that appearing in multiple episodes qualified him, while another editor distinguished a planned multi-episode story arc from a recurring role and challenged the sources calling it recurring. They also disputed whether the series’ Roy Harper should be linked to the comic-book character; one editor argued the connection was clear, while another required a source that explicitly confirmed it and accepted one source as meeting that standard.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should name Bose in connection with sponsored webisodes: one argued the sponsor was no more relevant than products appearing in regular episodes and that naming it amounted to advertising. Others argued the sponsor was central because the webisodes were created to promote its product, and that omitting the connection would obscure the promotional tie-in.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over describing the series as a loose adaptation of the comics: supporters pointed to substantial differences and cited sources using that description, while opponents argued that key characters and elements remain recognizable and the wording overstates the changes. Editors also disputed whether the series belonged in a category for LGBT-related television programs because it features significant LGBT characters; some argued that the category was for programs where LGBT identity or relationships are a defining theme or plot element, and suggested a separate category or list instead.

2012.summary: Editors questioned describing Dani as third because her exact placing was not announced on the show; replies argued she should be listed fourth, noting that the final did not establish second and third places and that she was not in the final dance-off.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to retain a section listing contestants’ past semifinal placements: one editor proposed correcting which countries had placed in particular years, while another said the section was minor trivia and its sources unreliable.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether academic material explaining that “pedophile” is sometimes used loosely belonged in the article: one argued it clarified terminology, while another said it created an unsupported link to Yiannopoulos. They also disputed how to describe his remarks about relationships between younger boys and older men, with one editor objecting that the opening paragraph’s use of “very often” was unsupported in that context and another suggesting wording that kept the phrase tied to his comments about positive experiences.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to remove the defunct My Vortexx website from the article: one editor called for its removal, while another argued that the link should remain as archival information that adds to the article.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Emily VanCamp should be described as a female lead: one argued that a report about her audition supported that wording, while another relied on Marvel’s press release listing her among the supporting cast.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe the film as a British-American co-production or as an American production made in the United Kingdom. The co-production argument pointed to British production credits and work, while opponents said the cited sources did not identify the film as British and argued that those credits alone did not establish its nationality.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether dance names in the tables should be capitalized throughout: one argued this matched earlier seasons and looked clearer, while another said only the first word should be capitalized unless a name includes a proper noun. They also disagreed over using verified social media accounts to source dance details and performance order; one editor considered them reliable firsthand sources, while another said social media was unreliable and that unsupported information about future events should be removed.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe an Avengers: Earth’s Mightiest Heroes episode: one wanted the article to say that both Hank Pym and Scott Lang appear, arguing that otherwise Lang could seem to be its main focus; another favored emphasizing Lang’s introduction because Pym’s connection to the film was already established and the article is about the film.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether Jeremy Renner should be listed as returning to play Hawkeye, with the disagreement centering on how clearly published reports supported that casting claim. Some argued that multiple reports, including Variety, identified Renner in the sequel, while others read those reports as assumptions based on director Joss Whedon discussing Hawkeye and said stronger confirmation was needed.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the plot summary should say Vision destroys Ultron: one argued that the final flash and surrounding events imply Ultron is killed, while others said the scene does not show what happens and favored saying only that Vision confronts Ultron’s last body.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over how much to say about gun-control debate after the shooting: some argued it merited a section, while others favored a brief mention or links to related articles, keeping the focus on the shooting.

Editors disagreed over how to describe Kurdish forces: one argued they opposed the government while seeking to stay out of the fighting, while another said some Kurdish militia fought rebels alongside government forces. They also disputed whether the article gave too much weight to Syrian state news reports, with one editor objecting that its claims were presented as fact and another saying those reports were included because little information came from rebel sources or journalists.

2026.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should retain sections about LGBTQ rights and immigration concerns: one argued that no harm directly related to the tournament had occurred, while another said the concerns were grounded in government actions and statements and should not be removed. In a separate exchange, editors contested how to describe Iran’s participation, including whether wording about the ongoing war should identify the United States and Israel as waging it or refer to the war without assigning that description.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over how much to say about the studio’s use of crunch time: one position called for fuller coverage of alleged broken promises and fan reaction, while others argued the controversy did not merit its own section and questioned wording about repeated promises. Editors also disagreed over whether to describe the game as an action-adventure title or an RPG, citing different descriptions from the developer and game stores.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether an online Doctor Who Appreciation Society fan poll could support claims that fans disliked the season: one editor cited the results as evidence of criticism, while others objected that the poll was limited and its averages were not clearly shown. They also disagreed over whether the reception section gave too much weight to professional reviews and too little to fan views, with one editor alleging that published criticism misrepresented broader audience reaction and others favoring established reviews over online opinion.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to add more context about DeSantis’s Guantanamo service, including his advice that force-feeding was legal, the United Nations’ view of force-feeding, and detainees’ allegations; opponents argued that the existing account was sufficient and that the proposed expansion gave the issue too much weight. Editors also challenged a COVID passage based on an encyclopedia, saying it copied wording and portrayed DeSantis as responsible for avoiding bad outcomes, while a defender disputed that interpretation but supported removing the material because of concerns about the source.

2019.summary: Editors disputed whether “Rojava” appropriately named the broader administration: some argued it was widely used for the polity, while others said it referred to a smaller Kurdish region and favored a North and East Syria name that better matched the administration’s scope.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “Loveeeeeee Song” should be identified as an album single: one said it had been sent to UK radio, while another argued it was not an official single because there was no promotion, single cover, music video, or confirmation from Rihanna or her team. A further comment questioned whether reports calling later tracks the fifth and sixth singles could establish this track as the fourth.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Tropical Storm Linfa warranted a separate article: opponents argued its reported deaths and damage were part of wider flooding involving multiple weather systems, while supporters said Linfa aggravated the disaster and its impacts merited fuller coverage. The discussion also questioned whether the existing flood article adequately covered Cambodia and whether reporting on Linfa was reliable enough to support a separate account.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail the article’s controversy section should include: one argued that remarks and their consequences belonged there, while another said it should avoid cataloguing contestants’ comments and remain brief.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether box-office coverage should use Box Office India figures alone or also report figures from other trade analysts; supporters of a separate account of conflicting reports pointed to a substantial gap between the estimates, while opponents favored relying on one source.
