They also disputed whether the film should be described as a worldwide blockbuster based on claims attributed to independent trade analysts, or whether the wording should attribute that label only to its production company.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether episode summaries should call Malcolm by his first name, as the page had generally done, or use “Merlyn,” which other editors said better reflected how the show identified him. A proposal to create separate season articles drew support from editors who wanted the information better organized, while others argued a split should wait until there was enough sourced production, casting, broadcast, and reception information to support those articles.

Editors disagreed over how to display the highest-grossing films’ box-office figures, with one defending the existing full-dollar table and another arguing for a different format and asking for a reason to retain that level of detail. A related disagreement concerned whether rounded figures such as “1.7 billion” were misleading or an acceptable summary, with discussion also raising ambiguity in the word “billion” across numbering systems.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the album’s critical reception: one request argued for “universal critical acclaim” instead of “generally positive” reviews. Editors responding said it was too early to use that stronger label and pointed to mixed reviews and the album’s review score in support of “generally positive.”

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the film’s characters identified publicly only as “Mason” and “Melina” could be named as Rick Mason and Melina Vostokoff, with one editor arguing the identities were clear from comic-book characters and reports, and others saying the names had not been officially confirmed and should not be presented as fact.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether allegations of election fraud and irregularities should receive a dedicated section in the article: some argued the claims merited coverage, while others said the proposed material was poorly supported or would give the allegations undue weight. Some editors favored mentioning specific claims within coverage of the relevant state contests rather than presenting them as a nationwide controversy.

Editors disagreed over what the article should count as a state win: some favored the candidate with the most votes, while others argued that delegate totals mattered, especially when delegates were split between candidates. One proposed solution was to show separate maps for the popular-vote leader and the candidate with the largest share of delegates.

Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraphs should mention market falls attributed by sources to referendum uncertainty: one editor argued they were important, while another said selecting them would make the introduction unbalanced and that they were better placed in the main article. They also disputed whether to list prominent supporters of each side in the introduction, with critics calling the selection one-sided and others defending it as representative; a shorter description naming the two official campaign groups was offered as an alternative.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include reports about a sting operation that allegedly showed six of seven party candidates accepting unregistered donations in exchange for favors: one argued it merited coverage given the party’s anti-corruption platform, while another urged caution because the claims were allegations and the sting came from a non-mainstream organization.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe the events as genocide or frame that label as an allegation, with one editor arguing that the label lacked broad legal or academic recognition and another rejecting the word “allegation.” They also disputed how to use a book that applies a broader, contested definition of genocide: some argued its claims should be explicitly attributed and contextualized, while others questioned whether it could support the article’s central characterization.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to remove the attendance and gross-revenue columns before figures were available; one wanted them removed, while others argued the columns could stay and tour pages did not need identical layouts.

Editors questioned which of two different audience figures reported by The Guardian and Digital Spy should be used, and later distinguished a peak that included ITV+1 from one that did not. They also disagreed over whether viewers objecting to judges’ decisions amounted to a notable controversy worth including, or was a recurring reaction that did not warrant coverage.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should include a map and a table tallying electoral votes based on state polling: one editor said the totals were uncited predictions, while another described the map as a picture of polling rather than election results. One proposal was to keep the map but remove the vote counts; a defender argued that the counts were calculations based on cited polls, not predictions of the election outcome.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether episode-viewership figures should be rounded to one or two decimal places: one editor proposed tenths, while others favored retaining hundredths. The discussion cited differing practices across television articles and the precision of the cited ratings data, while also noting concerns about uncertainty and repeated reversals.

2012.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to call the event a “massacre” or keep “shooting” in the article title: some favored “massacre,” while others argued that a title should follow the wording that reliable news sources commonly used and that it was too early to decide. They also disputed a sentence about whether Lanza could legally possess the handguns because he was under 21; one editor defended including it as a factual point, while another challenged the wording and changed “possess” to “obtain.”

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the election infobox should present coalitions or individual parties: some argued coalitions were informal and that party results should be shown, while others said coalitions mattered to the election and were how official results were reported. A later discussion noted that the Five Star Movement had the most votes among individual parties while the centre-right coalition had more votes overall, prompting objections that listing coalition leaders’ parties alongside coalition results could confuse readers.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the distributors’ statement about evaluating the global theatrical market explained the delay or merely described how they reached the decision; one view was that COVID-19 was the reason, while another favored including the statement as the distributors’ own, deliberately vague explanation. They also debated whether reporting about the financial consequences of closed theaters could be included: one editor called the reporting speculative, while another argued it was acceptable if clearly attributed to the news source and its reporting method.

2013.summary: Editors debated whether to title the article around Alexander’s murder or Arias’s trial: supporters of the murder title cited her conviction, while others favored a trial title because Arias drew more media attention and argued that murder wording could imply a point of view. Editors also disputed the reported number of stab wounds, with some relying on reports of 27 and another editor arguing that the autopsy report supported 29.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep the season marked as ongoing after November 30: some argued that available forecasts showed no further storm was expected, while others said it was too soon to rule one out. They also disputed the season overview’s final storm date: November 25 marks when Otto left the Atlantic basin, while November 26 marks when it dissipated in the Eastern Pacific.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Hurricane Beryl warranted its own article or whether its history and impacts could be summarized in the season article; arguments turned on its land impacts, amount of available detail, and unusual development. They also disputed how to describe Leslie after it became post-tropical: one editor argued that expected regeneration meant listing September 25 as its dissipation date could be misleading, while others said future regeneration was uncertain and should not be anticipated in the article.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Hurricane Pablo warranted a separate article, with supporters pointing to its unusual formation and record as the easternmost-forming hurricane, while opponents argued that those features alone did not justify a page. Opponents said the storm’s short duration and limited effects on land left too little to cover beyond its section in the season article; supporters compared it with other storms that had separate pages.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over what damage figure to list for Hurricane Sally, because estimates of $1–3 billion referred to insured losses while another cited estimate put overall losses at $7–8 billion. Some argued that the article should use at least $7 billion to reflect total losses, while others preferred keeping the current figure until AON issued another estimate.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should mention a possible link between Brie’s remark and earlier bullying of Kharma: one editor raised the connection, while another called it likely coincidence and said it belonged on other pages.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe the film as primarily Telugu or bilingual: one said it was mainly shot in Telugu with Tamil dialogue, while another cited a source for describing it as bilingual. They also disputed the reported worldwide gross: one editor used a 517-crore estimate from Box Office India instead of 600 crore, while another questioned treating that source’s estimate as more authoritative and argued that the figure should be marked as an estimate.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail to include in the tour’s set list, including songs and musical excerpts that some said were performed but that published reports did not consistently confirm; one editor argued that concertgoers’ accounts and videos were not enough to support those details. Another editor favored a more informative list but also supported removing unsupported items, noting that reports conflicted and that the set list remained uncertain.

Editors disagreed over whether criticism of the tribunal’s proceedings belonged in the protest article: some argued that concerns raised by international organizations were important context, while others said the material took attention away from the protest and belonged in a separate article. They also disputed how much to include about Jamaat-e-Islami’s demonstrations, with one view treating them as relevant opposition to Shahbag and another limiting coverage to protests directly responding to Shahbag.

2018.summary: Editors disputed whether the list overstated India’s overseas bases, with one editor challenging entries such as Farkhor as unsupported by evidence of an Indian air force presence and others saying the entries appeared well sourced. Farkhor was also debated separately: one editor argued there was no operating Indian air base in Tajikistan, while another cited books describing Indian involvement or joint operation and said the evidence was conflicting.

2013.summary: Editors questioned whether to include a transfer table, noting that it was repeatedly added and removed; one editor said they might support a short description of the transfer window but were not convinced by the table.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article could state that Cathy Newman received threats after her interview with Jordan Peterson, or should attribute the claim to Channel 4 editor Ben de Pear, whose statement they argued news reports were repeating. One side said news sources treated the threats as credible; the other stressed that reports offered few specific examples and that an investigation found no direct threats on Twitter, proposing wording that made clear the claim came from de Pear.

2017.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should say that many AfD supporters had racist, anti-Muslim or antisemitic tendencies; some objected that this presented contested claims as fact, while others defended the wording and its sources. Some proposed moving the material out of the opening paragraph and framing it as criticism of the party, while others supported keeping it there.

Editors disagreed over whether Melbourne Victory could be described as having qualified for the 2018 AFC Champions League before the remaining league matches were played; one editor argued that other teams could still finish second, while another’s stated reasoning relied on Victory’s points and goal-difference advantage.

2020.summary: Editors disputed whether McGregor’s infobox should list his height as 5 feet 8 inches, following Sherdog, or 5 feet 9 inches, supported by several other sources. Some favored Sherdog as a consistent source for MMA fighter details, while others argued that this article should use the more reliable independent sources that agreed on 5 feet 9 inches.

2014.summary: Editors discussed where to list “Black Widow” before its release as a single, with replies supporting keeping it among other charted songs until it was released.

2013.summary: The discussion records a request to add Australian tour dates and a follow-up saying the dates had been added.

Editors disagreed over whether the cast box should list every actor who played the Doctor, including those seen only in previously recorded footage, or reserve space for actors appearing in newly filmed scenes. Some argued that the on-screen credits warranted listing all the Doctors, while others said the archive appearances were better explained in the article text rather than the cast box.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe the film as a spin-off or a sequel: one editor pointed to its focus on a different character, while another said it needed reliable sources identifying it as a spin-off and noted that sources called it a sequel.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe the comics said to have informed Anarky’s characterization: one argued that calling them stories from the 1980s was inaccurate because only one relevant story appeared then, while another favored keeping the period reference to reflect a developer’s explanation. They considered describing the material as the earliest stories by the named creators, but also raised the possibility that the source’s account was too muddled to use.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep links for certification information: one objected to their repeated removal, while another questioned the linked site's reliability and said the information should be sourced directly from the RIAA when available.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether “Focus” should be classified as a non-album single or as part of the Dangerous Woman album era, since it appeared on the Japanese edition but not other editions; the discussion ended with it listed in that era with a note explaining the situation.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe the bombings as a terrorist attack: some pointed to official and news coverage, while others argued that the attackers’ motives were not established and the label should be left out or attributed. They also debated publishing photographs released by the FBI of people sought in the investigation; supporters said the images helped document it, while opponents cited privacy and the risk of implying guilt before the people were identified or charged.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to show a German flag for the race while its venue was still listed as unannounced; some argued that flags should wait until a circuit is named. Others argued that the race would be held in Germany, pointing to its name and the lack of any indication that it would take place elsewhere, and said the flag should remain.

2015.summary: Editors disputed whether GP Update was an appropriate source for reporting on Giedo van der Garde, after discussion of the site’s past financial support for him. One position was that this connection made the source unsuitable for his coverage; others argued that the particular report could still be used because its information was supported by other publications and showed no apparent bias.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the song’s title should be treated as “Beautiful,” with the hashtag understood as silent styling, or as “#Beautiful,” following its release listing on iTunes.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include reported commentary that the sequel’s prospects were uncertain, or to give only its scheduled release date and leave out discussion they considered speculation. One proposed describing the uncertainty in a separate sequel section rather than the opening paragraph, while another argued that only confirmed information belonged in the article.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether details revealed in CBS previews of unaired episodes should be added: some argued that clear information from an official preview could be used, while others said previews were unreliable or that episode events should wait until broadcast. Some objected that putting preview-based details in results tables made them look like events that had already aired, while others argued that certain details shown in the preview were clear enough to report.

Editors disagreed over whether the March should be described as an ongoing international grassroots movement or mainly as a worldwide protest event held on May 25, 2013, with organizers hoping to continue it. They also disputed whether major media had largely ignored the protests or covered them through news reports and wire-service stories, and how much space to give commentators who said coverage was inadequate.

Editors disagreed over how much detail to give the Xbox One’s proposed internet-connection and used-game rules: some argued these were major changes whose criticism deserved coverage, while others cautioned against emphasizing negative reactions without a counterpoint from Microsoft. They also disputed how to describe the initial response, with some favoring “mixed” because the console received praise as well as complaints, while another editor argued the initial reaction was mostly negative.

Editors disagreed over whether to call the event the murder of Lee Rigby before a conviction: some argued the term described the killing, while others favored a more neutral title until the court ruled. They also disputed how to present the attacker’s recorded statement, with some urging a complete transcript checked against the video and others favoring excerpts that matched published sources.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over how much criticism of the film belonged in the article: some argued that criticism from the merged material should remain, shortened and represented alongside defenses, while others said many entries were opinion pieces or strayed from the film and called for a much shorter, integrated account.

2013.summary: Editors disputed whether detailed, negative accounts based largely on Ortiz’s own interviews belonged in the article, with one side arguing that the claims lacked independent reporting or were presented out of context and the other insisting that the sourced material should remain. They also disagreed over whether to include incidents involving allegedly faked listing photos and rental listings as controversies, and whether an interview or television footage adequately supported those claims.

2025.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s infobox should count elected officials endorsed by or belonging to the Democratic Socialists of America, with supporters arguing that the figures show the organization’s electoral reach and resemble information given for party-like groups. Opponents argued that DSA is a nonprofit, not a political party, and that its endorsements and members in office cannot be counted clearly enough to present them as DSA representatives.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s coverage was out of balance: one argued that some sections, including awards, asylum and travel, received too much space relative to legal proceedings and public debate, while others said there was no agreed problem warranting a warning tag. They also disputed whether to include a report questioning claims by Snowden’s Russian lawyer; supporters considered the report relevant to how Snowden was presented, while opponents regarded the material as tangential and excessive.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should say Snowden was stuck in a Moscow airport transit area because the United States had canceled his passport. One position cited news reports describing him as unable to travel onward for that reason; another argued that reporting cast doubt on this account and that the paragraph should reflect that uncertainty.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the main article should include the full fixtures and results for the group stage or leave those details to a separate article. Some argued that fixtures were key information about the tournament; others said a short account of the most important events would avoid repeating details available elsewhere. They also debated how to order the material if the results stayed: one editor wanted the prose summary before them, while another argued that the results should be removed altogether.

2017.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should call the film critically acclaimed: one argued the wording overstated the evidence, while others pointed to review ratings and rating-site criteria to support it. They also disagreed over whether the film should be described as a box-office bomb or disappointment, with arguments focusing on its budget, worldwide ticket sales, and the need to attribute such judgments to sources.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to add a list of supposedly confirmed songs before the album’s official tracklist was announced: one editor argued the titles had been confirmed by Gaga and cited sources, while another said those sources did not establish that the songs would appear on the album. A further objection was that the album’s tracklist could change, making a list of confirmed songs premature.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Kimberly’s departure should be dated to Day 44, when she left the house, or Day 45, when it was confirmed she would not return and she decided to leave. They also disputed whether to include exact eviction percentages for Helen and Ashleigh: some editors argued they could be calculated from the announced 1.2% gap, while another objected that the exact figures lacked a source.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should state that Syrian government forces carried out the attack or describe responsibility as unresolved and attribute assessments to their sources. Some argued that the UN investigation and intelligence reports supported assigning responsibility, while others said the available evidence was circumstantial and should not be treated as proof.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Bloomberg’s criticism of claims about European “no-go zones” applied to Gatestone’s wording: some said the article called the claims false, while others argued that judgment concerned a different version of the claim and should not be attributed to Gatestone. They also disputed whether the opening paragraph should say Gatestone had been accused of making false claims about Muslims, with some supporting that summary of criticism and others calling it excessive and objecting to its wording.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over describing the film as Malayalam cinema’s first “family thriller”: one defended the framing as supported by sources, while another argued that the claim was not established and pointed to the director describing the film as a drama. They also disputed whether the film’s gross could be stated as 51 crore, with one editor citing a source that gave a regional breakdown and another questioning whether that source clearly supported the total and was reliable.

Editors disagreed over whether the season summary was too detailed and should be shortened to a concise account, or whether its length was comparable to summaries for other seasons and its detail captured key events. They also debated how to make the voting table fit screens and remain readable: some proposed removing information, while another editor argued that pre-veto nominations should stay and others wanted eviction vote totals retained or represented elsewhere.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the case should remain a separate article or be merged into the page about the exchange, with one editor arguing for a merge and another saying the case warranted its own page. They also disputed how to describe Jignesh Shah: an edit request challenged calling him the scam’s “mastermind” and proposed presenting his role as allegations, while another editor defended the article’s framing by citing a police chargesheet and a regulator’s finding, and argued that bail did not clear him.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should use “Czechia” and “Türkiye,” the names used by UEFA, or the more common English-language names “Czech Republic” and “Turkey.” Those favoring official names argued for following UEFA and FIFA, while others said the article should reflect names commonly used in English-language sources rather than official forms.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over what the table’s numbered placements should represent: one argued they should show each contestant’s final position when leaving the competition, while another said they reflected public-vote results and could not be changed without sourced voting information.

Editors disagreed over whether a Miami-area image accurately represented the pageant venue: one said the event was not being held in Miami, while another argued the image was valid for the region where it would take place.

Editors disagreed over whether detailed discussion of costumes belonged in the tour’s development section or should instead be incorporated into a concert summary; one editor argued that costumes were a defining part of the show and were discussed in many media sources.

2016.summary: Editors disputed whether the game should be described as multiplayer: one position cited earlier descriptions of rare encounters and possible interaction, while another pointed to reports that players could not see or interact with one another.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over which genres belonged in the album’s infobox, with one position favoring pop and electro-R&B, which it said appeared repeatedly in reviews, and rejecting alternatives such as hip-hop and neo-soul. Another view was that the infobox should name only one or two genres describing the album’s overall sound, rather than include genres associated with particular tracks.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Week 4 voting table should show separate Saturday and Sunday columns or one column, citing different precedents for how vote results had been presented in earlier series.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over a new weekly-score table that labeled judges’ scores and made them sortable: its proponent argued this improved comparison, while others favored the established format and said the changes were unnecessary or harder to read. They also disputed whether to keep a separate dance chart: one editor called it duplicate information, while others said it offered a convenient way to see which dances each couple performed.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the series’ final three episodes should be described as one three-part story or as separate stories; the discussion cited differing interpretations of magazine and other evidence, and one editor objected specifically to calling them a three-parter in the article’s opening paragraph. They also disputed how to group the final episodes in the table, with a cited source pairing some episodes together while another editor argued they should be treated as separate stories.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over how much production history belonged in the opening paragraph: one argued it contained too many details, while others defended summarizing the film’s development milestones there. They also differed over what context to prioritize, including the lead actor and the character’s earlier appearance versus the film’s place in the Marvel universe and its studio credits.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to mention the “Scare Master” leak and whether to hide its plot summary: some questioned the leak’s significance and whether its temporarily unavailable content could be verified, while others argued the iTunes release date counted as an airing and later pointed to a Canadian broadcast as verification.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over how much space the article should give possible “hard” and “soft” withdrawal arrangements: one wanted the mechanics of a hard exit emphasized and descriptions of Norwegian and Swiss models shortened, while another argued that options discussed in the media should be covered. Others warned against presenting those labels as settled or giving weight to forecasts, arguing that the distinction lacked an authoritative definition and the process remained uncertain.

2017.summary: Editors disputed whether the article’s economic-effects section gave too much weight to forecasts and overstated economists’ agreement, including by describing it as “overwhelming or near-unanimous.” One side sought more qualification and context about forecasting limits; another argued that the wording was supported by sources and that discussion of long-term assessments and short-term forecasting limits gave readers necessary context.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s sections on the UK’s domestic and bilateral impacts should be moved to a separate page: supporters said they were large and took up a disproportionate amount of space, while opponents argued they were concise and should not be split out. Opponents also argued that other parts of the article could be trimmed instead, and that the topic’s broad scope justified its length.

2016.summary: Editors questioned whether the article should describe Ethereum as software, a protocol, organizational entities, or one or both blockchains, with one view favoring coverage of all these closely connected subjects and another calling for clearer treatment of the two chains. They also disagreed over how much to include about Ethereum Classic: some favored keeping details within the Ethereum article while reliable coverage developed, while others argued the chains should be distinguished and Classic given its own section.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail the article should give to the disputed safety-car procedure at the 2021 Abu Dhabi race: some argued that describing it as an early withdrawal or emphasizing the race director’s error was inaccurate or excessive in Verstappen’s biography, while others said the error and its possible effect on the race should be included.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Eddie Thawne’s death should appear in his brief character description: one objected that it spoiled a season finale and argued such details belonged in fuller character coverage, while another defended its inclusion. The inclusion was defended as useful context for the character’s development and the actor’s departure, while the opposing editor argued that spoilers should be placed with consideration for where readers encounter them.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether the infobox should list violent opposition groups alongside pro-government colectivos: one argued there was no evidence of an organized opposition group and that opposition leaders had called for peaceful protests, while another said violent opposition groups were documented and should also be included.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether reports were enough to state that Tom Holland would appear as Spider-Man: some treated the trade-press reports as definitive, while others argued they were based on unattributed rumors and the article should not present the appearance as certain.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe the political affiliations of referendum observers as context for judging their credibility, with one position arguing that those backgrounds mattered and another objecting that their significance could not be inferred without supporting sources. Some editors favored a general account of the observers, while others opposed labeling their affiliations a concern or detailing individuals when the discussion did not establish that these details were relevant to the whole group.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe characters Bucky and Pronk as a married gay couple based on a filmmaker’s tweet: one editor argued the tweet confirmed it, while others said a tweet was not enough to establish the claim or that it represented Disney’s position.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether the title’s “pro-Russian” label described the events fairly: critics said it characterized one side rather than the conflict as a whole, while defenders said it identified the unrest and distinguished it from earlier protests. They also disagreed over whether the broader article should be framed as unrest or conflict: some stressed that it covered protests beyond the armed fighting, while others considered conflict the more accurate term for events involving extensive violence.

Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should report accounts that the plane remained capable of flying for hours after losing contact and had headed west. Some argued the reporting was sufficiently supported to summarize, while others said the account was a non-definitive working theory and should not appear in the opening paragraph.

Editors disputed whether to describe the twins as American: some argued that their official accounts saying they had become U.S. citizens supported that wording, while another questioned whether citizenship established nationality and objected to relying on self-published material. Other editors pointed to reports describing the twins as Romanian, while a response argued those reports predated their later citizenship and did not rule out describing them as American.

2015.summary: Editors disputed whether to add the 2017 Spider-Man film to the list: a request cited claims that Marvel and Sony had confirmed its place in the shared universe, while the response declined the change without reliable verification that the film itself belonged there.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether an announced film should be described as being about “mutants” or the X-Men, with one view favoring the broader term until the specific team was confirmed and another interpreting the announcement as referring to the X-Men. They also disputed whether Disney+ shows announced alongside the films belonged in this film list: some favored grouping Marvel Studios projects together, while others argued that the page should remain focused on films and television should stay on a separate list.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to describe Russia’s change of Crimea’s status as an “annexation” or use the broader term “incorporation”; one proposal argued the latter avoided taking a side, while opponents said it softened or obscured what happened. They also disputed whether opinion polls showing support among Crimeans should be included: some editors objected that the results were cherry-picked or lacked context, while another supported including them if presented neutrally and with reliable sources.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Lily Rabe should be placed in a named cast category after reports said she would appear in one episode: some argued that appearance made her a special guest, while another editor said no source established how she would be credited. A reviewing editor likewise argued that the cited reports did not expressly classify her as regular, special guest, or recurring cast.

Editors disagreed over whether to keep charts based on reported Ebola cases and deaths: critics argued that unreliable figures and changes in reporting made the charts misleading. Supporters said the figures could still show broad trends and that the charts were useful when their limitations were explained.

2015.summary: Editors disputed whether the announced attendance of more than 76,000 was credible, with one comment citing a report that the actual number in the stadium was about 67,000 and questioning the venue’s capacity. Others argued that floor seating and the stadium’s expandable capacity could make the announced figure possible, while also allowing that the competing attendance information might be wrong.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to present the Donetsk People’s Republic as a claimed state structure or primarily as a war faction, with some pointing to its governing bodies and others arguing that it had little practical governance. That disagreement shaped the choice of infobox: some favored a state-style box, while others preferred one for a war faction or another type of organization.

Editors disagreed over whether the two-part “Smash the Mirror,” broadcast as a two-hour special, should count as one episode or two, with some proposing to wait for episode titles or separate ratings and another editor arguing it was one longer episode rather than two. Other editors pointed to ABC’s recap and streaming pages splitting the story into two parts and argued that each part should have its own row in the season’s episode table.

Editors disagreed over whether Russia belonged in the article’s list of parties to the fighting: some argued that reports of Russian troops and support made it a participant, while others said Russia should be described as accused of involvement rather than as a belligerent. They also disputed whether U.S. military aid warranted listing the United States as a supporter in the infobox; one view treated the reported equipment and training as support, while another argued that the aid was too limited to make the country a party to the conflict.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to put a report of about 2,000 Russian military deaths in the article’s summary box: some argued it should be left out or discussed only in the article text because the original claim had not been verified, while others favored including reported estimates with attribution. The disagreement also concerned whether the reported figures should be presented as a range, with some editors arguing that multiple news outlets made the claim sufficiently reportable and others emphasizing that those outlets had not independently confirmed it.

2016.summary: Editors disputed whether the page needed separate ratings tables in addition to its episode tables, with one editor calling the extra tables duplicative and excessive. Another editor defended separate tables for DVR viewing figures, while the objection was that the tables repeated information and presented live, delayed-viewing and share figures in a confusing way.

2022.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should describe the regiment outright as neo-Nazi or instead explain its origins and contested associations; supporters of the direct label cited sources describing it that way, while opponents said newer sources were more cautious and that the article blurred the military unit with related political groups.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether news coverage was substantial enough to justify a standalone article: one pointed to coverage in major publications, while another argued that most reports only briefly mentioned the chant while focusing on a separate diplomatic incident. A critic also described the article as political promotion and questioned its historical value, while arguing that the chant’s importance to the meme made the article consequential.

Editors disagreed over including Ben Shapiro’s opinion that political views shaped film critics’ reactions: supporters called it noteworthy and argued that Breitbart could be cited for attributed opinions. Opponents said the quote’s placement after named critics could make it seem directed at them, and argued that Breitbart was questionable and the passage raised concerns about claims concerning living people.

2015.summary: Editors questioned how to describe a source’s claim that departures from the books had upset fans, which was discussed in connection with season ratings: one preferred “deviations” to “divergences,” while another wondered whether to rely on an article version whose wording had changed and suggested the versions might address different audiences.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over how much the background should emphasize Palestinian factions’ unity as a factor in the fighting: one side said it received too much prominence and lacked sources explicitly linking it to the conflict, while others argued that it was relevant context that should remain. Editors also disputed whether the article’s photographs adequately represented both sides; some objected that images focused on damage in Israel, while others said image choices should reflect source coverage and were limited by the availability of legally usable photographs.

Editors disagreed over whether to include a detailed table of scores from the film’s Battle of the Bands tournament: one editor proposed adding it, while another argued it was trivia rather than material suited to an encyclopedia article.

Editors disagreed over how to describe responsibility for the crash: one position called for presenting Ukraine’s and Russia’s accusations side by side and noting that no independent investigation had yet assigned responsibility, while another argued that the article should give greater weight to the account supported by most reliable sources. The dispute also concerned whether Russian claims should receive equal space or be treated differently because editors considered their sourcing and support weaker.

2018.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should include the Netherlands and Australia’s formal statement holding Russia responsible, with some arguing it was significant and deserved prominence while others considered it political or too much detail for the opening paragraph. They also disagreed over how the infobox should describe the missile’s connection to Russia, including whether wording risked implying that Russian forces fired it when that had not been established in the discussion.

2014.summary: Editors disputed whether the grand-jury proceedings should be described as atypical: some favored comparison with usual proceedings, while others argued that this lacked context because the jury was examining the case rather than following the more common process of considering charges already brought. They also disagreed about whether that comparison fairly described the proceedings.

2018.summary: Editors questioned whether a five-pronged spear should be called a “trident” or a “quindent,” while replies pointed to the film’s use of “trident” and argued that the article should follow reliable sources.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over how the opening paragraph should summarize reviews: some defended a sourced roundup praising the film, while others argued the wording should reflect the wider review coverage in the article rather than rely on that early summary. They also debated whether to characterize the overall reception as positive and how to describe criticism of the story.

2016.summary: Editors disputed whether the film was based on Kipling’s works or on the animated film, with one editor arguing that sources supported the former description and calling the latter an unsupported opinion.

2017.summary: Editors debated how the opening paragraph should describe the casting criticism: some favored calling it a whitewashing controversy, while another preferred wording that said the casting drew accusations of whitewashing from Western critics. They also disagreed over including Japanese-American actresses’ views that beauty standards in Japan help explain the limited local reaction; one editor questioned whether their interview represented a Japanese perspective, while another argued it added a perspective otherwise missing from the article.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening should foreground harassment and sexism or give more space to supporters’ stated concern about ethics in video game journalism. They also disputed whether claims that the ethics concerns had been disproven should be stated directly or framed as conclusions reached by news sources, with concerns about both accuracy and neutrality.

2015.summary: Editors debated how to present Gamergate supporters’ stated aim of improving ethics in video-game journalism alongside reports of harassment. They disagreed over whether to describe the ethics claims as a genuine stated goal, a justification for harassment, or both.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe audience response: some argued that news coverage of fan dissatisfaction warranted inclusion, while others said the online ratings driving the discussion could be skewed and that the scale of dissatisfaction was unclear. Some favored summarizing reported criticisms of the film, including its treatment of Rey’s parentage, Snoke, and Luke, while others wanted discussion grounded in critics’ analysis rather than audience polls.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe the film as divisive among audiences, or foreground positive results from controlled polls and treat negative online ratings as less representative. They also disputed how much space to give claims that online ratings had been manipulated: some argued that those claims and the company’s response deserved inclusion, while others said the response that no unusual activity was detected should weigh against presenting manipulation as a live possibility.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to rename the article “Umbrella Revolution” or “Umbrella Movement,” or retain “2014 Hong Kong protests”: supporters cited usage and specificity, while opponents said no alternative was clearly dominant and questioned its framing. They also disputed whether coverage of protest organization, cleanliness and logistical support belonged in the article: some wanted sourced accounts retained, while others considered the section too long or promotional and sought shorter, more neutral wording.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over how the voting-history table should describe Julia during the first five weeks, with proposals including “Non-HouseGuest,” “Not Eligible” and “Not in house.” They also disputed whether votes cast while the twins alternated should be credited to Liz, the identity they shared in the game, or attributed to Julia when she cast them.

2024.summary: Editors corrected an infobox entry that incorrectly listed the Philadelphia Eagles instead of the Cleveland Browns as Garrett’s team from 2017 to 2024.

2015.summary: Editors differed over whether colored cells should be used in the results table: one argued that the text remained readable without the colors, while another said the colors still had to meet accessibility standards. The discussion also raised concerns about symbols, color contrast, and making the table key easy to navigate.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include Krennic’s visit to Vader in the plot summary: some argued the scene mattered, while others questioned its role in driving the plot and pointed to the word limit for plot sections. They also debated how to describe coverage of the film’s computer-generated images, with one editor arguing that criticism was overrepresented and that reviews offered mixed reactions, while others questioned whether the section warranted a controversy label.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Proplyd 133-353’s listed radius should be treated as an upper limit: one argued that dust would not materially distort the estimate, while another said the estimate depended on an unproven assumption that surrounding dust did not affect the measurements. They also differed over its classification, with one editor arguing that it was likely planetary-mass and another noting that the cited models did not conclusively distinguish a planet from a brown dwarf.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should describe the film as planned to be a sequel, with some favoring cautious wording because it was unreleased and others arguing that the qualifier cast unnecessary doubt on its relationship to the previous film.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article’s record-setting box-office claim should note that it was not adjusted for inflation; one editor sought that qualification, while others argued that figures are normally presented without inflation adjustments. They also disputed how much detail belonged in the plot summary: a proposal sought added explanations and character moments, while editors argued that some material belonged in an analysis section or that the summary should stay concise.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should give a budget range because sources reported different figures, or distinguish a $260 million gross budget from a $217 million net budget; one editor argued that the figures should not be labeled gross and net without evidence. They also disputed how to identify Steven Barr’s character: while one source was said to credit him as Volleybot, the article’s Topspin identification was challenged as relying on a fan-edited wiki rather than a reliable source.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep a separate “competitive races” section: critics called it redundant and said its assessments were speculative, while its author argued it could be improved rather than discarded. Several editors proposed moving sourced material into state-specific coverage and removing claims they considered unsupported.

2016.summary: One editor removed several sources used for box-office figures as unreliable, citing a site that described its numbers as unofficial and unconfirmed and other sources the editor considered unsuitable; the sources were later restored without explanation, leaving their use contested.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether evidence about Bulgarian T-72 tanks justified listing them as delivered to Ukraine: one cited a military source, while another argued that tank components did not prove whole tanks had been supplied. The disagreement also concerned whether intelligence assessments and reporting about British AS-90 guns were strong enough to include; one editor defended the source, while the other sought firmer confirmation and said the available evidence was speculative.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the season’s contestant table should label performances as “high” and “low,” with some arguing the categories were hard to determine consistently and others supporting their continued use. Supporters said the labels conveyed how contestants performed, while a critic argued that disputed interpretations without independent sourcing should not be presented as settled results.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should formally classify the siege as terrorism, with some supporting removal of a terrorism label and others arguing that the attacker’s stated claims and public descriptions supported keeping it. Opponents of the label argued that no organizational direction was established and that experts disputed whether the event qualified as terrorism, while supporters pointed to statements by officials and other sources describing it that way.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the charts table should include country-specific charts for international artists when the album had also appeared on that country’s overall album chart: one editor argued those overall-chart positions should be used, while another said the international charts were separate charts and could also be included.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over how to describe Whiterose, with one arguing that the character should be called a cross-dresser unless the show or reliable sources established a transgender identity, and another pointing to the character’s feminine self-reference and comments by the actor and creator as evidence that she is transgender. The discussion also disputed whether the article needed to clarify the character’s sex at birth or physical traits; one editor said the term “transgender woman” could be ambiguous, while another argued that such clarification was unnecessary.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the organisation’s name should appear as “Spectre” or “SPECTRE”: some said the film did not establish it as an acronym, while another argued that the established name should be capitalized. They also disagreed over whether to name Blofeld in the opening paragraph; some wanted the reveal kept out of that prominent position, while others argued his return was notable enough to mention there and that the article need not conceal plot details.

Editors disagreed over whether the background should include concise information about France’s Muslim population and social context: one position argued this helped readers understand the reporting and the event, while another considered it too far from the article’s focus. The opposing concern was that including demographic information could suggest a connection between population growth and the attackers’ actions; the proposal’s supporter argued the suggested wording did not assign blame to Muslims as a group.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over how to record the scheduled Rusev–Reigns bout, which became a brawl before the opening bell: one argued it should be excluded from the results table because no match began, while another said the confrontation belonged there as a no-contest or in a footnote.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the cast section’s long character quotations were useful information or unnecessary material that made the section cumbersome. Some argued that worthwhile details should be retained in shortened or paraphrased form, while others wanted the block quotations removed, with useful points paraphrased and padding discarded.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over how much detail the event’s storylines needed: some wanted substantial cuts to a section they considered overly long, while another argued the event’s extended build-up justified exceeding the usual recommended length. They also disputed whether discussion of negative reactions to Roman Reigns belonged in the event’s background: some considered it relevant and professionally presented, while others argued it was negative in tone and better placed in the storyline section or elsewhere.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to label The Undertaker as part of Raw in the participant list: one pointed to his recent and expected appearances, while another argued that the list should reflect his official status on the event date, when WWE did not list him under a brand.

2015.summary: Editors differed over whether to mention “The Main Event” as another short: one asked whether it belonged in the article, while a reply characterized it as film footage rather than a new short.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the plot summary should describe the post-credits scenes, especially the second scene, which one editor argued was a joke unrelated to the plot. Others argued that the scenes should be mentioned because they are part of the film and similar franchise films include such scenes, while one editor supported mentioning only the mid-credits scene.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to identify Zendaya’s character as Michelle Jones or only as Michelle: some argued that sources supported the surname and helped explain her nickname, while others said the film itself never calls her Jones and argued that its credits should guide the name used.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether actors should be classified as recurring after appearing in multiple episodes, or whether that label required a reliable published source. They also disputed whether Denis O’Hare should be credited as playing both Nick Pryor and Liz Taylor, or only Liz Taylor, treating Pryor as part of her backstory.

Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should say Clinton denied sending or receiving classified information, or more narrowly that she denied handling material marked classified at the time; one participant argued the narrower wording could imply an admission, while another defended it as reflecting her stated position after classified material was reported on the server. They also challenged wording that described emails as containing classified information, with opponents saying it overstated the evidence because some material was classified later or was not marked when sent.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should include reports of hacking attempts and experts’ views that foreign governments may have accessed Clinton’s server. Some argued that the coverage was too limited and that there was no evidence of a successful hack; others said the reported attempts and security experts’ assessments merited discussion, while distinguishing the possibility of access from proof that it occurred.

Editors disagreed over whether the “Supergirl” episode counted as part of the 2016 crossover event, or whether it only set up the crossover in its closing moments. Some argued that official promotions and news reports described a four-part event beginning with “Supergirl”; others said the crossover’s story unfolded in three episodes of the other series, with “Supergirl” serving only as a teaser.

2015.summary: Editors disputed whether to describe the crash as a murder-suicide or use the less specific phrase “deliberate flight into terrain,” with some arguing that reports supported the stronger label and others saying it went beyond what sources established. Those urging caution accepted that the crash was intentional but argued that calling it murder required evidence of intent to kill the passengers, not just evidence of deliberate action.

2024.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should say more about the Post Office’s alleged failure to disclose known problems with Horizon during prosecutions and court proceedings; one editor argued that omitting these points concealed the scandal’s central issue, while another defended reverting a broad rewrite pending discussion. The disagreement concerned how prominently the introduction should frame the alleged non-disclosure and the resulting convictions, rather than whether those topics appeared elsewhere in the article.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the opening paragraph should mention criticism of the film’s narrative: one argued the sources reflected only early festival reviews and that the overall assessment should wait for more reviews, while another said prominent critics supported mentioning the flaw. The objector said detailed criticism belonged in the critical response section, while the other editor argued that leaving it out would be misleading.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include the widely reported exchange between Rowling and Stephen King: one argued it was too fleeting to merit inclusion, while others said it was relevant to the ongoing public debate about her views. They also disputed how to frame the section about her comments on transgender people, with one position favoring a heading focused on the people affected and another proposing a broader title about comments on gender.

2015.summary: Editors questioned whether the nominations table needed UK-versus-US colors, with one saying housemate identities and nomination details were already explained elsewhere and that the colors looked messy and differed from earlier series. They also considered whether an eviction should be labeled as the housemate’s choice or Austin’s, then agreed on Austin’s choice because he made the final eviction decision.

Editors discussed whether the squad section should include players’ appearance and goal totals, transfer fees and time at the club; one editor opposed adding them, while the contributor questioned why similar statistics appeared on another club’s season page.

Editors disagreed over whether the article’s country-style infobox could make Liberland seem like an established country, or whether its disputed status was clear enough that the infobox did not imply success. They also disputed whether to show the flag in the infobox: one editor said its prominent placement could mislead readers, while another argued that it existed and had been reproduced by major publishers.

Editors disagreed over whether to rename the article “Europe’s refugee crisis,” with supporters calling “refugee” more precise and an opponent preferring the existing title because it was more widely used.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Chalamet’s reported possession of French and U.S. passports was sufficient to describe him as a French citizen: one editor said it supported that description, while another noted that a French passport was not conclusive proof of citizenship.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the election article should use an infobox with party leaders’ photos or a more compact results-style box, with some arguing that the photos and extra details made it too large and others defending the information the format could show. They also disputed which parties the box should include, proposing different combinations that ranged from the main parties to a wider selection including smaller and regional parties.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether claims about white farmers in South Africa were a distinct conspiracy theory or one regional form of a broader theory about white populations, and whether the article should separate these topics or explain their connection more clearly. That disagreement shaped objections to naming people as advocates: some editors argued that reporting their South Africa comments did not establish support for the broader theory, while others said sources connected that case to the broader conspiracy and names could be included with context.

2016.summary: Editors questioned wording that presented Martin Shkreli’s offer to buy the album as potentially affecting its release, arguing that the proposal was unlikely to be accepted and did not need consideration. The discussion also challenged the legal argument behind that framing, though the excerpts do not show a defense of it.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the election page should have a summary box before voting: some wanted it removed until results were known, while others argued it should remain as a link to earlier election pages. They also disputed which parties belonged in the box: one editor objected that it omitted the Brexit Party, while another questioned including it before the party’s number of candidates was clear.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the upcoming Batman film should be listed as “The Batman” or as an untitled Batman film. One position treated “The Batman” as the current working title because the filmmaker and reliable sources used it, while the other argued that the film had no confirmed title and that using the name could mislead readers. The discussion also contested whether a working title should be used in the article’s film list when it had not been officially confirmed as the final title.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list a proposed Harley Quinn and Joker film in the article. One editor argued that it had been reported by multiple sources, while another considered the available reporting too prone to repeating rumors and favored waiting for confirmation from an established source.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the planned Blackhawk film belonged in the DC Extended Universe: some argued it should be included based on its connection to DC films and related characters, while others said the available reporting did not confirm a connection to the shared film universe. The disagreement also touched on whether reports linking a separate Joker origin film to the universe were firm enough to justify its inclusion.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over how to summarize critics’ reactions in the opening paragraph: some considered using a broad rating-based description more appropriate than selecting one review or a small group of critics, which one editor argued could misrepresent the overall response.

2016.summary: Editors disputed whether the article gave too much space to controversies, including rally violence, at the expense of campaign developments such as support, results and strategy; some proposed shortening or moving material elsewhere. Others argued that controversy was central to the campaign and that separating it risked glossing over widely reported statements and reactions.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether John F. Kennedy’s character should be described as a president, or as a politician who might appear before becoming president; some argued that the available sources identified him only by the presidential title, while others said his earlier appearance could not yet be ruled out. They also disputed how to list actors credited as guests despite significant appearances: one proposal separated them by season as guest cast, while an opposing view favored keeping the usual cast layout and noting their guest status in a note.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to include a quote from an anonymous Oscar voter in the film’s critical or industry response: some considered its publication in a reliable source enough to include it in the industry section, while others argued that the voter’s anonymity and lack of clear relevance made the quote unsuitable or merely trivia.

2016.summary: Editors discussed whether to present the season’s events in an episode table or a prose summary: one editor favored episode entries that could explain alliances and why people were targeted, while another proposed either using different formats for different editions or choosing one format for all seasons.

2019.summary: Editors disputed whether Hulk Hogan’s 2002 entries should include “Hollywood” before his name; one editor argued that comparable nicknames were omitted for other wrestlers and that full announced names should be listed consistently.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the driver table should keep a column for entrants: some said it repeated information and could be removed, while others argued it showed official team names and should remain. They also disputed how to identify Red Bull’s power unit: one position was to name the Renault-built unit rather than its TAG Heuer branding, while another favored the name used by the team and argued that a note could clarify the branding.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article gave too much space to criticism of Trump’s positions: one editor argued that the page was overly long and criticism-heavy, while others defended including analyses by experts and fact-checkers as context for understanding the positions. They also disputed how to frame the article’s discussion of his political philosophy, including whether critical assessments and descriptions by others should be condensed or given less prominence.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the film’s reception section, which one editor described as mostly positive, should include more negative reviews to avoid selecting only favorable criticism. One editor argued for a roughly even account of positive and negative views, while another cautioned that giving criticism equal space could overstate its importance for a well-received film.

Editors disputed whether the article should describe the Proud Boys as far-right, with one position arguing that the label is an interpretation and should be replaced by the group’s own description of its ideology. Others argued that the label was supported by independent news sources and should remain in the article.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over how much character information belonged in the article: one argued for retaining details such as Zac’s black belt, while another objected to the amount of detail and said minor character information did not belong.

2013.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to list Sergey Sirotkin as a Sauber race driver for 2014: some cited the team principal’s statement that he would race if he earned a required licence, while others argued that this conditional statement did not establish he had a race seat. The dispute also concerned whether the table should track drivers described as signed or only those explicitly confirmed to race, with supporters defending the signed-driver approach and critics calling it misleading when a contract’s terms were unclear.

2014.summary: Editors disagreed over how to order the teams-and-drivers table: some favored sorting by car number, arguing it gave readers a visible pattern, while others preferred alphabetical order or last season’s team standings because the new driver-chosen numbers made the old arrangement harder to follow. They also debated whether to list drivers who took part only in first practice; supporters saw them as participants in the season’s race weekends, while opponents argued their role and contribution were too varied to make an uncontextualized list useful.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed whether the article should present Kim Davis’s life or focus on the marriage-license controversy, with some arguing the controversy was the main source of her notability and others supporting a separate biography. They also disputed whether the controversy article’s title should include Davis’s name or identify the event by its location and subject instead.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the team’s headquarters and practice facility, City National Arena, merited a mention in the main article: one argued it was important to understanding the team, while others considered it too minor for the team’s history. They also differed on where any mention belonged, with support for a brief note in team information rather than the franchise-history section.

2015.summary: Editors disputed whether G.A. Parwez belonged in the article’s list of Quranists: one argued that he rejected the label and that the cited source did not support it, while another considered an unattributed label questionable and suggested it would need to be attributed to specific sources.

Editors disputed whether accounts that the gunman singled out Christians should be included: some cited multiple reports, while others questioned whether the reports were independent or sufficient to establish whom he targeted. They also disagreed over including the college’s rules on firearms, with one editor calling the policy notable and another arguing it did not play a role in the shooting.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the film’s language description should include Hindi and Telugu, with some treating reports that it was filmed in those languages as sufficient and others arguing those languages referred only to dubbed releases or were reported unreliably. A separate question was whether to list six release languages, though the discussion distinguished dubbing and release languages from languages in which the film was made.

2018.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to mention “Robot 2” or “Robot 2.0” as an alternative name for the film; a supporter pointed to news coverage using those names, while opponents questioned how widely they were used. Opponents argued that the names were unofficial and that an alternative title should be included only if it was an official title, rather than a name used by some media outlets.

2016.summary: An editor proposed rewriting the paragraph under “Accolades,” describing it as grammatically messy; the discussion shown does not establish a broader disagreement about the article’s content.

2015.summary: Editors disagreed over whether a brief passage about an event at the pageant should be presented as a controversy: one argued it was relevant and supported by evidence, while another called it a plain mistake rather than a controversy.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Donald Trump should appear in the 2020 election infobox: supporters argued that his likely reelection bid justified inclusion, while opponents said he had not declared and that naming him so early would predict an uncertain outcome. The discussion closed with a finding against listing him as the Republican Party’s presumptive incumbent.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether Donald Trump’s campaign filings and rally meant he should be called a declared candidate, or whether he should remain a potential candidate until he formally announced a run. They also disputed how much evidence should be needed to list people as possible candidates: some wanted to limit celebrity speculation, while another argued that people should be included when multiple sources speculate about them, even without expressed interest.

2020.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the Libertarian and Green candidates belonged in the prominent election summary box: some favored the existing rule based on access to enough state ballots to win, while others argued for a polling threshold instead. After most major news organizations projected Biden as Georgia’s winner, editors disagreed over whether to update the election map before every outlet had made the same call; some favored waiting for unanimity, while others said a majority was sufficient.

2017.summary: Editors disputed whether to include an incident in which two local volunteers were reported to have attended an execution and celebrated: supporters cited reporting and the organization’s disciplinary response, while opponents questioned the source’s reliability and whether the incident merited coverage. They also disagreed over the opening paragraph’s description of criticism as a disinformation campaign, with one position calling for allegations to be presented before responses and the other arguing that reliable sources supported the campaign framing.

2018.summary: Editors disputed whether the opening paragraph should describe the White Helmets as targets of a disinformation campaign, with some arguing that this wording adopted one side’s interpretation and others defending it as an accurate summary of reliable reporting. A proposed alternative would present allegations of links to foreign governments or jihadist groups alongside the supporters’ characterization of those allegations as disinformation; editors also debated whether this framing belonged in the opening paragraph.

2017.summary: Editors disagreed over whether to keep three guest performers with limited appearances in the article’s cast section: one editor removed them, while another objected to making those decisions unilaterally and called for agreed criteria for inclusion.

2019.summary: Editors disagreed over whether fact-checking belonged in its own section or should be included alongside the claims it addressed; one editor said some checks had no obvious place elsewhere, while another preferred relevant prose rather than a separate section. They also disputed whether four debunked claims warranted inclusion: one editor called them minor and questioned why they were selected, while another argued the referenced information should be kept, possibly in a different section.

2022.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the film’s original writers should be included in its writing credits: one editor argued that they were not involved in the production, while another said writers can receive credit when their screenplay was used, even without involvement in the new production. The objection also questioned whether the Writers Guild had certified those credits and favored describing the film as based on an earlier film, while other editors argued the article should follow the film’s credits and the guild’s decision.

2016.summary: Editors debated how to present the cast because some performers appear as characters who portray other people in the fictional documentary, creating a distinction between the performers’ in-story roles and the people they reenact. Some proposed a separate section for the documentary’s cast, while another proposal kept one cast list and showed reenactment roles beneath the performers’ in-story characters.

2017.summary: Editors disputed whether box-office material justified calling the film the highest-grossing war film, objecting that the cited table covered World War I films rather than war films generally and that such rankings needed direct sourcing and attribution. Editors also disagreed over whether to classify the film as feminist: one editor argued that its leading female character and cited commentary supported the label, while others said sources did not commonly and consistently define it that way.

2016.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the ratings table should include demographic audience figures as well as total viewers. One editor argued that demographic figures added useful context about the show’s performance, while others said including only selected age groups could skew impressions and that total viewership was the more relevant measure.

2023.summary: Editors disagreed over whether the article should describe the film’s audience reception as more positive than critics’ reviews, with one view favoring that context and another cautioning against putting audience reception scores in the opening paragraph. They also disputed whether to include user-submitted scores at all: some argued they were needed to explain the audience–critic gap, while others said the article could describe audience response without listing those scores. The opening paragraph’s wording about generally positive audience reception was also challenged.

Editors disagreed over whether the article should call the film a “box-office bomb” while it was still playing in theaters, with one side arguing that press coverage supported the label and another preferring less definitive wording at that stage. Some editors also challenged whether the cited articles explicitly used the term, arguing that reports of underperformance did not establish a broader press consensus that the film was a bomb.
